course.title: Macroeconomics: How Economies Grow, Slow and Recover
course.description: How the Australian economy is measured, why prices rise, how the Reserve Bank and the Budget respond, and what makes an economy grow. Each lesson uses real figures and statements from the RBA, the ABS and Treasury to practise reading evidence and judging a decision.
course.audience: A curious adult who has met supply and demand and wants to follow news about GDP, inflation, interest rates and the Budget. They need percentages and the ability to read a table, and no algebra. They may have a mortgage or a pay rise and a sense that the headlines do not add up.

paragraphs: How the Australian economy is measured, why prices rise, how the Reserve Bank and the Budget respond, and what makes an economy grow. Each lesson uses real figures and statements from the RBA, the ABS and Treasury to practise reading evidence and judging a decision.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a GDP, unemployment or CPI release and say which measure answers your question and what it leaves out.
You'll be able to tell whether a rise in unemployment or in a price index is a real signal or a small movement within survey error.
You'll be able to say whether an episode of inflation looks driven by demand, by costs or by expectations, and what evidence would separate them.
You'll be able to trace a loan through two banks' balance sheets and say what limits bank lending.
You'll be able to trace a rate rise from the cash rate to spending and prices, and judge from data whether it has worked yet.
You'll be able to judge a budget deficit against GDP, debt and interest, and say who is making each claim in a budget paper.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Economics: Markets and Strategy, Maths Foundations.

modules.title: Measuring an economy
modules.description: Reading the headline figures for output, work and prices, and knowing what each one counts and leaves out.

modules.title: Inflation
modules.description: Where price rises come from and what they cost, using the 2026 oil shock and the RBA's own statements.

modules.title: Money and monetary policy
modules.description: How banks create money, how the RBA sets the cash rate and how a rate change reaches spending and prices.

modules.title: Cycles and fiscal policy
modules.description: Reading booms, slowdowns and recessions, then the Budget as a tool and what it can and cannot do.

modules.title: The wider economy and a full reading
modules.description: The dollar, the current account and long-run growth, then a whole central bank statement read start to finish.

concepts.title: GDP
concepts.summary: The market value of the final goods and services produced in an economy in a period, which the ABS estimates from production, income and expenditure and publishes each quarter.

concepts.title: Real GDP
concepts.summary: GDP with the effect of price changes removed, so that it moves only when the volume produced moves; the ABS publishes it as chain volume measures.

concepts.title: Nominal GDP
concepts.summary: GDP at current prices, which rises when output rises and also when prices rise.

concepts.title: GDP per person and per hour
concepts.summary: Output divided by population, or by hours worked; the second is the ABS's measure of labour productivity in the national accounts.

concepts.title: What GDP leaves out
concepts.summary: Unpaid household work, the distribution of income, and spending that only replaces what was lost, such as rebuilding after a disaster.

concepts.title: Employed, unemployed, not in the labour force
concepts.summary: The ABS sorts people aged 15 and over by what they did in a reference week: one hour of paid work is employed; no job, looking and available is unemployed; the rest are outside the labour force.

concepts.title: Unemployment rate
concepts.summary: Unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force, so it moves when the number of jobseekers moves and also when the labour force changes size.

concepts.title: Underemployment and underutilisation
concepts.summary: Underemployed workers have a job but want and could take more hours; the underutilisation rate adds them to the unemployed.

concepts.title: Participation rate
concepts.summary: The share of people aged 15 and over who have a job or are looking for one.

concepts.title: Seasonally adjusted and trend
concepts.summary: Two ways the ABS smooths a monthly series; the ABS says trend is the best guide to underlying behaviour.

concepts.title: Sampling error
concepts.summary: The Labour Force Survey is a sample, so a small monthly change can lie inside its confidence interval.

concepts.title: Consumer Price Index
concepts.summary: The change in the cost of a standard household basket of goods and services, with each item weighted by how much households spend on it.

concepts.title: Headline and underlying inflation
concepts.summary: Headline is the whole CPI; underlying measures set aside items with unusually large price changes so that temporary factors do not hide broad pressure.

concepts.title: Trimmed mean
concepts.summary: The average price change of the middle 70 per cent of the basket by spending, once every item is ranked by how much its price changed.

concepts.title: An index is not a price level
concepts.summary: A CPI index number shows how much a price has risen from a base, so it cannot say which of two items is dearer.

concepts.title: Annual and monthly change
concepts.summary: The inflation target is an annual rate; a monthly change is one month's movement.

concepts.title: Demand-pull inflation
concepts.summary: Inflation that arises when total demand exceeds the supply the economy can produce sustainably, so that prices rise on a wide range of goods and services.

concepts.title: Cost-push inflation
concepts.summary: Inflation that arises when the cost of producing falls on supply, such as dearer oil, so that firms produce less and charge more.

concepts.title: Inflation expectations
concepts.summary: What households and firms believe about future prices, which can feed into wage and price setting; they are anchored when they stay near the target through a spike.

concepts.title: Capacity pressure
concepts.summary: Demand pressing on the economy's potential output, which cannot be observed directly and is inferred from evidence such as unemployment against the NAIRU.

concepts.title: Stagflation
concepts.summary: Stagnant output and high or rising unemployment together with high inflation, which a large or persistent supply shock can cause.

concepts.title: Real and nominal
concepts.summary: A real value is a dollar value less the effects of inflation, so a pay rise lower than inflation is a fall in purchasing power.

concepts.title: Real interest
concepts.summary: The interest a lender receives after inflation; if inflation is higher than expected when a loan was agreed, the lender gets less purchasing power than planned.

concepts.title: Costs of high inflation
concepts.summary: Lower purchasing power, wage and price chasing, distorted spending and investment, frequent repricing and loss of competitiveness.

concepts.title: Costs of very low inflation
concepts.summary: Deflation can delay spending, firms find it hard to cut real wages, and policy has less room to push real interest rates below zero.

concepts.title: Flexible inflation target
concepts.summary: An annual CPI rate of 2 to 3 per cent, with the Board aiming for the midpoint and looking through temporary changes.

concepts.title: Currency and deposits
concepts.summary: The two main forms of money are banknotes and coins, which the central bank backs, and deposits, which are liabilities of private institutions and make up most of modern money.

concepts.title: Balance sheet
concepts.summary: A bank's assets (loans, cash) against its liabilities (deposits) and equity.

concepts.title: Lending creates deposits
concepts.summary: When a bank makes a loan it typically credits the borrower's deposit account, so loans and deposits rise together across the system, and repayment reverses it.

concepts.title: Limits on lending
concepts.summary: Liquid assets to meet withdrawals, capital to absorb losses, and willing borrowers and a bank willing to lend.

concepts.title: Exchange Settlement balances
concepts.summary: Banks' deposit accounts at the RBA, the cash that settles payments between banks.

concepts.title: Cash rate
concepts.summary: The rate banks charge each other on overnight loans, which the Monetary Policy Board sets a target for.

concepts.title: Policy interest rate corridor
concepts.summary: The RBA pays interest on banks' settlement balances 0.1 points below the target and lends at 0.25 points above, which keeps trading between banks inside that range.

concepts.title: Funding costs and lending rates
concepts.summary: Funding costs are what banks pay savers and bond holders; lending rates are what borrowers pay and also reflect competition and credit risk.

concepts.title: Monetary Policy Board
concepts.summary: The nine-member body that sets monetary policy independently of the government and explains each decision.

concepts.title: Tightening and easing
concepts.summary: Raising the cash rate target to restrain demand, or lowering it to support demand.

concepts.title: Transmission
concepts.summary: How a change in monetary policy settings flows through to interest rates (first stage) and then to activity and inflation (second stage).

concepts.title: Channels
concepts.summary: The saving and investment channel, the cash-flow channel, the asset prices and wealth channel and the exchange rate channel.

concepts.title: Lag
concepts.summary: Some estimates put the maximum effect of monetary policy at one to two years, with large uncertainty.

concepts.title: Financial conditions
concepts.summary: How tight or loose borrowing, asset prices and the exchange rate are together; the RBA judges whether they are restrictive.

concepts.title: Demand against supply
concepts.summary: Policy aims to slow demand until it matches what the economy can supply.

concepts.title: Business cycle
concepts.summary: Fluctuations in output growth around the growth of potential output, in four phases: expansion, peak, contraction and trough.

concepts.title: Potential output
concepts.summary: The level of output the economy can reach using its resources sustainably without pushing up prices.

concepts.title: Technical recession
concepts.summary: Real GDP falling in each of two quarters in a row, the definition the media use most.

concepts.title: Broader recession tests
concepts.summary: Weak or falling growth that lasts, together with a significant rise in unemployment, or else a rule based on the unemployment rate alone.

concepts.title: Kinds of downturn
concepts.summary: Supply shocks, tightening against inflation, financial busts and shutdowns each produce a recession by a different route.

concepts.title: Underlying cash balance
concepts.summary: The Government's headline budget result: receipts less payments, as a deficit or surplus.

concepts.title: Gross and net debt
concepts.summary: Gross debt is the face value of government securities on issue; net debt subtracts selected financial assets and uses market value.

concepts.title: Debt as a share of GDP
concepts.summary: A way to judge the burden of debt against the size of the economy.

concepts.title: Net interest payments
concepts.summary: Interest paid less interest received, the cost of carrying the debt.

concepts.title: Structural balance
concepts.summary: The budget result with the estimated effects of commodity prices and the economic cycle removed; it is estimated and not observed.

concepts.title: Automatic stabiliser
concepts.summary: A feature of taxes and benefits that moves the budget towards deficit in a downturn and towards surplus in a boom without a new decision.

concepts.title: Discretionary fiscal policy
concepts.summary: A change in taxes or spending that the government decides on.

concepts.title: Multiplier
concepts.summary: The ratio of the change in national income to the change in spending that caused it; spending by one person is income to another, so the first round is followed by more.

concepts.title: Leakages
concepts.summary: Saving, taxes and imports take some of each round out of domestic spending, which lowers the multiplier.

concepts.title: Crowding out
concepts.summary: Extra government borrowing or spending that reduces private investment or spending, more likely when the economy is at capacity.

concepts.title: Exchange rate
concepts.summary: The relative price of one currency in terms of another; AUD/USD of 0.75 means one Australian dollar buys 75 US cents.

concepts.title: Appreciation and depreciation
concepts.summary: An appreciation is a rise in the Australian dollar's value, and a depreciation is a fall.

concepts.title: Drivers of the dollar
concepts.summary: Interest rate differentials, the terms of trade and commodity prices, trade flows and, over short periods, risk sentiment.

concepts.title: Terms of trade
concepts.summary: How the prices Australia gets for its exports compare with the prices it pays for its imports.

concepts.title: Current account
concepts.summary: The balance of goods, services and income flows with the rest of the world, matched by the capital and financial account.

concepts.title: Aggregate supply
concepts.summary: What the economy can produce, set by its labour, its capital and how efficiently they are used.

concepts.title: Labour and multifactor productivity
concepts.summary: Output per hour worked, and output per unit of labour and capital combined.

concepts.title: Diminishing returns
concepts.summary: Adding more of one input, holding others fixed, adds less and less to output.

concepts.title: Technological progress
concepts.summary: New methods that let the same inputs make more; in the Solow model it is given from outside, and endogenous growth theory tries to explain it.

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.summary: Small differences in annual growth become large gaps in income over decades.

concepts.title: Decision statement
concepts.summary: The Board's media release on the day, giving the decision, the reasons, the uncertainties and the vote.

concepts.title: Statement on Monetary Policy
concepts.summary: The RBA's quarterly assessment of the economy, with forecasts and risks.

concepts.title: Forecast and assumption
concepts.summary: A forecast is the staff's central view; the cash rate in it is a technical assumption taken from market pricing.

concepts.title: Risks
concepts.summary: Ways the outcome could differ from the central forecast, in both directions.

concepts.title: Forward approach
concepts.summary: What the Board says it will do next, which in 2026 was data-dependent and not a commitment.

lessons.title: Reading a GDP headline

lead.text: So what is the figure a measurement of? **Gross domestic product**, or **GDP**, is the market value of the final goods and services produced in an economy over a period of time. The word *final* matters: a loaf of bread counts, and the flour inside it doesn't count a second time, because its value is already in the price of the loaf. Each quarter the ABS gathers data from households, firms and government bodies and works the figure out.

There are three ways to add up the same thing. The ABS can count what was produced, the income that producing it earned, or the spending on what was produced, and the RBA's explainer describes them as three routes to the same figure. The data are never complete, so the three answers differ a little, and the ABS and Australian economists mostly look at the average of the three.

That settles what GDP counts, which is production valued at market prices. It doesn't yet tell us how to read a growth rate, and the first thing to ask there is whether the prices in the figure were allowed to change.

Take the ABS's 0.8% first. It's a growth rate for GDP measured in dollars at the prices of the time, and we call a figure like that **nominal**. Dollars of production can grow for two reasons, because more was made or because what was made sold for more, and a nominal figure can't tell them apart. The 0.4% is the **real** figure, which the ABS publishes as chain volume measures. It takes the effect of price changes away, so it moves only when the volume produced moves.

afterFigure.text: The ABS's commentary explains the gap in this quarter. It reports that the GDP price deflator, its measure of price change across everything GDP covers, rose 0.4%, so about half of the 0.8% was more output and half was higher prices. The RBA gives the rule: the growth rates of real GDP and of prices add up to something close to, but not exactly equal to, nominal growth.

Over the year to June 2026 the gap was far wider, with 5.3% in current prices against 2.1% in volume. That is why economists normally talk about real growth, because, as the RBA puts it, real growth shows more truly how much a country is producing.

steps.headline: An economy that makes only apples goes from 100 kg at $2 a kg to 104 kg at $2.05 a kg. How much does it grow in nominal and in real terms?

workedSteps.text: In the first year the value of production is the volume multiplied by the price, which is what nominal GDP records.
The second year has more apples at a higher price.
Nominal growth is the change in the dollar value, divided by where it started.
Real growth leaves the price out and compares only the volumes.
The price rose as well, and the same method shows by how much.
The RBA, whose example this is, notes that adding the growth rates (4% and 2.5% make 6.5%) comes close to the nominal 6.6% without matching it, because the two effects multiply and do not simply add.
So of the 6.6% nominal growth only the 4% says the economy produced more apples, and the rest is dearer apples.

lead.text: The ABS's table doesn't stop at one row. Beside [[real GDP|GDP with the effect of price changes removed. Met in 'Real and nominal'.]] it reports GDP per person and GDP per hour worked, and for the year to June 2026 the three read 2.1%, 0.7% and -0.2%. They cover the same year and they look as if they disagree, so what we need is the question that each row answers.

afterFigure.text: Total output answers how big the economy is and how fast it's growing. Per person answers whether the average person is producing more, and it can fall while the total rises if the population grows faster; the RBA's example is GDP up 2% in a year when the population is up 4%. Per hour answers how much each hour of work now produces, which the ABS lists under productivity. The last column of the table compares June 2026 with June 2025.

Put the three rows together for the year. The gap between 2.1% and 0.7% is population growth, roughly 1.4% over the year. Output per hour slipped 0.2%, so the 2.1% can't have come from each hour producing more; since output is output per hour multiplied by hours worked, hours must have risen by roughly 2.3%.

reveal.text: The same year of output gives 2.1%, 0.7% or -0.2% depending on what it is divided by, so the denominator is part of the question being asked.

steps.headline: Over the year to June 2026, GDP rose 2.1% while GDP per hour worked fell 0.2%. Where did the growth come from?

workedSteps.text: Output is output per hour multiplied by hours worked, so growth in output combines growth in each of the two.
workedSteps.math: output = output per hour × hours worked

workedSteps.text: The ABS reports output per hour down 0.2%, so each hour of work produced very slightly less than a year before.
Output still rose 2.1%. Decide what has to have grown for that to happen.
So the year's growth came from more hours of work, and each hour was not more productive.

lead.text: GDP counts what is produced and sold at a price, and that rule leaves out some things that are plainly useful. The RBA gives a clear case: when parents look after their own children the work is left out of GDP, but when a paid childcare worker does the same job it is counted. The work and the child are the same, and the payment alone moves it across the line.

Wikipedia's article on GDP states the general version, that unpaid work at home and elsewhere has no place in GDP, and it reports a calculation that puts the value of unpaid work in Australia at over half of GDP. That is one estimate, and the article notes that figures for other countries swing widely with the method, but even a cautious figure shows how much sits outside.

GDP also says nothing about who receives the income. The RBA puts it plainly: GDP says nothing about how national income is shared across the population, so income may have risen for everyone or have gone mainly to certain groups. Wikipedia's article adds that GDP per person is an average, and that the income of poorer residents can fall even as the average rises.

A third limit is less obvious, because here GDP does count the activity and the activity still isn't a gain. The RBA's example is the first spending to rebuild buildings and infrastructure following a natural disaster, which lifts measured economic growth. Builders, suppliers and equipment hire are all producing goods and services at market prices, so they are in GDP, yet the community has only got back what it had before.

A rise in GDP therefore tells us that more was produced, and it doesn't tell us whether the production made anyone better off. The RBA's wording for the whole family of limits is that GDP leaves out wider aspects of economic welfare. GDP remains the standard measure of the size and growth of an economy, and these limits are the reasons to read it with other figures beside it.

This country is not Australia, and its figures are invented. Its [[nominal|GDP in dollars at the prices of the time. Met in 'Real and nominal'.]] growth is the figure in the news, and each row of the ABS table takes one more thing away from it.

reveal.text: The order of the steps doesn't matter, because each one divides out a single thing: prices to reach real output, then the population to reach output per person. The ABS table does the same work for Australia.

lessons.orientation: Read a GDP announcement and say whether the figure is real or nominal, whether it describes total output, output per person or output per hour, and what GDP leaves out.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read a GDP release, say which row answers your question, and say what that row leaves out.

blocks.text: Every quarter the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) estimates how much the economy produced, and the news boils the result down to one percentage. For the June quarter of 2026 the ABS published two, and one was twice the size of the other, although both described the same three months of the same economy.

Two honest figures for one economy must be measuring different things. Reading a GDP headline well means knowing which thing a number measures, and then choosing the number that answers the question you have.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a GDP release and say whether a figure is real or nominal, whether it is total, per person or per hour, and what it leaves out.
intro.whyItMatters: Later lessons on inflation, interest rates and the Budget keep returning to these figures, so it helps to know what each one counts.

recap.keyIdea: A GDP headline is real or nominal, total, per person or per hour, and it counts only what is produced and sold at a price, so you choose the row that answers your question.

blocks.text: You saw one quarter's growth come out as 0.8% in dollars and 0.4% in output, because half of the dollar figure was higher prices, and you saw the year to June 2026 read 2.1% in total, 0.7% per person and -0.2% per hour. Each row was true, and each answered a different question. Whichever row you read, GDP leaves out unpaid work, says nothing about who receives the income, and counts spending that replaces what was lost as growth without making anyone better off.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn from output to work and ask which of the ABS's labour market figures answers a given question.

lessons.title: Which unemployment measure

lead.text: Start with how the ABS decides who is unemployed, because the answer isn't anyone without a job. Each month the ABS runs the Labour Force Survey, which asks around 50,000 people about a reference week, and it sorts everyone aged 15 and over into three groups. A person is **employed** if they did at least an hour of work for wages, profit, commission or payment in kind. A person is **unemployed** if they weren't employed, had actively looked for work at some time in the past four weeks and were available to start. Everyone else is **not in the labour force**.

The tests are exact in both directions. Someone who has accepted a job that starts within four weeks, and who would have been free to start in the reference week, counts as unemployed, because the ABS treats them as waiting to start work. Someone with no job who isn't looking, perhaps because they're studying or caring for family or retired, is outside the labour force, and so is someone who has stopped looking. When that person would probably work given the chance, the RBA calls it **hidden unemployment**: they aren't counted as unemployed, though they're often described as discouraged workers.

Employed and unemployed people together are the **labour force**. That gives two rates that sound alike and answer different questions. The **unemployment rate** is the number of unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force, and the **participation rate** is the share of the population aged 15 and over who are in the labour force.

steps.headline: In the RBA's example, 12.6 million people are employed, 0.7 million are unemployed and 20.0 million are aged 15 and over. What are the two rates?

workedSteps.text: The labour force is everyone who is employed or unemployed.
The unemployment rate puts the unemployed over the labour force, and not over the whole population.
The participation rate puts the labour force over the population aged 15 and over.
The remaining 6.7 million people are outside the labour force, and neither rate counts them as unemployed.

lead.text: The unemployment rate answers one question, which is whether people who want work are finding it. The ABS publishes other measures for other questions. **Underemployed** workers have a job but want, and are available for, more hours than they have. The ABS counts them as employed, so the unemployment rate never sees them, and the **underemployment rate** shows them as a percentage of the labour force. Add them to the unemployed and divide by the labour force and you have the **underutilisation rate**, the share of the labour force whose time isn't fully used. The participation rate shows how much of the population is in the labour market at all, and the employment-to-population ratio compares the number of people with jobs with the population.

afterFigure.text: Each button names a question and highlights the measure that answers it. For October 2026 the five rows read 4.9%, 6.2%, 11.1%, 66.6% and 63.3%, and they didn't all move the same way: unemployment rose 0.1 points, underemployment fell 0.1, participation fell 0.2 and employment to population fell 0.3. The RBA treats the underemployment rate as a further gauge of the labour market, because a high rate can mean that the demand for labour is weak compared with its supply. The ABS says it works out changes from unrounded figures, so a change can differ from the gap between the rounded ones, as the unemployment rate's 4.7% to 4.9% shows beside its stated rise of 0.1 points.

lead.text: The unemployment rate has a denominator, and the denominator moves too. The RBA says the rate moves when the number of unemployed people changes and also when the size of the labour force changes, and that participation tends to follow the business cycle: when firms are hiring and offering higher wages there's more reason to start looking. So if people who weren't looking begin to look, the labour force grows, and the unemployment rate can rise even though nobody has lost a job. Wikipedia's article on unemployment draws the consequence that the participation rate can explain how the unemployment rate goes up in a period when employment goes up as well.

The RBA made exactly this reading of the September quarter of 2026. Its November Statement says the unemployment rate climbed further than expected, averaging 4.6%, and that this "appears" to be "largely" the result of more people joining the labour force than anticipated, with cost-of-living pressures behind it, while employment growth held up. Those two hedging words matter, because they mark an assessment made from the data and not a count.

steps.headline: In the earlier economy, 0.1 million people outside the labour force start looking for work and none find a job. What happens to the two rates?

workedSteps.text: No one has lost a job, so employment is still 12.6 million. The new jobseekers move from outside the labour force into the unemployed.
The labour force grows by the same 0.1 million.
Put the new number unemployed over the new labour force and compare it with the earlier 5.3%.
The unemployment rate has risen with no job lost, and participation has risen as well.

lead.text: In 2020 the Australian Government paid employers a wage subsidy called JobKeeper to help them keep their employees. The RBA's explainer on the pandemic describes what that did to the unemployment figures.

The October change in the unemployment rate was 0.1 points, and it comes from a survey of about 50,000 people. A sample can't match a full count, and the ABS says so directly, noting that results vary from month to month because of sampling. The ABS therefore prints a **95% confidence interval** for the main monthly changes, a range which, in the ABS's words, has about nineteen chances in twenty of containing the real movement.

afterFigure.text: For the unemployment rate the change was 0.1 points and the interval runs from -0.1 to 0.3, so the true change could have been a small fall, no change or a rise of up to 0.3 points. The 43,500 fall in employment has an interval running from a fall of 109,500 to a rise of 22,500. When an interval includes zero, the survey can't rule out that nothing changed, and a single month is weak evidence of anything. The ABS adds its own advice to treat short-term changes with some caution.

diagram.alt: Four bars show the ABS 95% confidence interval around each October 2026 monthly change: unemployment rate +0.1 points (-0.1 to 0.3), participation -0.2 (-0.4 to 0.0), employed people -43,500 (-109,500 to 22,500) and unemployed people +17,800 (-19,600 to 55,200). A dashed line marks no change.

lead.text: The ABS publishes each series in two forms. A **seasonally adjusted** series removes the patterns that repeat every year, such as the jobs that exist only in one season, like fruit picking and holiday work, which are the RBA's examples, and the RBA notes that the ABS publishes its labour statistics this way. The **trend** series goes further and removes the month-to-month variability as well. The ABS says the trend is the best guide to what the labour market is doing underneath.

afterFigure.text: Both lines show the same months. The seasonally adjusted line jumps around the trend by a tenth or two in most months, while the trend climbs steadily through 2026, from 4.3% in March to 4.8% in October. The rise of 0.5 points over seven months is the kind of change a single month can't show and a run of months can.

diagram.alt: A line chart of the unemployment rate each month from January 2024 to October 2026 in two forms. The seasonally adjusted line moves up and down by a tenth or two from month to month, with a low of 3.7% in February 2024 and 4.9% in October 2026. The smoother trend line stays near 4.0% through 2024, then climbs from 4.3% in March 2026 to 4.8% in October 2026.

lessons.orientation: Choose the labour force measure that answers a question, place people in the ABS categories, and judge whether a one-month movement is more than survey noise.
lessons.nextAction: You can now place people in the ABS categories, pick the measure that answers a question, and judge a monthly movement against its margin of error.

blocks.text: In its release for October 2026 the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported two things that sound like one story. The unemployment rate rose to 4.9%, and the number of people employed fell by 43,500 on the month, seasonally adjusted. Together they read like a simple tale of job losses.

The tale is less simple than it looks, because each figure counts a particular group of people in a particular way, and a single month's movement comes from a survey with its own margin of error. What does the 4.9% count, who does it leave out, and when is a month's change big enough to mean something?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place people in the ABS labour force categories, choose the measure that answers a question, and judge whether a one-month movement means anything.
intro.whyItMatters: The RBA weighs jobs against inflation, so you need to know what each labour market figure counts before reading its decisions.

recap.keyIdea: Each labour force measure answers its own question, the unemployment rate counts people who are looking and available, and one month's change is weak evidence until the interval or the trend supports it.

blocks.text: You sorted people by the ABS tests and saw the unemployment rate sit beside underemployment at 6.2% and underutilisation at 11.1%. You saw the rate rise with no job lost when more people started looking, and you read the October rise of 0.1 points against an interval from -0.1 to 0.3 and a trend that had climbed from 4.3% to 4.8% since March. The habit to keep is to ask which group a measure counts, and then whether the movement is larger than the survey's own uncertainty.

recap.nextHook: Next we move from jobs to prices and read the ABS's monthly consumer price index.

lessons.title: What the CPI measures

lead.text: Start with what the ABS actually measures. It collects prices for thousands of items, groups them into 87 categories and 11 groups, and every month it works out how each item's price has changed from the month before and combines those changes into one figure for the whole basket. That figure is the **Consumer Price Index**, or **CPI**, which the RBA describes as the change in what it costs households to buy a basket of goods and services. The ABS publishes it monthly.

A monthly release therefore carries two figures that answer different questions. The change in the month, 0.8% for September 2026, says how much prices rose since August. The change over the 12 months to September, 4.3%, compares prices with September a year earlier. The RBA's target is for annual consumer price inflation, so the 12-month figure is the one to hold against it.

steps.headline: Books rise from $20 to $20.50 and an hour of childcare from $30 to $31.41, with childcare 73% of spending. What is inflation for the basket?

workedSteps.text: Inflation for one item is the change in its price divided by its starting price. For a book:
Childcare is worked out the same way.
A plain average of the two would give each item an equal say.
The CPI weights each item's inflation by its share of household spending, and the weights add to one.
The RBA, whose example this is, adds that the ABS uses data on household spending to set and update the weights of the real basket.

lead.text: The figure the target is written for is the whole CPI, which the RBA calls **headline inflation**. Headline has a weakness, which is that some prices move a great deal for reasons that say little about the state of the economy. The RBA's examples are unusual weather that disrupts supply and infrequent changes in tax rules. So the RBA also looks at **underlying inflation**, which sets aside the items with particularly large price changes. A price change across a broad range of items is another matter, because in the RBA's words it may indicate a shift in economic conditions, and that is the kind of change the RBA may respond to by changing the cash rate.

afterFigure.text: The line chart plots headline and one underlying measure, the trimmed mean, for the 12 months to each date. At the 2022 peak headline reached 7.9% in December and the trimmed mean 6.8%, so the underlying measure was lower, though far above the 2 to 3 per cent range the RBA shades in the chart.

diagram.alt: A line chart of annual headline CPI and trimmed mean inflation from September 2022 to September 2026, with the target range of 2 to 3 per cent shaded. Headline peaks at 7.9% in December 2022 and the trimmed mean at 6.8%. Both fall towards the band by mid 2025, then rise again to 4.3% and 3.6% in September 2026.
diagram.caption: ABS, September 2026. Quarterly points until December 2024, then monthly points.

lead.text: In Australia the RBA names the trimmed mean and the weighted median as the most important indicators of underlying inflation. The trimmed mean comes from a ranking. The ABS orders all 87 items by their price change over the month, seasonally adjusted, then trims away the items with the largest changes, whether rises or falls, and takes the weighted average of what remains, which is the middle 70 per cent of items. The **weighted median** is simpler: it is the inflation rate of the item in the middle of that ranking, the 50th percentile by weight. The figure shows the steps with 20 invented items of equal weight.

afterFigure.text: Because the items at the two ends are set aside, one extreme price can't drag the result around. The ABS also publishes the CPI excluding volatile items, which always removes the same items, fruit and vegetables and automotive fuel, while the items removed from the trimmed mean and the weighted median change each month, depending on which had the largest price changes. For September 2026 the ABS reports 3.6% for the trimmed mean, 3.4% for the weighted median and 3.7% for the CPI excluding volatile items, all of them below the headline 4.3% and above the target range.

diagram.alt: Three views of the same 20 invented items, drawn as bars of the price change in a month, from -4.8% to 9.4%. First they are ranked, then the three smallest and three largest are set aside, then the middle 14, which is 70 per cent, are averaged. The average of all 20 is 0.8% and the trimmed mean is 0.4%.

lead.text: The RBA gives an example of a price change that underlying measures are built to see past.

An annual figure of 4.3% is an average over 11 groups, and the groups differ a great deal. In the 12 months to September 2026 transport rose 8.7%, with automotive fuel up 23.6% the main contributor, and in the month of September alone fuel rose 9.4% because of higher world oil prices. Housing rose 5.2%, and within it electricity rose 12.8%, which the ABS puts mostly down to Commonwealth electricity rebates ending during the year. Clothing and footwear rose 0.4%.

afterFigure.text: Fuel and electricity are both rises in single categories with stated causes, world oil prices and the end of rebates, and each lifts the annual figure without showing that prices are rising broadly. The RBA's November Statement says that fuel has risen sharply but that inflation has also been broad-based, with sizeable price increases across a range of market services. The RBA's rule of thumb is to look through temporary changes and to watch for persistent ones, such as faster wage growth that is sustained across the whole community.

lead.text: The CPI has limits that matter when you read it. It measures the rate of price changes and not the price level, so an index number says how far a price has risen from a base period and can't say which of two items costs more. It prices the basket in the eight capital cities, which are home to roughly two thirds of Australian households, and it weights each item by average spending, so a household with no car, an item with a weight of almost 3% in the basket, faces a different mix from the average.

That is why the RBA says the CPI is often used to measure the cost of living but is not an ideal indicator of it: what the RBA calls cost-of-living inflation is the rise in what a household must spend to keep up its standard of living, and the ABS publishes other indexes aimed at that. The CPI also uses a fixed basket, and because households shift towards items that rise least, the RBA says the CPI is biased upwards a little, one reason the target isn't set at zero.

lessons.orientation: Read a CPI release: choose headline, trimmed mean or a breakdown by group for the question being asked, and tell a one-off price change from broad-based inflation.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read a CPI release, choose headline or underlying inflation for a question, and tell a step in one category from broad price rises.

blocks.text: On 28 October 2026 the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) released the consumer price index for September, and its key statistics gave three numbers in four lines. Over the 12 months to September, prices rose 4.3%, and a second measure of inflation read 3.6%. In the month of September alone, prices rose 0.8%.

Three numbers about one set of prices will each answer a different question. Which of them belongs beside the RBA's target, and what is the second measure for? Both answers depend on how the CPI is built.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between headline and underlying inflation for a question, read a CPI release by group, and tell a one-off price rise from broad-based inflation.
intro.whyItMatters: The RBA sets interest rates by watching inflation, so you need to know which measure it is watching and what each one leaves out.

recap.keyIdea: The CPI is a spending-weighted rate of price change, headline and underlying measures answer different questions, and a rise in one category is different from price rises across the basket.

blocks.text: You built a small CPI by weighting each price change by spending, held the annual figure of 4.3% against the target and not the month's 0.8%, and saw how the trimmed mean sets aside the largest movers to give 3.6%. Reading the groups showed fuel and electricity lifting the annual figure from single categories, while the RBA's own words about market services pointed to price rises that are broad. The index itself is a rate of change and not a price level, and it is not any one household's cost of living.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask where inflation comes from, and what separates pressure from demand from pressure from costs.

lessons.title: Where inflation comes from

lead.text: The RBA groups the main causes of inflation into three: demand-pull, cost-push and inflation expectations. **Demand-pull** inflation arises when total demand for goods and services, which the RBA calls aggregate demand, rises above the supply the economy can sustainably produce, and this excess demand pushes up prices on a wide range of goods and services, and in the RBA's phrase it pulls inflation higher. **Cost-push** inflation starts on the supply side: a higher price for an input such as oil or raw materials adds to production costs, so firms tend to produce less and to raise their prices. And **inflation expectations**, the beliefs that households and firms hold about future prices, can move prices themselves, since a firm that expects higher inflation may raise its prices faster and a worker who expects it may ask for higher wages.

Each cause puts a different question to the data. For demand-pull the question is whether demand is pressing on what the economy can produce, for cost-push whether the cost of inputs has risen, and for expectations whether people's beliefs about future prices have moved away from the target. The RBA considers all three when it analyses and forecasts inflation.

Demand-pull and cost-push both push prices up, so prices alone can't tell them apart. What separates them is what happens to output. When demand rises, firms sell more, so output and employment rise along with prices. When costs rise, supply falls and firms produce less at each price, so prices rise while output falls.

afterFigure.text: The first piece of evidence, then, is whether prices are moving with output and jobs or against them. Two more help. One is how broad the price rises are: the RBA says excess demand puts pressure on a broad range of goods and services, while a cost shock shows first in the items it touches, as an oil price rise shows first in petrol and then in freight and groceries. The other is what people expect, which the surveys and bond prices the RBA watches can show. Real episodes mix the causes, so the task is to judge which is doing most of the work.

In the second, the supply curve shifts left and the meeting point moves up and to the left: prices rise and output falls.

lead.text: The supply an economy can sustainably produce is called its potential output, or full capacity. At that level the labour and machines are being used as intensively as they can be without pushing up inflation, and demand above it creates **capacity pressure**. Demand can be measured fairly well from the quarterly GDP figures, but potential output can't be observed and has to be inferred from other evidence. One clue is unemployment: there is a rate of unemployment consistent with stable inflation, which the RBA calls the NAIRU, and when unemployment is below it inflation will tend to rise.

The Board's first decision of 2026 reads as a demand-side case. On 3 February it said that some of the increase in inflation reflected greater capacity pressures, which in turn reflected the greater momentum in demand: private demand had grown much more strongly than expected, led by household spending and investment. It added that labour market conditions looked a little tight, with unemployment a little lower than expected. Strong demand, a tight labour market and rising inflation fit together as demand-pull.

Costs enter through inputs, and the RBA's explainer takes oil as the example. A rise in the price of oil, an input to many industries, raises petrol prices first, then the cost of moving goods about, and so the prices of items such as groceries. In March 2026 the Board added this to its picture. It said the conflict in the Middle East had pushed fuel prices up sharply and that, if the rise lasted, it would add to inflation, and that short-term measures of inflation expectations had already risen. The data later showed the pass-through. The Budget paper from Treasury reports that a 32.8% rise in automotive fuel prices in March lifted headline inflation to 4.6% over the 12 months to March, and the ABS recorded automotive fuel up 23.6% over the 12 months to September, with a 9.4% rise in the month of September on higher world oil prices.

By May the Board said higher fuel prices were adding to inflation and that there were signs of what it called second-round effects, with the rise starting to reach the prices of other goods and services. It described this as an impulse on top of the high inflation recorded early in the year, which it put down to capacity pressures, so two pushes were at work together and the Board treated them as separate. Labour costs belong on the cost side too. Labour is a large share of most firms' costs, and the RBA says the effect of a rise in wages depends on productivity as well: if wages grow faster than labour productivity, each unit costs more to produce, and prices tend to follow.

Expectations are the third cause and the hardest to see, because nobody can observe them directly. The RBA relies on surveys that ask people about the outlook, and on the prices of financial assets such as government bonds. What matters is whether they are **anchored**. If households and firms expect inflation to return to the central bank's target whatever current inflation is, their expectations are anchored to it, and a spike from a cost shock fades because nobody changes how they set prices and wages. If their expectations move away from the target, they become unanchored, and a spell of high inflation turns persistent because everyone adjusts to expecting more. The RBA concludes that a central bank finds it much easier to manage inflation when expectations are anchored.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the same cost shock produces the same spike in both cases, and the difference is where people expect inflation to settle. That is why it matters that the Board's March statement reported a rise in short-term measures of inflation expectations alongside the fuel price rise: expectations help decide whether the price rise is a passing spike or the start of something that lasts.

In the anchored case expected inflation stays inside the range and actual inflation falls back into it. In the unanchored case expected inflation climbs, and actual inflation stays high.

lead.text: A cost shock puts the Board in a difficult spot, because it can push its two goals in opposite directions. The RBA's mandate is price stability and full employment, and over the longer term the RBA says they usually go hand in hand. But a negative supply shock, a sharp rise in energy prices for example, can push inflation higher while pulling activity and employment down. If the shock is large or persistent it can reduce both current output and the economy's potential output, and the unusual combination of stagnant output, rising or high unemployment and high inflation is called **stagflation**. The RBA's example is the 1970s, which had two oil price shocks, among them the 1973 embargo after which oil prices quadrupled.

How does monetary policy choose between the goals? The RBA says it depends, and that expectations are the main consideration. If the shock lifts households' and firms' expectations of future inflation, the Board may need to raise the cash rate to bring them back down, because higher expectations feed into wage and price setting and could push inflation higher still. If expectations remain steady, the Board may choose to overlook the shock and wait for inflation to come down by itself. A strong record of low and stable inflation helps, because when people believe inflation will come back to target, they build less of it into their wages and prices.
The last case is about the cost side again, in a firm that isn't in the news.

lessons.orientation: Given a description of an inflation episode, say whether demand, costs or expectations are doing the work, what evidence would separate them, and what each implies for policy.
lessons.nextAction: You can now say whether demand, costs or expectations are doing the work in an episode of inflation, and what each implies for policy.

blocks.text: In February 2026 the RBA's Monetary Policy Board said that some of the rise in inflation reflected greater capacity pressures. By March it also named sharply higher fuel prices from the conflict in the Middle East, and its later statements added that firms were passing costs on to prices.

Which of these is doing the work matters, because a cause on the demand side calls for a different response from one on the cost side, and a third possibility, that people expect prices to keep rising, can feed on both. How does the RBA tell the three apart, and what evidence does it use?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether demand, costs or expectations are doing the work in an episode of inflation, what evidence separates them, and what each implies for policy.
intro.whyItMatters: The RBA's 2026 decisions rest on a diagnosis of why prices are rising, so reading them means knowing the three causes.

recap.keyIdea: Inflation can be pulled by demand, pushed by costs or sustained by expectations, and which one dominates is judged from the evidence around prices and decides how the RBA responds.

blocks.text: You saw that prices rising with strong output and jobs point to demand, and prices rising as output falls point to costs. You read the RBA's 2026 statements as a demand-side case in February, with a cost shock from fuel added in March and May, and you saw why expectations decide whether a supply shock fades or lasts. A rate decision can't lower the price of oil, but it can slow demand and keep expectations from moving, which is what the Board said in June.

recap.nextHook: Next we count what inflation costs, who gains and loses from it, and why the RBA's target is 2 to 3 per cent.

lessons.title: What inflation costs and why the target is 2 to 3

lead.text: Return to the worker. The RBA's explainer states the idea in one sentence: a real value is a dollar value, which it also calls a [[nominal|A figure in dollars at the prices of the time. Met in 'Reading a GDP headline'.]] value, with the effects of inflation removed. For income, that means the question to ask of any pay rise is how it compares with the inflation over the same period.

The target range answers a different question. It describes what the RBA aims for on average, and it can't say what prices actually did to her pay this year, because only this year's inflation applied to this year's pay. The comparison is also one of size. A pay rise that is smaller than inflation is a fall in purchasing power, and a rise that is larger is a gain.

steps.headline: In the RBA's example a worker's pay rises from $100 to $105 in a year when prices rise 2%. What happened to the worker's purchasing power?

workedSteps.text: Nominal income rose by 5 on a starting figure of 100.
To find the real change, subtract inflation from nominal growth, which is the rule of thumb the RBA uses.
The exact figure asks how much the 105 buys when prices are 2% higher, compared with what the 100 bought a year ago.
The worker can buy about 3% more goods and services than before, so purchasing power rose.

lead.text: The RBA says that a target of 2 to 3 per cent inflation avoids the costs of inflation that is too high and of inflation that is too low. Begin with too high. The first cost is the one in the opening question: if prices rise faster than people's nominal incomes, they can afford fewer goods and services over time. The second follows from it, because workers may seek larger wage increases to compensate, higher wage growth raises firms' costs, and firms may then raise prices further or employ fewer workers.

Third, decisions get distorted. If households expect higher inflation they may buy sooner than they planned to avoid paying more, and businesses have to update their prices more often while consumers spend more time comparing them. Fourth, a higher inflation rate lowers the real return on an investment, which is part of how inflation reaches savers and lenders. The RBA adds that a country whose inflation is higher than others' can become less competitive, unless its currency depreciates.

Inflation that is too low has costs of a different kind, and the RBA names three. If consumers expect prices to fall they may delay purchases, so falling prices, a situation the RBA calls deflation, can lead to lower spending, and businesses may react by laying off workers or cutting wages, which pushes demand and prices down further.

The second cost comes from pay. A business in difficulty that needs to cut its workers' real wages will usually let nominal wages grow more slowly than prices, and if inflation is very low there is little room to do that, so it may lay off workers instead. Wikipedia's article on inflation makes the same point: nominal wages are slow to adjust downward, and moderate inflation lets real wages fall even when nominal wages are kept constant. The third is about policy. In a sharp fall in demand, monetary policy may need real interest rates below zero, and a very low inflation target makes them harder to reach.

Inflation doesn't hit everyone alike, because many dollar amounts are fixed in advance. The RBA makes the point for lenders: if inflation turns out higher than expected when a loan was agreed, the lender ends up with less than planned, because inflation eats into the purchasing power of the interest received. Wikipedia's article on inflation states the other side. Debtors with a fixed nominal rate of interest see the real interest rate fall as inflation rises, and purchasing power moves away from people whose income is fixed in dollars, such as some pensioners whose pensions aren't indexed to the price level, towards people with variable incomes whose earnings may keep pace.

What decides who gains is whether a dollar amount was fixed before the surprise and whether it adjusts afterwards. A fixed repayment weighs less in real terms when prices rise faster than expected, and a fixed income buys less. Both effects run the other way when inflation turns out lower than expected.

Australia's target is for annual consumer price inflation to stay between 2 and 3 per cent. The measure used is the percentage change in the CPI, which suits a target because it covers the prices of what households buy, is produced independently by the ABS, is publicly available, and has a history that does not get revised. The range sits where inflation is low enough not to significantly influence people's economic decisions. It dates from the early 1990s, by which time inflation had already settled at around 2 to 3 per cent, and the lowest average inflation other countries had seen over many years was a little over 2 per cent.

A lower target would be costly. The slower growth in spending and investment needed to hold inflation lower would reduce output growth and raise unemployment. Inflation close to zero also limits the room for monetary policy to push real interest rates below zero and the room for firms to cut real wages, and the RBA adds that the target has to be high enough to allow for the CPI's upward bias, which comes from its fixed basket.

The target is flexible. The RBA sets policy so that it expects inflation to come back to the midpoint of the range, and it separates temporary changes in inflation, such as supply disruptions or seasonal sales, which it looks through, from persistent ones, such as faster wage growth that is sustained across the community. Inflation above the target may signal that the economy is overheating, and inflation below it may signal spare capacity.

The RBA publishes average annual inflation for three periods, two before inflation targeting and one after it. CPI inflation averaged 9.3% over 1976 to 1984, 6.3% over 1985 to 1992 and 2.6% over 1993 to 2024, and underlying inflation averaged 8.6%, 6.3% and 2.7%. The RBA adds that since the early 1990s CPI inflation has averaged a figure inside the target range, with expectations in line with it, and that it is difficult to be precise about when the target started.

afterFigure.text: Not everyone agrees that targeting inflation is the best framework. Wikipedia's article on inflation targeting reports a criticism from supporters of a nominal income target, who say that a focus on the price level alone makes inflation targeting neglect shocks to output. A framework can be well suited to its main aim and still leave something out.

lessons.orientation: Say who gains and who loses when inflation differs from what was expected, explain why the target is 2 to 3 per cent and not zero, and judge a pay rise against a given inflation rate.
lessons.reviewLabel: What inflation costs and why the target is 2 to 3
lessons.nextAction: You can now judge a pay rise against inflation, say who gains and loses when inflation surprises, and explain why the target is 2 to 3 per cent.

blocks.text: A worker's pay rose 3.5% over the 12 months to September 2026 (an invented figure). That is above the 3 per cent top of the RBA's target range, which can make it sound like a generous rise, but the ABS reports that consumer prices rose 4.3% over the same 12 months.

How inflation compares with the pay, prices, interest rates and incomes it touches decides who gains and who loses from it, and the same reasoning explains why the RBA aims for 2 to 3 per cent and not for zero.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to judge a pay rise against inflation, say who gains and loses when inflation surprises, and explain why the target is 2 to 3 per cent and not zero.
intro.whyItMatters: The RBA's target is the yardstick for every decision in this course, and its costs explain why it acts when inflation moves.

recap.keyIdea: What matters is inflation set against what people are paid, owe and earn, so too much and too little inflation both cost something, and the 2 to 3 per cent target balances them.

blocks.text: You saw a pay rise of 3.5% turn into a small fall in purchasing power against 4.3% inflation, and a pay rise of 5% against inflation of 2% turn into a gain of about 3%. Inflation that is too high eats purchasing power, sets off pay and price claims, and distorts spending, while inflation that is too low delays spending and leaves little room to cut real wages or real interest rates. Fixed dollar amounts, such as a loan repayment or an unindexed pension, move in value when inflation surprises, and the record since the early 1990s shows lower average inflation without showing what caused it.

recap.nextHook: Next we move from prices to money and ask how banks create it when they lend.

lessons.title: How banks create money

lead.text: The Reserve Bank says that money in a modern economy takes two main forms: currency, which means banknotes and coins, and deposits, which are balances in accounts at banks and other authorised deposit-taking institutions. Currency is physical and deposits are digital, and deposits make up the greatest share of the money in a modern economy.

The two forms differ in who stands behind them. The Reserve Bank backs currency, so there is no risk that it fails to pay. A deposit is a **liability** of the privately owned institution that holds it, which means an amount the institution owes and has to hand back when the depositor asks, and the RBA puts the risk of that failing in Australia as extremely low.
Since most money is a bank's promise to pay, we can ask where a new promise comes from when a bank makes one. The rest of the lesson answers that from a bank's own records.

A bank keeps its records as a **balance sheet**, which lists what the bank holds on one side and what it owes on the other. The first side holds its **assets**: cash, and the loans that borrowers owe to it. The second holds its liabilities, such as the deposits it owes to customers, and its **equity**, the money its owners put in. The two sides always add to the same total, because whatever the bank holds was either owed to someone or supplied by its owners.

The Reserve Bank's Bulletin of September 2018 follows a made-up island that has no banks until two open, their owners putting in $100 and $50. Each bank keeps that money as cash, so Bank A shows cash of 100 against equity of 100, and Bank B shows cash of 50 against equity of 50. There are no deposits yet and no loans.

steps.headline: Bank A lends $80 to a customer who pays a business that banks at Bank B. What happens to the two balance sheets?

lead.text: Each line below changes only the numbers it names. Use the buttons on the figure to see both balance sheets after the loan, after the withdrawal and after the payment.

workedSteps.text: Bank A agrees to the loan. It records the borrower's promise to repay as a loan, which is an asset, and it credits the borrower's account with the funds, which is a deposit and so a liability. Nothing has left the vault, so cash is still 100.
Both sides still match. Assets are cash of 100 and the loan of 80, which make 180, and the other side is the deposit of 80 and equity of 100, which also make 180.
The borrower withdraws $75 in cash to pay a business. Bank A's cash falls by 75, and so does the deposit it owes, which leaves 5 in the borrower's account.
The business pays the $75 into its own bank, Bank B. Bank B's cash rises by 75, and it now owes the business a deposit of 75.

Add up across the two banks. Loans total 80, and deposits are 5 at Bank A and 75 at Bank B, which also total 80. One loan has created deposits equal to its size, although most of the deposit now sits at the other bank.

reveal.text: The deposit follows the payment, and the amount follows the loan. Next we try a loan with different banks and a different borrower.
The deposit is there as soon as the loan is made. Everything after that moves it around, and nothing in the later steps adds to it.

lead.text: Lending creates deposits, and the process runs backwards when loans are repaid. The RBA says repaying a loan typically extinguishes deposits: the borrower's balance goes and the loan goes with it, so the total of money falls by the same amount.

A new deposit is not always new money. The RBA's example is a business that takes the cash it earned during the day to the bank, which raises its deposit balance. That creates a deposit but not money, the RBA says, because the business has swapped one form of money, cash, for another, a deposit. Money is created only when the total of currency and deposits rises, and the usual way it rises is that a bank lends.

reveal.text: Lending and repaying are mirror images, which is why the amount of money in the economy rises and falls with the amount of lending.

steps.headline: Bank B lends $40 to a second borrower, who pays a merchant that banks at Bank A. What do the two balance sheets show at the end?

lead.text: Carry on from the end of the first case. Bank A holds cash of 25 and a loan of 80, against a deposit of 5 and equity of 100. Bank B holds cash of 125 against a deposit of 75 and equity of 50. Fill in the lines marked for you.

workedSteps.text: Bank B agrees to lend $40. It records the loan as an asset and credits the borrower with a deposit, so both sides of its balance sheet rise by 40 and its cash is untouched.
The borrower withdraws all of the $40 in cash to pay a merchant. Decide which lines of Bank B's balance sheet change.
The merchant pays the $40 into Bank A. Bank A's cash rises by 40 and so does the deposit it owes the merchant.
Now add up both banks. Bank A's deposits are 5 and 40, and Bank B's are 75. Compare total loans with total deposits.

lead.text: If lending creates deposits, can a bank lend as much as it likes? The Reserve Bank says it cannot, and the island case shows why. Suppose Bank A had agreed to lend a customer $120 instead of $80, a case the Bulletin considers itself. The customer could withdraw the whole amount, and Bank A holds only $100 of cash, so it could not pay. That is the limit of **liquidity**: a bank needs enough cash and other liquid assets to meet withdrawals.

The same loan would also be bigger than all of Bank A's equity of 100. The RBA says that if the borrower could not repay, the bank's equity would be wiped out, and that is the limit of **capital**: loans have to be backed by enough of the owners' money to absorb losses from defaults.

Two more limits come from the business of lending. The return on a bank's loans has to cover what it pays for deposits and other funding and what it costs to run, and the bank needs a borrower who wants the loan. The RBA's case study says that making loans, and so deposits, depends on the borrower deciding to approach the bank and on the bank deciding to lend.

afterFigure.text: The Bulletin adds that central bank money once had close links to the growth of bank balance sheets and credit through reserve requirements of the fractional kind, and that these requirements have been removed and replaced by the market's and the regulator's requirements on liquidity and capital. Wikipedia's article on money creation lists Australia among the countries with no reserve requirement, and says the old multiplier idea, in which reserves were multiplied up to a limit, has largely been abandoned as an explanation.

If Bank A had lent 120, it would hold cash of 100 against a deposit of 120, and a loan of 120 against equity of 100.

reveal.text: Liquidity and capital limit what a bank can do, and borrowers decide whether it is asked to do it. The Reserve Bank's own part comes next.

lead.text: The Reserve Bank has two jobs in this story. It issues the banknotes that banks buy from it as their customers want cash, and banknotes are a liability of the Reserve Bank and not of any commercial bank. It also gives banks accounts of their own, which hold what it calls **Exchange Settlement balances**.

Banks use these balances to make payments to each other, some on behalf of their customers, and the RBA treats them as the equivalent of cash for banks. In the island case the customer carried $75 in notes from one bank to the other. In the real system two banks would settle such a payment through their accounts at the Reserve Bank. The next lesson, 'The cash rate and the rates you pay', shows how the Reserve Bank's interest rates on those accounts keep the rate that banks charge each other near its target.

The Reserve Bank can also create deposits itself, for example when it buys government bonds from households and businesses, who then deposit the proceeds in the banking system and so add to total deposits.

reveal.text: Money is created when the total of currency and deposits rises. A payment between accounts moves it, and a loan adds to it.

lessons.orientation: Trace a loan through two banks' balance sheets, say why lending creates deposits, and name what limits how much banks lend.
lessons.nextAction: Find out how the Reserve Bank's cash rate is set, and how a change in it reaches the rates you pay.

blocks.text: When a bank approves a $30,000 car loan, the money is in your account the same afternoon, and you can pay the dealer from it straight away. It is natural to ask where the bank found $30,000 so quickly.

A common answer is that the bank lends out money other customers deposited earlier. The Reserve Bank gives a different account, one that changes how we should think about where money comes from and what stops a bank lending as much as it likes. We'll follow one loan through a bank's records and see which account holds up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a loan through two banks' balance sheets, say why lending creates deposits, and name what limits how much a bank can lend.
intro.whyItMatters: Most money is bank deposits, so how a bank makes one decides how much money exists and what keeps the banks in check.

recap.keyIdea: A bank that makes a loan creates a matching deposit, so lending creates money and repayment removes it, and what limits a bank is its cash, its capital, the return on its loans and whether anyone wants to borrow.

blocks.text: You followed Bank A's $80 loan through two balance sheets. The loan appeared as an asset and the deposit as a liability, and when the borrower paid a business at Bank B the deposit moved there while the total stayed at 80. Repaying a loan reverses the process, and paying cash into an account swaps one form of money for another without adding any.

The limits the RBA names are the cash a bank needs to pay out, the capital it needs to absorb losses, a return that covers its costs and a borrower who is willing to ask. Wikipedia adds that Australia has no reserve requirement, which fits the RBA's Bulletin, so the old multiplier story no longer explains what holds lending back.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the Reserve Bank's own rate, the cash rate, and how a change in it reaches the rates people pay.

lessons.title: The cash rate and the rates you pay

lead.text: The cash rate is the price in one particular market. Banks lend to and borrow from each other overnight, and the interest rate on those loans is called the cash rate. What they trade is a deposit at the Reserve Bank, which the RBA calls an [[Exchange Settlement balance|A bank's deposit account at the Reserve Bank, used to settle payments between banks. Met in 'How banks create money'.]] and treats as the equivalent of cash for a bank. The Board sets a **target** for the cash rate, and the Reserve Bank then keeps the market rate close to that target.

It does this with two rates of its own. The Reserve Bank currently pays banks interest on their balances at a rate 0.1 percentage points below the target, and it is willing to lend balances to banks at a rate 0.25 points above the target. A bank has no reason to lend to another bank for less than it earns by leaving the balance with the Reserve Bank, or to borrow from another bank for more than the Reserve Bank charges. Those two rates are the lower and upper bounds of what the RBA calls the **policy interest rate corridor**, and banks have an incentive to trade among themselves inside it.

afterFigure.text: The corridor is tied to the target, so the whole band moves whenever the target does, as the two views show.

reveal.text: The corridor works through incentives. The Reserve Bank leaves banks free to trade, and the floor and the ceiling give them reasons to stay inside the band.

steps.headline: From the cash rate to your rate

lead.text: The Board's target is for one rate, and the rates you meet in daily life are set by banks. The RBA says the cash rate has a strong influence over the rates that households and businesses get on deposits and pay on loans. It also says the cash rate is only one influence, because conditions in financial markets, competition and the riskiness of different loans can all change the gap between the cash rate and the rate you pay. That gap is called the **spread**, and it varies over time.

Speed differs along the way. Changes in the cash rate are typically passed on quickly to **market reference rates**, which are measured from frequent trades in financial markets and used as benchmarks for pricing bonds and other debt, and the RBA's example is the bank bill swap rate. Deposit rates are less directly influenced and take some time to respond, because banks have discretion in setting them. Deposits make up around two-thirds of Australian banks' funding and bonds around a third, and the rates banks pay on these different sources of funds do not always change by the same amount, or as fast, as the cash rate.

afterFigure.text: Lending rates come last, and the bank chooses them. The RBA says a bank sets its lending rates to make lending as profitable as it can, within the level of default risk it is willing to take.

diagram.alt: A chain from the cash rate to the rates you pay. The cash rate passes quickly to market reference rates and more slowly to deposit rates, and both feed into lending rates, which also depend on competition and credit risk.

reveal.text: The cash rate is a strong influence on the rates a bank pays and charges, and each bank decides how fast to follow it.

lead.text: Several bodies turn up in a story about interest rates, and each has a different job. The **Monetary Policy Board** of the Reserve Bank decides the target for the cash rate. The RBA's explainer says it has nine members: the Governor as chair, the Deputy Governor, the Secretary to the Treasury and six others. It meets eight times a year and decides by majority vote, with the chair holding an additional casting vote if one is required, and it announces its decision at 2.30 pm on the meeting's second day.

The Board is independent of the government when it sets monetary policy, a principle the RBA calls generally accepted internationally and says helps stop monetary policy being manipulated for political purposes. Other jobs belong to other bodies. The Australian Bureau of Statistics calculates and publishes the consumer price index, which the Board watches but does not produce. The Government delivers the Budget. Each commercial bank decides its own deposit and lending rates.

The Board explains itself in public. There is a media conference after each meeting, minutes follow two weeks later, the Statement on Monetary Policy appears four times a year, and the Governor appears twice a year before a committee of the House of Representatives.

reveal.text: The Board's job is narrower than a headline makes it sound. Next we read what it decided in 2026.

lead.text: The Board announced seven decisions between 3 February and 3 November 2026, and together they read like a data series. The target went to 3.85 per cent on 3 February, 4.10 on 17 March and 4.35 on 5 May. It was left at 4.35 on 16 June and again on 11 August, then raised to 4.60 on 29 September and to 4.85 on 3 November.

Every rise was 25 basis points. The statements give the size of the move in basis points and the new level, so the unit can be read off the series: 3.85 to 4.10 is 0.25 of a percentage point, and the statement calls that 25 basis points. A rise in the target is a **tightening** of monetary policy. The RBA says tightening raises interest rates in the economy and helps bring inflation back towards the target, but that it is also likely, all else equal, to slow economic growth and push unemployment up. Lowering the target is an **easing**.

Four of the seven statements say the decision was unanimous, and three were made by majority. The latest, on 3 November, had six members vote to raise the target to 4.85 and three vote to leave it at 4.60. A majority decides, and a split shows how close the call was.
