lessons.orientation: Say what the cash rate is and who sets it, trace a change to the rates households pay, and read the Board's 2026 decisions as a data series.
lessons.reviewLabel: The cash rate and the rates you pay
lessons.nextAction: Follow a cash rate rise past the banks to spending and prices, and judge from data whether it has worked yet.

blocks.text: On 3 November 2026 the Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Board lifted its target for the cash rate by 25 basis points, from 4.60 to 4.85 per cent, the fifth rise of the year. The announcement is about one rate, yet most people care about others: the rate on a home loan, on a credit card or on a savings account.

Who sets which of those rates, and how does a decision made by one board reach them? We'll follow the cash rate outward, and then read the Board's decisions of 2026 as a series, including the votes and the two meetings at which it held.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what the cash rate is and who sets it, trace a change to the rates households pay, and read the Board's 2026 decisions as a series.
intro.whyItMatters: A headline about the cash rate is about one rate set by one board. Knowing who sets the others, and how quickly they follow, tells you what a decision means for you.

recap.keyIdea: The Board sets a target for one rate, the cash rate, and banks set the rest, some quickly and some slowly, so a decision reaches households through each bank's own choices.

blocks.text: You saw that the cash rate is the rate on overnight loans between banks, and that the Reserve Bank keeps it near the Board's target by paying 0.1 points below the target on settlement balances and lending at 0.25 above. Market reference rates follow a change quickly, while deposit rates and lending rates follow at each bank's pace and by amounts the bank chooses.

Reading the 2026 decisions as a series showed five rises of 25 basis points and two holds, three decisions made by majority, and a hold in June that was followed by a rise in September. The ABS, the Government and each bank have jobs that the Board does not.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows a rate rise past the banks to spending and prices, and asks how soon a Board can tell whether it has worked.

lessons.title: How a rate change travels

lead.text: A change in the cash rate target reaches spending and prices in two stages. The RBA's explainer sets them out in two steps: changes in monetary policy first affect interest rates in the economy, and changes in interest rates then affect economic activity and inflation. 'The cash rate and the rates you pay' covered the first stage, which is how the cash rate reaches [[market reference rates|Rates measured from frequent trades in financial markets and used as benchmarks. Met in 'The cash rate and the rates you pay'.]], deposit rates and lending rates. This lesson is about the second stage.

The second stage works through demand. Higher interest rates lead households and businesses to spend and invest less, so demand grows more slowly. The Board's statements in 2026 say what it wants from this: demand has to grow more slowly, so that [[capacity pressures|Demand pressing against what the economy can supply. Met in 'Where inflation comes from'.]] ease and inflation can return to the target. The RBA's explainer describes a fall in rates, in which demand at first runs ahead of supply because supply takes time to respond, and says higher rates have the opposite effect.

diagram.alt: Two stages from a rate rise to prices. In stage one the Board raises the target and market, deposit and lending rates rise. In stage two households and firms spend and invest less, demand grows more slowly than supply, and price rises slow. Below, an arrow marks a lag of one to two years to the maximum effect.

lead.text: The RBA names four main channels through which a change in interest rates reaches spending. Its explainer describes each for a fall in rates, so a rise works in the opposite direction.

In the **saving and investment channel**, a higher rate on deposits gives households more reason to save and less to spend, and higher lending rates make borrowing to buy a house or to invest in equipment dearer, so demand for assets such as housing weakens and business projects are harder to justify. The effect is more direct for firms that borrow than for those that use the owners' own funds.

In the **cash-flow channel**, borrowers with variable-rate loans pay more in interest and have less left to spend, while savers earn more interest on their deposits. The two effects pull in opposite directions, and the RBA says the borrowers' effect is the larger, so spending falls overall.

In the **asset prices and wealth channel**, higher rates weigh on the prices of housing and shares, which leaves owners with less wealth to spend from and gives banks less value to lend against. In the **exchange rate channel**, a rise in Australian rates against those overseas typically lifts the Australian dollar, which makes imports cheaper and Australian exports dearer to overseas buyers. The RBA says this channel matters most for export-oriented sectors and for firms that compete with imports.

diagram.alt: Four channels, shown one at a time. Saving and investment: dearer loans weaken demand for housing and investment. Cash flow: borrowers pay more and savers receive more, and the borrowers' effect is larger. Asset prices and wealth: falling prices leave owners less wealthy and banks with less to lend against. Exchange rate: a higher dollar makes imports cheaper and exports harder to sell.

reveal.text: The four channels start from different places, and a single rise sets all of them going at once.
The cash-flow channel works in both directions. It still lowers spending overall, because the RBA says borrowers' loss is larger than savers' gain.

lead.text: How long should a Board wait before judging a rise? The RBA says the effect on activity and inflation arrives with a lag, since households and businesses need time to change what they do. Some estimates put the maximum effect between one and two years after the change. The RBA stresses that these estimates are very uncertain, because the shape of the economy shifts over time and conditions vary, so the delay for any one rise can vary too.

A lag makes early evidence hard to read. Soon after a rise some channels may have responded while others have not, and inflation, which the Board is aiming at, may have barely moved. The RBA's account of the early 1990s shows a case where the lag ran longer than expected. It says that recession grew mainly out of attempts to rein in excess demand at home, cool speculation in commercial property and bring down inflation, and that rates were pushed up very high because tighter policy was slower than anticipated to bear down on demand and prices.

The Board's statements in 2026 let us see which channels had shown up by each meeting. The figure sets out what four statements said about consumer spending, the housing market, business investment and borrowing, and the labour market. Use the buttons to move through the year.

A pattern runs through them. Consumer spending is described as slowing or easing at the first three dates, and in November the Board says the economy is slowing and expects higher rates and lower housing prices to weigh on household consumption. The housing market is described as turning from June. Business investment and credit are described as strong at every date. Unemployment came in above expectations in April, the labour market had softened slightly more than expected by August, and by November the Board says unemployment has risen.

afterFigure.text: Two cautions come from the November Statement on Monetary Policy. It says that by September house prices stood almost 5 per cent under their March high, and puts that down to higher interest rates and to tax changes announced in the federal budget, so rates were not the only cause. It also says the rise in unemployment looks largely like more people than expected joining the labour force under cost-of-living pressure, while employment kept growing.

The sources do not settle the argument. They show what each side of it could point to.

lessons.orientation: Trace a cash rate rise through the four channels to spending and inflation, and judge from data whether it has worked yet given a lag of one to two years.
lessons.nextAction: Read GDP and unemployment data to say where the economy is in the cycle, and test whether a downturn is a recession.

blocks.text: By 16 June 2026 the Board had raised the cash rate target three times since February, to 4.35 per cent, and its statement still said that inflation was too high. A commentator says the rises have failed, on the reasoning that if they were working, prices would already have eased.

The RBA's explainer on how policy reaches the economy says something about how long that should take. We'll follow a rise from the banks to spending and prices, through four channels, and then read the Board's own evidence in 2026 to see how far it had got.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a cash rate rise through four channels to spending and inflation, and judge from data whether it has worked yet.
intro.whyItMatters: Whether a rate rise has worked depends on when you look and which part of the economy you look at, and the 2026 evidence points in different directions.

recap.keyIdea: A rise in the cash rate reaches spending and prices in two stages and through four channels, and because the maximum effect can take one to two years, judging whether a rise has worked means reading the evidence channel by channel as well as watching inflation.

blocks.text: You traced a rise through two stages, banks' rates first and then demand and prices. You sorted its effects into the saving and investment, cash-flow, asset prices and wealth, and exchange rate channels, and saw that for a retired couple with deposits the cash-flow channel works in both directions, with the borrowers' effect the larger.

The Board's 2026 statements show spending and housing responding from June while business investment and credit stayed strong, and the November Statement says there is significant uncertainty about how restrictive financial conditions are. The RBA's account of the early 1990s shows why a Board takes the lag seriously.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from rates to the cycle itself, and asks how to tell a slowdown from a recession.

lessons.title: Booms, slowdowns and recessions

lead.text: An economy's output usually grows over time, but not smoothly. The RBA calls the fluctuations in the growth of output the **business cycle**, and it measures them against the steady growth of what it calls **potential output**, which is the level of output the economy can reach when it uses its people, equipment, natural resources and technology at a sustainable pace and without pushing prices up unduly. Output here means real GDP.

The RBA divides a cycle into four phases. In an **expansion**, demand for goods and services grows, firms take on workers, and wages and prices usually rise, until the expansion reaches a **peak**. In a **contraction**, demand falls back, firms cut jobs and growth in wages and prices slows, until the contraction reaches a **trough**. The phases vary in length, and the RBA says the expansion usually lasts longer than the contraction. News stories tend to call a strong expansion a boom and a spell of weak growth a slowdown, and the four phases give the more exact words.

diagram.alt: A stylised wave of actual output moving above and below a rising dashed line of potential output, with a peak, a trough and a second peak marked, a contraction between the first peak and the trough, and an expansion between the trough and the next peak.
diagram.caption: A stylised picture and not data. The RBA measures the cycle against potential output, which grows steadily.

lead.text: The ABS publishes quarterly growth in real GDP, and the figure shows every quarter from June 2018 to June 2026. Most columns are small and positive, and two features stand out. In the June quarter of 2020 GDP dropped 6.8 per cent, which the RBA says is a bigger quarterly fall than any in its records, after a fall of 0.2 per cent in March. And it fell by 1.8 per cent in the September quarter of 2021, between two rises.

The second view compares each quarter with the same quarter a year earlier. It tells a calmer story about September 2021, because the year as a whole was still 4.7 per cent higher. It also shows how far growth has slowed since 2021, to 2.1 per cent through the year to June 2026, and the large 2020 fall makes the quarters of 2026 look tiny, so it is worth reading their numbers directly: 0.9, 0.3 and 0.4 per cent in the last three quarters.

reveal.text: A trough is the end of a fall, and growth figures show it as the last negative quarter. The next screen sets three ways of telling whether a fall counts as a recession.

steps.headline: Three ways to call a recession

lead.text: The RBA says there is no single definition of a recession, though the different descriptions share features in output and in the labour market. Three are in use, and on the same data they can disagree.

The one most often used in the media is the **technical recession**, in which real GDP shrinks for two quarters running. The RBA's own description is broader: a prolonged stretch of weak or falling output together with a large rise in unemployment, since unemployment is a reliable and timely summary of many bad developments. A third approach uses the unemployment rate alone, and signals a recession when it rises by more than a pre-specified amount. Some commentators also apply the two-quarter test to GDP per person, which takes population growth out of the figure. The figure sets out what each of the three needs to see and a weakness the RBA names for each.

afterFigure.text: Apply them to 2020. Real GDP fell 0.2 per cent in the March quarter and 6.8 per cent in June, two quarters in a row, so the technical test is met. The RBA puts the June fall at about 7 per cent and says unemployment topped out near 7.5 per cent in mid-2020, which fits the broader description as well. On the technical definition, the RBA says, Australia had gone 29 years without a recession, since the early 1990s.

diagram.alt: A table of three tests for a recession. The technical test needs two quarters in a row of negative real GDP growth. The RBA's description needs weak or falling growth that lasts, alongside a large rise in unemployment. An unemployment rule needs unemployment to rise by more than a pre-set amount. Each has a weakness the RBA names.

On the data in the ABS release, the clear tests are not met. The tests that turn on an amount or a judgement need a reader to say how much counts, which the RBA leaves open.

lead.text: Recessions have different causes, and the cause shapes how the economy behaves. The RBA's account of Australia's recessions gives four kinds, and the figure sets them side by side.

The recession of the mid-1970s came after the world price of oil roughly quadrupled. Costs of production rose and other economies in recession bought less, so output contracted, yet high inflation lingered, a combination the RBA calls [[stagflation|Falling output and high inflation together. Met in 'Where inflation comes from'.]]. The early 1980s recession came when central banks tightened policy to cut inflation that had become entrenched, and in Australia drought and weak global demand added to it. The early 1990s recession, the RBA says, grew mainly out of attempts to rein in excess demand at home, cool speculation in commercial property and bring down inflation, with rates pushed very high because tighter policy was slower to work than expected.
The 2020 recession was different again. To manage the public health problem many activities had to stop at once, and the RBA points to how fast output fell and unemployment rose as well as how far.

reveal.text: The kind of shock is a clue to the path the economy takes. The RBA's own list shows that a single recession can have more than one cause at work.

lead.text: A recession leaves marks that outlast it. The RBA says some people who lose their jobs in a recession stay out of work for a long time even after growth returns to normal, because their skills may have grown rusty, because employers may suspect so, and because a recession can hasten changes in how the economy is organised. After each recession the unemployment rate tends to settle above where it began, and it falls slowly.

The early 1990s fit this. Wikipedia, quoting the former Governor Ian Macfarlane, dates the recession from the September quarter of 1990 to the September quarter of 1991, with GDP falling 1.7 per cent, employment 3.4 per cent and the unemployment rate rising to 10.8 per cent. It adds that a slow recovery began around the September quarter of 1991, while unemployment kept rising until late 1992, and the RBA's own figure for the peak is just over 11 per cent. The two sources date the episode differently, the RBA as 1991-92 and the quotation from the September quarter of 1990, so a careful reader notes which dates each source gives.

The RBA adds that business failures in a recession cause a permanent loss of output, and that a recession can have a longer-term effect on public debt, as governments collect less tax and need to fund more support. The next lesson, 'Budgets, deficits and debt', reads the Budget to see what that debt looks like.

reveal.text: The tests can disagree, and an honest verdict says which test it used.

lessons.orientation: Read GDP and unemployment data to say where an economy is in the cycle, test whether an episode is a recession by more than one definition, and match a downturn to the kind of shock behind it.
lessons.nextAction: Read a Budget table and judge a deficit by its size against GDP, the path of debt and who is making each claim.

blocks.text: The ABS measured Australia's real GDP as falling 1.8 per cent in the September quarter of 2021, after growth of 0.7 per cent in June and before growth of 3.7 per cent in December. Newspapers often use a rule of thumb to decide whether a fall like that means a recession, which is two quarters in a row of falling GDP.

The RBA says there is no single definition of a recession. We'll see where the economy sits in its ups and downs, test the same data against more than one definition, and see why the answer depends on which definition you use.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read GDP and unemployment data to place an economy in the cycle, test an episode against more than one definition of recession, and match a downturn to its cause.
intro.whyItMatters: Whether an episode is called a recession depends on the test used, and an economy can hurt households without meeting the most common test.

recap.keyIdea: Whether an episode is a recession depends on the test, because two negative quarters, a sustained weak output with a significant rise in unemployment, and an unemployment rule can disagree on the same data, and the cause of a downturn shapes how it plays out.

blocks.text: You read quarterly GDP from 2018 to 2026 and saw that one negative quarter, September 2021, is not a technical recession, while 2020 meets the technical test and fits the RBA's broader description. For 2026 the technical test is not met, and the unemployment tests turn on how large a rise counts as significant, an amount the RBA does not give.

The RBA's account links downturns to different shocks: an oil price shock in the 1970s, tighter policy against inflation in the 1980s, a property boom and tightening in the early 1990s, a financial crisis in the 1890s and a shutdown in 2020. It also says the effects last, in long-term unemployment, business failures and public debt.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson reads a Budget table to judge a deficit, which is where the public debt that recessions add to shows up.

lessons.title: Budgets, deficits and debt

lead.text: Table 3.1 of the Government's 2026-27 Budget Paper sets out its main totals year by year. Its headline measure is the **underlying cash balance**, which is receipts less payments, shown in dollars and then as a share of [[GDP|The value of what an economy produces in a period. Met in 'Reading a GDP headline'.]]. For 2026-27 receipts are $798.1 billion and payments are $829.6 billion, so the balance is a **deficit** of $31.5 billion, which is 1.0 per cent of GDP.

The row of shares is the more useful reading. Wikipedia's article on government debt says GDP measures what an economy produces in a year, which is why debt is set against it as an indicator of the burden and why countries of different sizes can be compared. Along the row of shares the deficit holds at 1.0 per cent of GDP from 2025-26 to 2028-29, although the dollar figure moves between $28.3 billion and $34.4 billion. It then narrows to 0.7 per cent for 2029-30, after 0.4 per cent in 2024-25, and the Government expects the budget to come back into balance in 2034-35 and to show a surplus equal to 0.8 per cent of the economy by 2036-37.

diagram.alt: Two views of Table 3.1 of the 2026-27 Budget paper. In dollars, payments exceed receipts in every year from 2024-25 to 2029-30, so the underlying cash balance is a deficit each year, 31.5 billion in 2026-27. As a share of GDP it is 0.4 per cent in 2024-25, 1.0 per cent for the next four years and 0.7 per cent in 2029-30, with a surplus of 0.8 per cent projected for 2036-37.

lead.text: A deficit and debt are different things. The deficit is the gap in one year, and debt is what has built up from borrowing to cover gaps over the years. Wikipedia's article on government debt says changes in debt over time reflect mainly borrowing due to past deficits.

The Budget table gives two measures of debt. **Gross debt** is the face value of the government securities on issue at the end of the financial year, which is what the Government repays to its investors at maturity. **Net debt** starts from the interest-bearing liabilities, counts the securities at market value, and subtracts some of the financial assets the Government holds, such as cash, deposits, advances and some investments and loans. The Budget calls net debt a broader measure of the Government's financial obligations.

In 2026-27 gross debt is 34.0 per cent of GDP and net debt is 19.9 per cent, a gap of 14.1 points. The Government projects that gross debt will top out in 2028-29 at 35.8 per cent of GDP, then fall away to 27.2 per cent by 2036-37, and that net debt will reach 21.9 per cent in 2029-30 and 15.1 per cent by 2036-37. **Net interest payments**, the interest the Government pays less the interest it receives, go from 0.6 per cent of GDP in 2026-27 to 0.9 per cent in 2029-30, and to 1.0 per cent by 2036-37. In dollars that is $19.9 billion rising to $31.7 billion between 2026-27 and 2029-30.

reveal.text: A share of GDP lets one row be read against the economy, and it is the reading the Budget itself uses for its main totals.
The two measures answer different questions, and the Budget gives both so that a reader can pick the one that fits.
Where a document gives figures and no reason, the honest reading says so and leaves the reason to be found.

lead.text: Not all of a deficit comes from the Government's own settings. Receipts and payments also move with the economy and with commodity prices, and the Budget separates that part out in the **structural budget balance**. It starts from the underlying cash balance and removes the estimated effects of **cyclical** factors, which are deviations of commodity prices and of economic activity from their long-run levels that affect receipts and payments only for a time.

The Budget points out that the structural balance is estimated and not observed, which makes it sensitive to the assumptions behind it, and that price swings linked to the conflict in the Middle East add to the uncertainty. It puts the structural deficit at a peak of 1.6 per cent of GDP, reached in 2025-26, a year in which the cash deficit is 1.0 per cent. It also says that cyclical factors lift the cash result in both 2025-26 and 2026-27, mostly because commodity prices are high, and that this help fades as prices drift back to the long-run levels the Budget assumes.

reveal.text: The structural figure is an estimate, and the Budget says so. It is a way of asking how much of the deficit would be left if the temporary help were taken away.

lead.text: A Budget paper is the Government's own account, and its sentences are of different kinds. Some are definitions, such as the notes under the table that say what gross debt, net debt and net interest mean. Some are forecasts, which depend on assumptions about growth, prices and policy, such as the peak of gross debt in 2028-29 and the return to balance in 2034-35. Some are the Government's judgements about its own work, such as its claim that its budget is stronger and more sustainable. And some report what other bodies say, such as the paper's note that Australia is one of just nine countries holding AAA ratings from all three major agencies.

The Government is the speaker in all four, but the way to check each differs. A definition can be looked up in the notes. A forecast has to be judged by its assumptions. A judgement is open to argument, and a report of what others say can be checked with those others.

reveal.text: Sorting the sentences by kind shows what you would need in order to check each one.

lead.text: A Budget paper is one voice. The Wikipedia article on government debt, written by volunteer editors and not an official source, gives others. It says one major reason for borrowing is to cushion shocks: when a downturn cuts tax revenue and raises spending on benefits, borrowing lets a government keep services running, whereas cutting spending or raising taxes at that moment would, the article says, make the downturn worse. The RBA says something close in its account of recessions, that a recession can add to public debt because governments collect less tax and need to fund more support.

The article also sets out the case for caution. It says a "deficits bias" can arise when groups disagree about spending, because politicians are tempted to win popularity by deficit spending, and that rising debt may lift interest rates and squeeze out private investment, since governments and firms compete for the same funds. Which of these arguments applies to Australia's deficit is a judgement that neither source makes for the reader.

reveal.text: A claim about debt is worth weighing by who makes it and what it rests on, whether it comes from a Budget paper, an encyclopedia article or a radio host.

lessons.orientation: Read a budget table and judge a deficit by its size against GDP, the path of debt, the interest bill and whether it is cyclical or structural, while noting who is making each claim.
lessons.nextAction: Tell automatic stabilisers from discretionary measures, and judge whether a fiscal boost adds to output or to prices.

blocks.text: The Government's 2026-27 Budget has $31.5 billion more going out than coming in over the year. That is a large number of dollars, but a dollar figure only means something against a scale.

We'll read the Budget's own table to see what it compares the deficit with, follow the path of debt and the interest bill, and ask a second question that a Budget paper makes unavoidable: whose claim is each sentence?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a Budget table, judge a deficit by its size against GDP, the path of debt, the interest bill and whether it is cyclical, and say who is making each claim.
intro.whyItMatters: A deficit of billions sounds alarming or trivial depending on what it is compared with, and the paper that reports it is the Government's own account.

recap.keyIdea: A deficit is judged against the size of the economy, the path of debt, the interest bill and how much of it is cyclical, and in a Budget paper each sentence has to be read for what kind of claim it is and who is making it.

blocks.text: You read Table 3.1 in dollars and as a share of GDP, and saw a deficit of 1.0 per cent of GDP in 2026-27, gross debt projected to peak at 35.8 per cent in 2028-29, and an interest bill rising from 0.6 to 0.9 per cent of GDP by 2029-30. The structural deficit of 1.6 per cent in 2025-26 is larger than the cash deficit because commodity prices are temporarily helping the cash figure.

The Budget is the Government's own account, with definitions, forecasts, its own judgements and reports of what others say, and each needs a different check. Wikipedia gives other voices, on borrowing as a shock absorber, on deficits bias and on the household analogy, each of which should be attributed to the article and weighed. Whether Australia's deficit is a problem is a judgement the sources leave to the reader.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what automatic stabilisers and discretionary measures do to a downturn, and what limits a fiscal boost.

lessons.title: Stabilisers, multipliers and their limits

lead.text: That built-in response has a name. Wikipedia describes **automatic stabilisers** as features of government budgets, mainly income taxes and welfare payments, that reduce swings in GDP without the Government taking any new action. When incomes fall in a recession, households pay less tax, and because income tax is generally progressive, the tax collected tends to fall faster than incomes do. More people are also entitled to unemployment and other benefits. Both effects leave households with more to spend than they would otherwise have had, so demand is held up.

In a boom the same rules run the other way. Rising incomes bring in more tax and fewer people claim benefits, so the budget moves towards surplus and takes some heat out of demand. Wikipedia cites a 2013 estimate by the US Congressional Budget Office that in fiscal 2009 stabilisers added 32.9% to the size of the deficit, and that 60% of the 1999 surplus was attributed to them.

A **discretionary** measure is the other kind, because someone has to decide it: a change to a tax rate, a new payment, a new project. The difference matters when you read a [[deficit|The amount by which spending exceeds revenue in a year. Met in 'Budgets, deficits and debt'.]]. A widening deficit in a downturn can come entirely from rules already in place, so it doesn't show that anyone chose it.

reveal.text: The 2026-27 Budget says part of its $11.8 billion of increased social security payments comes from indexation that runs by itself at a higher rate. A single line of a budget can therefore be partly automatic.

lead.text: Spending by one person is income for someone else, and that is what the multiplier is about. The RBA's example is a business that spends $10 million building a wind farm in a small town. The money goes to engineers and builders, and if they spend 8 of every 10 extra dollars they earn and save the other 2, they spend $8 million in the town's shops and businesses. Those businesses and their workers receive $8 million of income and spend 8 of every 10 of those dollars in turn. The share of an extra dollar of income that people spend is called the **marginal propensity to consume**, and in this example it is 0.8.

afterFigure.text: Each round is 0.8 times the one before: $10 million, $8 million, $6.4 million, $5.12 million, and the rounds keep shrinking without ever quite stopping. Added together they give $50 million of additional GDP. The ratio of that final rise in GDP to the first $10 million of spending is the **multiplier**, and the RBA writes it as 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5. In the second case in the figure, where people spend only 5 of every 10 dollars, each round is half the last, the multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 2, and the same $10 million adds $20 million.

diagram.alt: Bars for the rounds of spending that follow a $10 million wind farm. With 8 of every 10 dollars spent, the rounds are $10 million, $8 million, $6.4 million and $5.12 million, then $20.48 million over all later rounds, a total of $50 million. With 5 of every 10 spent they are $10 million, $5 million, $2.5 million and $1.25 million, then $1.25 million over all later rounds, a total of $20 million.

reveal.text: With only 2 of every 10 dollars passed on, the rounds are $10 million, $2 million, $0.4 million and so on, which add up to about $12.5 million. The more of each dollar people save, the closer the multiplier gets to 1.

lead.text: Saving is one way a round can stop short, and there are others. Part of what people earn goes in tax, and part of what they spend goes on imports, which pays foreign producers and leaves nothing for the next person in the town. We call saving, taxes and imports **leakages**, because each takes some of every round out of domestic spending. Wikipedia says the size of the multiplier depends on the marginal propensity to consume and on the marginal propensity to import, the share of extra income spent on imports.

Here is an invented version of the wind farm. The engineers spend $8 million, but $2 million of that buys imported equipment, so only $6 million becomes income for someone in the town. Now 6 of every 10 dollars are passed on instead of 8, and the same $10 million adds 10 ÷ (1 − 0.6) = $25 million, which is half of the RBA's $50 million.

Government spending brings some money back as well. Wikipedia notes that when the money is spent in a shop the shopkeeper pays more tax, so the net cost to the Government of spending $1 is likely to be a little less than $1.

How large the multiplier is depends on what the economy is doing when the money arrives. Wikipedia's account is that extra demand from government spending can be met by extra production, without pushing up prices, when many workers and machines are idle. The rounds in the first figure then really do happen, because each round of spending is matched by new work. When the economy is already at capacity, meaning that anyone who wants work has it and firms are using all their equipment, there is nothing idle to put to work. The extra demand then competes for the same workers and materials, and it shows up more in prices than in output.

afterFigure.text: Wikipedia calls the offsetting effect **crowding out**. It says the extent of resource crowding out depends on the economic situation: at capacity, a government that suddenly raises its deficit competes with private firms for scarce resources and the stimulus is offset, while below capacity the same stimulus is much more effective. A second channel works through borrowing, where the Government competes with private borrowers for funds and pushes interest rates up.

The article also reports that multipliers below one have been measured in some cases, and it quotes The Economist in 2009 saying that economists are deeply divided about how well such stimulus works. That is a reason to treat the multiplier as an estimate that depends on conditions and not as a fixed number.

diagram.alt: Two drawings of output before and after extra demand, with a dashed line marking capacity. With spare capacity, output after the boost is higher than before and still below the line. At capacity, output cannot rise above the line and the extra demand is marked as spilling into prices, imports and crowded-out private spending.

reveal.text: Spare capacity decides whether extra demand finds idle resources or has to compete for ones in use. Two more things change the size, and the next screen takes them in turn.

steps.headline: Who spends it, and the central bank

lead.text: The first is who receives the money. Wikipedia reports an argument that help aimed at the poorest households has a bigger multiplier than help aimed at richer ones, because those households' spending is held back by their incomes, so they spend a bigger share of anything extra and do it sooner. The article adds that someone on a high income may spend almost none of a small extra amount in the short run.

The second is the central bank. Wikipedia says how potent a stimulus is may depend on how accommodating the central bank is, and that if the central bank raises interest rates in response to the extra borrowing and spending, to contain overheating, the stimulus does less. It also describes a view held by many economists that monetary policy is the better tool for steering the business cycle, with fiscal stimulus most useful when interest rates cannot fall further.

None of the sources for this course gives an estimate of the multiplier for Australia, so we don't offer one. Wikipedia does report that in 2012 the IMF said the multipliers its staff used in forecasting were about 0.5, while its results suggested a range of 0.9 to 1.7 since the Great Recession, which shows how far an estimate can depend on the circumstances.

reveal.text: The first round is the same size either way. What differs is how much of it is spent, and spending is what starts the next round.

lead.text: The 2026-27 Budget gives us a case to apply all this to. The Government delivered a $2.9 billion package that more than halved the fuel excise for a temporary three months, reducing the excise on petrol and diesel by 32 cents, which takes nearly $23 off a full 65-litre tank. In the same year the RBA raised the cash rate target five times, to 4.85 per cent on 3 November. The excise cut answered dearer fuel, and the RBA's rises answered dearer fuel together with capacity pressures in the economy.

The Budget argues that this kind of shock suits fiscal policy better than monetary policy. It says fiscal policy offers many instruments, each of which can be tailored to a particular problem, and that this fits it to a supply shock such as the global oil shock more than monetary policy. That is the Government's view of its own measures, and it is an argument to weigh. Two questions help: what is each tool aimed at, the price of one good or demand across the economy, and what do we know about the economy's spare capacity when the measure arrives?

reveal.text: Neither source weighs one tool against the other, so the comparison is ours to make from what each tool does.

lessons.orientation: Tell automatic stabilisers from discretionary measures, and judge whether a fiscal boost is likely to add to output or to prices given spare capacity, who receives the money and how the central bank reacts.
lessons.nextAction: You can now tell an automatic stabiliser from a decision, and judge whether a boost to spending is likely to add to output or to prices.

blocks.text: When a recession arrives, the government's budget deficit usually grows, even if nobody in Parliament has voted for anything. Fewer people are earning, so less income tax is collected, and more people qualify for payments such as unemployment benefits, so more money goes out. In a boom the same rules push the budget the other way.

Governments also make choices of their own, such as cutting a tax or paying for a project, and then a second question arises: how much does one extra dollar of spending add to what the economy produces? The answer turns out to depend on the circumstances, and the 2026-27 Budget contains both kinds of measure, which makes it a good place to look.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell an automatic stabiliser from a decision, and to judge whether a boost to spending is likely to add to output or to prices.
intro.whyItMatters: Budgets and rate decisions are reported side by side, and weighing them takes a way to ask what each can do in the conditions of the day.

recap.keyIdea: Automatic stabilisers move the budget with the economy without a decision, and the multiplier, the final rise in GDP per dollar of first spending, depends on leakages, spare capacity, who spends the money and how the central bank reacts.

blocks.text: You separated rules that act on their own from decisions, followed the RBA's wind farm through its rounds and saw how saving, taxes and imports cut them short. A boost does most for output when resources are idle, when the money goes to people who spend it at home and when the central bank doesn't lean against it. At capacity, more of it shows up in prices or crowds out private spending. The sources give no Australian multiplier, and the Government's claim that fiscal policy suits a supply shock is an argument to weigh against what the RBA says about excess demand.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at the Australian dollar, what moves it, and what a move does to exports, imports and prices.

lessons.title: The dollar and the current account

lead.text: An exchange rate says how much of one currency a unit of another will buy. The Australian dollar is usually quoted against the US dollar, because the US dollar is the most traded currency in the world, and AUD/USD is the number of US dollars you receive for each Australian dollar you convert. When the Australian dollar becomes worth more, we call it an **appreciation**, and when it becomes worth less, a **depreciation**. In the figure, the same Australian dollar buys 70, 75 or 80 US cents.

afterFigure.text: One pair of currencies can mislead, because the dollar can rise against one currency and fall against another. For a broader view the RBA uses a **trade-weighted index**, which prices the dollar against a basket of currencies weighted by Australia's trade with each partner. It generally moves less than any single rate, because changes against different currencies partly offset each other.

Australia has floated its dollar since 1983, so its value comes from how many people want to buy Australian dollars and how many want to sell them. The RBA steps in only on rare occasions, such as when trading becomes disorderly.

reveal.text: The RBA's interest rate decisions still matter, because interest rates are one of the things that raise or lower the demand for Australian dollars. The next screen takes the drivers in turn.

lead.text: Because the dollar floats, its price rises when more people want Australian dollars than want to sell them. The first thing the RBA names is the gap between Australian interest rates and those overseas. All else being equal, higher Australian rates make Australian assets that pay interest more attractive, so more money flows in and less flows out. That raises the demand for Australian dollars and reduces their supply, and the dollar ends up higher than it would otherwise be. Lower rates work the other way.

The second is the **terms of trade**, the ratio of Australia's export prices to its import prices. The RBA says the two have moved closely together over a long period, and that commodity prices have a large influence, because commodities are a large share of exports. When the price of iron ore rises, export prices rise, buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for the same tonnes, and the dollar tends to appreciate. The mining investment boom from the mid-2000s to 2013 also brought large inflows of foreign investment, and in 2011 AUD/USD reached a record 1.10.

afterFigure.text: The third driver, risk sentiment, matters over short periods. The RBA says the Australian dollar tracks other financial markets: it typically appreciates when global share prices rise and depreciates when they fall, as investors become more or less willing to take on risk. Several drivers can act at once and pull in different directions, so a rule about one of them says what to expect only when the others stay the same.

Higher Australian interest rates shift demand right and supply left, so the price rises. Higher export prices shift demand right, so the price rises. Investors turning cautious shifts demand left, so the price falls.

reveal.text: The sources don't say which driver mattered most in 2026, only that the dollar rose while these two pointed in opposite directions. Several drivers acting at once is the usual position.

lead.text: A move in the dollar changes the price of Australian goods against foreign ones, and everything else follows from that. The RBA's explanation uses a depreciation. Australian goods and services become cheaper for foreign buyers, so export volumes rise, while imports become dearer for Australians, who shift towards locally made goods, so import volumes fall. More output and income raise the demand for workers, and imported goods cost more, which adds to inflation both directly and through higher wages and costs. An appreciation has the opposite effect on activity and inflation.

The effects arrive with a lag. Firms that sell imported goods often price them in Australian dollars, so each firm decides when to pass a change in cost on, and exchange rates are volatile enough that many wait until a move looks lasting. The RBA says most estimates put the largest effect on activity and inflation between one and three years after the move.

The ABS June quarter 2026 national accounts show an appreciation at work. Prices of imported consumption goods fell in the quarter, which the ABS puts down partly to the appreciation. The ABS also lists the appreciation, along with the temporary fuel excise cut and weak travel demand, among the reasons that consumption prices grew more slowly.

It would be natural to expect a depreciation to improve the trade balance quickly, and the RBA explains why it can do the opposite for a while. What counts for the balance of payments is the value of exports and imports, which means prices as well as quantities. The direct effect of a depreciation is immediate: imports cost more in Australian dollars, which tends to lower the value of net exports, meaning exports less imports. The indirect effect, more export volume and less import volume, comes later. So in the short run a depreciation is likely to lower what net exports are worth, and over time, as volumes respond, it is likely to raise it. The RBA says this pattern is sometimes called the **J-curve**.

afterFigure.text: The same slow response of volumes that delays the effect on activity also explains why net exports can look worse before they look better.

diagram.alt: A curve for the value of net exports after a depreciation. It starts at zero, dips below the starting level, then climbs above it. The dip is labelled as import prices rising at once and the climb as volumes responding.
diagram.caption: An illustration of the pattern the RBA calls the J-curve. It is not drawn from data.

reveal.text: The RBA doesn't say how long the dip lasts, so the sensible conclusion is to wait for more data, and not to rule the effect out.

steps.headline: Two sides of the balance of payments

lead.text: The balance of payments records the dealings between people and firms living in Australia and everyone else, and the RBA divides it into two accounts. The **current account** records the flow of goods, services and income: the trade balance, which is exports less imports, the income earned from or paid to the rest of the world, such as wages and dividends, and transfers. The combined **capital and financial account** records changes in who owns what, such as shares, bonds, businesses and bank deposits bought across borders.

Every transaction is entered twice, once as a credit and once as a debit of the same amount, so the two accounts offset each other and the total is zero. The figure uses three of the RBA's examples. An iron ore shipment is a credit in the trade balance, and the trade credit that the buyer owes until it pays is a debit in the financial account. A holiday in Bali is a debit in the current account, with a matching credit in the financial account as money moves out of Australian bank accounts to overseas businesses.

afterFigure.text: The RBA draws a lesson for Australia from this. The country has tended to borrow from overseas to invest in its economy. The capital flowing in is a credit and gives a capital and financial account surplus, and that surplus has its counterpart in a current account deficit, part of which is the interest Australia pays on its international borrowing. The sources for this course don't give the size of the current account balance, so we don't quote one.

diagram.alt: A table of three of the RBA's examples. An iron ore export of $100 million is a plus in the current account and a minus in the financial account. A $5 million Bali holiday is a minus and then a plus. US shares for $20 million have no current account entry. Net of the three: plus $95 million in the current account, minus $95 million in the financial account, zero in total.

Pass-through isn't complete on the day, which is why a lower dollar and higher import prices can be separated by months.

lessons.orientation: Explain what moves the Australian dollar, predict what a move does to exports, imports and inflation, and read a current account deficit as the other side of capital inflows.
lessons.reviewLabel: The dollar and the current account
lessons.nextAction: You can now read an exchange rate, say what is likely to move the Australian dollar, and explain why a current account deficit has a matching capital inflow.

blocks.text: The RBA explains exchange rates with a simple case: at an AUD/USD rate of 0.75, an Australian dollar changes into 75 US cents. That number is the price of our currency in someone else's. It changes every day, and each change alters what Australian exporters earn, what imported goods cost in the shops and how much of the country's income is paid abroad.
Before asking what moves the number, it is worth being sure which way it points, because quotes of this kind are easy to read backwards.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read an exchange rate, say what moves the Australian dollar and what its moves do, and explain why a current account deficit has a match.
intro.whyItMatters: A move in the dollar changes the cost of imports, the earnings of exporters and the path of inflation, so reading it correctly helps with many headlines.

recap.keyIdea: The Australian dollar floats, so supply and demand set it, with interest rates, the terms of trade and risk sentiment among the drivers. Its moves change prices with a lag, and a current account deficit is matched by capital flowing in.

blocks.text: AUD/USD gives the US cents one Australian dollar buys, so a lower number is a depreciation. Higher interest rates and higher export prices tend to lift the dollar, risk sentiment moves it from day to day, and the drivers can point in different directions, as the ABS and RBA figures for 2026 showed. A fall in the dollar raises import prices at once and changes volumes later, so the value of net exports can dip before it improves. The balance of payments has two sides that always offset each other, and Australia's borrowing from overseas to invest is one reason for its current account deficit.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at why some economies grow faster than others, and how more inputs differ from better productivity.

lessons.title: Why some economies grow faster

lead.text: Every rise in output comes from one of two sources. Firms can use more inputs, meaning more workers, more hours or more equipment, or they can produce more from the inputs they already have. The RBA defines productivity as the output you get from a given quantity of inputs. Wikipedia names the two kinds of growth: growth from more inputs alone, such as a larger population, is **extensive growth**, and growth from using inputs more efficiently is **intensive growth**. Our World in Data adds why the difference matters: before economies began to grow, one person could gain only if another lost out.

Take the RBA's toy factory worker, who makes 120 dolls in a 40-hour week. That is 3 dolls an hour, which is her **labour productivity**, her output divided by the hours she works. If she works 50 hours at the same rate she makes 150 dolls, so her output has grown by a quarter and her productivity hasn't moved. That is why the ABS publishes GDP per hour worked: it removes the effect of working more hours.

Productivity isn't observed directly. The ABS measures output and inputs, and productivity is calculated by dividing one by the other. Labour input is usually hours worked, which captures overtime and leave better than a head count does. The other widely used measure is **multifactor productivity**, or MFP, which divides output by labour and capital combined, so a change in MFP is a change in output that changes in inputs can't explain.

The RBA's toy factory shows the calculation, using indexes that start at 100. In year 2 the factory's output index rises to 107 while its combined input index rises to 105, so its MFP index is 107 ÷ 105 × 100 = 101.9. MFP has grown by 1.9%: the factory made 7% more with 5% more inputs, and the 1.9% is the part that the extra inputs don't account for.

Short-run figures need care. In a downturn output falls by more than inputs, because firms can't change their inputs quickly, so measured productivity falls, and in a boom it rises. The RBA says economists therefore often study productivity over long periods that include several cycles.

steps.headline: An invented bakery's output index rises from 100 to 104 and its combined input index from 100 to 106. Has its multifactor productivity risen or fallen?

workedSteps.text: MFP is output divided by combined inputs, so compare the two indexes in year 2, as the RBA did for the toy factory.
workedSteps.math: MFP index = output index ÷ combined input index × 100

workedSteps.text: Output has grown by 4 and inputs by 6. Decide which way the ratio will move before working it out.
The calculation confirms it. The index is below its starting value of 100, so the bakery gets less from its inputs than it did.

reveal.text: The RBA gives the reason as the difficulty of measuring output in non-market industries, where prices don't reflect supply and demand. The absence of a measure isn't evidence of a rise or a fall.

lead.text: The RBA uses a **production possibility frontier** to show two ways for a business to raise productivity. The frontier marks the most of two goods, X and Y, that the business can produce with its inputs and technology. A business inside the frontier is not using its inputs as well as it could, so moving it up to the frontier raises output with the same inputs, which the RBA calls efficiency. It says microeconomic reform, such as policies on competition, trade, tax and regulation, has supported efficiency in Australia over the past few decades. A business on the frontier can still do better by expanding what is possible. New technology or knowledge, often built into faster computers or more powerful machines, moves the frontier outward, and the RBA calls that expanding capacity.

afterFigure.text: Spillovers add to both. When knowledge is shared between businesses, directly through industry innovation hubs or indirectly when workers change jobs, one firm's improvement lifts others. The RBA says the gains can show up as higher wages, lower prices or higher profits, and that unit labour costs, the labour cost of making one unit of output, fall as labour productivity rises.

diagram.alt: Two drawings of a production possibility frontier for two goods, X and Y. In the first, point A inside the frontier moves up to point B on it, which is more of both goods from the same inputs. In the second, point B on the frontier moves to point C on a frontier further out, which is more of both goods after new methods.
diagram.caption: The RBA's two ways to raise productivity. Use the buttons to compare them.

lead.text: The RBA calls productivity growth the main source of rising living standards over the long run, and its reason is **diminishing returns**: holding the other inputs constant, each extra worker or machine adds less to output than the one before. More inputs alone can't keep output per worker rising.

Wikipedia reports that the Solow-Swan model, developed in the 1950s, builds this in. Capital accumulates through investment and wears out through depreciation, so with no technological progress, output per worker eventually reaches a **steady state** where the two balance. Technological progress is what lifts output per worker even in the steady state. The model takes the pace of technological progress as given from outside, and Wikipedia says its failure to explain why technology improves is one of its limitations. Endogenous growth theory, developed in the 1980s by economists including Robert Lucas and Paul Romer, set out to explain that progress from within the model.

Wikipedia also reports a famous estimate by Solow that technological progress explained about 80 per cent of the long-run increase in US income per person. It is an estimate for one country from one model, and it isn't a settled share for every economy.

reveal.text: That is why the model needs technological progress to explain growth that lasts, and why economists asked where it comes from.

lead.text: Small differences in growth rates matter more than they look, because growth **compounds**. Wikipedia notes that in 1870 GDP per person in the United Kingdom, at $4,808, was about 20% above that of the United States at $4,007, and that by 2008 the positions were reversed, with $36,130 in the UK and $46,970 in the US. The average growth rates behind that were 1.47% a year in the UK and 1.80% in the US, a gap of about a third of a percentage point, kept up for 138 years.

afterFigure.text: The second case in the figure is an illustration with no data behind it: two economies that start equal and grow at 1% and 2% a year. After 35 years the faster one has about 2.0 times its starting income and the slower about 1.4 times. After 70 years the figures are 4.0 and 2.0, so an economy that grew a point faster each year ends with twice the income of the other.

The 2026-27 Budget puts the same idea in policy terms. The Government says a comprehensive productivity package, which helps reduce regulatory costs, supports higher living standards, and it calls improving productivity central to its plan to grow the economy. Those are the Government's claims about its own package, and the evidence for them isn't in these sources.

diagram.alt: Two drawings. The first compares GDP per person adjusted for inflation: the United Kingdom $4,808 in 1870 and $36,130 in 2008, the United States $4,007 in 1870 and $46,970 in 2008. The second shows two growth paths from the same start: income at 1% a year reaches 2.0 times its start after 70 years, and at 2% a year it reaches 4.0 times.
diagram.caption: The first case uses figures Wikipedia reports. The second is an illustration with no data. Use the buttons to compare them.

blocks.text: In 'Reading a GDP headline' you read the ABS rows for the year to June 2026, with GDP up 2.1%, GDP per person up 0.7% and GDP per hour worked down 0.2%. That lesson was about which row answers which question. This one asks what a rise in output is made of, because a figure like 2.1% is usually read as good news about how well off people are becoming, and that depends on where the growth came from.

Growth in output has to come from somewhere. Either more labour and equipment is being used, or more is being made from what is already in use. Which of the two it is has large consequences for living standards, so the first job is to learn to tell them apart.

recap.keyIdea: Output grows by using more inputs or by getting more from them, and because inputs have diminishing returns, productivity growth is the main long-run source of rising living standards, whose small yearly gaps compound.

blocks.text: Output can rise because more inputs are used, as in the first invented economy at the start of the lesson, or because more is made from the same inputs, as in the second. Productivity is calculated from output and inputs, it swings with the cycle, and the RBA names efficiency and new capacity as its two sources. Diminishing returns mean that more inputs alone slow down, which is why the Solow model needs technological progress and why endogenous growth theory tries to explain it. Small differences in growth rates compound into large gaps, as the United Kingdom and United States, and South Korea and Ghana, show.

recap.nextHook: Next we read a central bank statement closely, separating its decision, its evidence, its outlook and what the Board says it will do.

lessons.title: Reading a central bank statement

lead.text: A **decision statement** is the media release the Monetary Policy Board publishes on the day of each meeting. It opens with the decision in one sentence: whether the Board raised, held or lowered the cash rate target, by how much and to what level. The reasons follow, and they fall into three kinds. Some sentences give evidence, meaning what has already happened to inflation, growth, housing and jobs. Some give the outlook, meaning what the forecasts expect and which risks could make the outcome differ. And some give the Board's approach, meaning what it says it will pay attention to and do. The statement ends with the vote.

afterFigure.text: In practice a paragraph often mixes the kinds, so you need to sort sentence by sentence. A statement also does a second job: it explains and justifies the decision, so the evidence it chooses is part of the argument and not a neutral report. The RBA releases the Board's minutes two weeks after the meeting, and the forecasts behind the decision come out in a separate document.

For each variable it gives the forecast at six dates, and beneath it, in brackets, the previous forecast, so you can see what moved. The figure shows the unemployment rows.

afterFigure.text: A forecast is the staff's central view, the outcome they judge most likely, and it isn't a promise. The Statement says so by naming risks in both directions. It judges the risks to inflation to be skewed to the upside, and it also describes a downside: inflation could fall faster than forecast if capacity pressures ease sooner. Some rows in the table are assumptions and not forecasts, such as the cash rate you met in the opening question, and a note under the table says which.

reveal.text: The Statement gives the same account in words: activity in 2026 has come in a little above what was expected, helped by data centre investment, while tighter monetary policy and a weaker housing market are expected to hold growth under trend.

lead.text: A single statement tells you where the Board stands, and a pair of them tells you what moved it. Compare four things between the two dates: the decision, the new information the Board cites, the outlook it gives, and the wording of its approach. The February and March statements show how. On 3 February the Board raised the cash rate target to 3.85 per cent, citing greater capacity pressures and private demand that had strengthened more than expected. By 17 March it had raised it again, to 4.10 per cent, and the statement had something new in it: the conflict in the Middle East had pushed fuel prices sharply higher, which would add to inflation if sustained. That new item is the one to look for, because it points to what the Board thought had changed in the weeks between meetings.

The same method works on the outlook. A forecast that has moved later or higher is a change in the Board's view, and the Statement's table lets you measure it. Compare like with like, though, because a forecast for the end of 2027 is a different thing from the inflation figure published last week.

reveal.text: Source A said the Board would leave the rate unchanged while it assessed how the economy was evolving, and Source B says some of the upside risks had begun to materialise. A change in the evidence is what moved the decision.

steps.headline: What the Board says it will do

lead.text: The last part of a statement says what the Board will pay attention to and do, and none of the 2026 statements committed it to a path. Every statement says the Board will keep watching the data and its assessment of the outlook and risks, and will use them to guide its decisions. Some add a sentence about what it would do if things went a certain way. In June, when it held the rate, it said it would do what it considers necessary, and it named a further rise in the target as one of the things that might be required. In August it said the same, with a further rise if upside risks materialise. In September it raised the rate.

afterFigure.text: Read the last column against the row below it. This is the course's own reading of the table, and the RBA doesn't make it. Three statements mentioned a further rise, and the next meeting held once and raised twice. Of the four that did not, the first three were followed by two rises and a hold, and the November statement has no later meeting yet. So in this year's record the wording shows what the Board is prepared to do, and it doesn't work as a timetable.

Votes behave the same way in this record. The vote line gives a count, and a split vote says the members weighed the same evidence differently: in March four of the nine preferred to leave the rate unchanged, and in November three did. The count doesn't give the dissenters' reasons, and the minutes, which come two weeks later, aren't among our sources.

diagram.alt: A table of the Board's 2026 decisions. 3 February: raised to 3.85, unanimous, no further rise mentioned. 17 March: raised to 4.10, five to four, no. 5 May: raised to 4.35, eight to one, no. 16 June: held at 4.35, unanimous, yes. 11 August: held at 4.35, unanimous, yes. 29 September: raised to 4.60, unanimous, yes. 3 November: raised to 4.85, six to three, no.

lessons.orientation: Read a Monetary Policy Board decision and the Statement on Monetary Policy overview, separate the decision, the evidence, the outlook and the Board's stated approach, and say what changed from one statement to the next.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read a central bank statement, separate its decision, evidence, outlook and approach, and say what changed from one statement to the next and what it leaves open.

blocks.text: On 3 November 2026 the Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Board raised its cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, a rise of 25 basis points, and the same day it published a statement explaining why. A statement like that is easy to skim for the number and the verdict, yet it contains several different kinds of sentence: what was decided, what has been observed, what is expected, and what the Board says it will do next. Mixing them up is how a headline comes to say more than the Board did.
The RBA's forecast table lists a cash rate for each of the years ahead, and it is worth asking what kind of number that is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to separate the decision, the evidence, the outlook and the approach in a central bank statement, and to say what changed since the last one.
intro.whyItMatters: Statements and the news about them are written to explain a decision, and reading them closely shows what was said and what was left open.

recap.keyIdea: A decision statement separates a decision, the evidence so far, the outlook and the Board's approach, and a careful reader keeps them apart, compares each statement with the last, and treats forecasts, assumptions and votes as information and not as promises.

blocks.text: You sorted the sentences of the 3 November statement by what they do, read the forecast table with its previous values and its note, and compared pairs of statements for new information and a shifted outlook. The Board's forecasts are central views with risks on both sides, the cash rate in the table is an assumption taken from market pricing, and, in the course's own reading of the 2026 table, neither the closing wording nor the vote predicted the next decision. With these habits you can read the next statement for what it says and for what it leaves open.

questions.prompt: These two sentences come from the same ABS release. Which of the two figures better shows how much more Australia produced in the quarter?
hints: Ask which figure would still change if nothing more were made and every price went up.
The ABS describes one figure as nominal and the other as chain volume measures. Which one is tied to the amount produced?

acceptedIdeas: The 0.4%, because it takes out price changes and so tracks the volume that was produced
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 0.4%, because it takes out price changes and so tracks the volume that was produced

choices.label: The 0.8%, because it counts every dollar produced and so gives the fuller picture
The 0.4%, because it takes out price changes and so tracks the volume that was produced
Both equally, because each is a growth rate for the same GDP over the same quarter and nothing else

extracts.text: The Australian economy rose 0.4% in seasonally adjusted chain volume measures. In nominal terms, GDP rose 0.8%.
extracts.who: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Australian National Accounts: National Income, Expenditure and Product (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The ABS's key statistics for the June quarter 2026

questions.onCorrect: The 0.4% is the real figure, the ABS's chain volume measure with price changes removed. The 0.8% is nominal, so it also includes higher prices.

misconceptions.feedback: Nominal growth does count every dollar, and that is the trouble: a dollar total also rises when prices rise, with nothing more made. The 0.8% includes the effect of price changes.
They cover the same quarter, but they don't count the same thing. One is in dollars at the prices of the time and the other has the price changes taken out, so they can't both show volume.

questions.prompt: Why does the real growth figure for this apple economy compare 104 kg with 100 kg and leave the prices out?
hints: Real growth is meant to answer one question. What is it?
If the apples had cost the same in both years, would the kilograms have changed?

acceptedIdeas: The kilograms show how much was produced, so leaving out prices removes the effect of the price rise
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The kilograms show how much was produced, so leaving out prices removes the effect of the price rise

choices.label: Prices are only estimates, so economists avoid them wherever they can and compare quantities instead
The price rise is already inside the kilograms, so counting it again would double its effect on growth
The kilograms show how much was produced, so leaving out prices removes the effect of the price rise

questions.onCorrect: Real growth compares volumes so that it moves only when the amount produced moves. The price effect belongs to nominal growth.

misconceptions.feedback: Prices are recorded like any other data. Real growth leaves them out because the question is how much was produced, and a price rise says nothing about that.
Kilograms are a quantity and contain no price. It's nominal growth that mixes volume and price together.

questions.prompt: Someone asks whether the average Australian produced more in the year to June 2026 than a year earlier. Which ABS figure answers that, and what does it show?
hints: The question is about the average person, not the whole economy and not one hour of work.
Which row shares output out over the population?

acceptedIdeas: GDP per person, which shows a small gain in what the average person produces
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GDP per person, which shows a small gain in what the average person produces

choices.label: GDP in chain volume measures, which shows a large gain for the average person
GDP in current prices, which shows the biggest gain for the average person
GDP per hour worked, which shows a loss for the average person's output
GDP per person, which shows a small gain in what the average person produces

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by the population takes out growth that came only from there being more people. Here it cuts the 2.1% for the economy to 0.7% for the average person.

misconceptions.feedback: That row is total output. It rose 2.1%, but part of that came from there being more people, so it can't tell you about the average person.
The current price row includes price rises, so it grows faster than output does. It also covers the whole economy and not the average person.
That row divides by hours of work and not by people. It answers whether each hour produced more, and a person can produce more in total by working more hours.

questions.prompt: Output rose 2.1% over the year even though output per hour fell 0.2%. What must have risen to make up for it?
hints: Output is output per hour multiplied by hours worked. If the first factor edged down and the product still grew, what about the second?
Both rows are in the same table and are measured the same way, so they have to fit together.

acceptedIdeas: Hours worked, which more than made up for the small fall per hour
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hours worked, which more than made up for the small fall per hour

choices.label: Hours worked, which more than made up for the small fall per hour
The price of each hour's output, since a fall in volume is offset by dearer goods
Output per person, because output per person moves with total output
Nothing needs to have risen, because the ABS must have made an error in one of the two rows

questions.onCorrect: Output equals output per hour multiplied by hours worked, so a small fall per hour and a 2.1% rise in output together mean hours worked rose by roughly 2%.

misconceptions.feedback: Output and output per hour are both about how much was produced, so a price change can't bridge the gap. What is missing from the product is the number of hours worked.
The ABS reports output per person up 0.7% over the year, well short of 2%. It moves with total output only if the population stays the same.
The two rows are consistent with each other. Output is output per hour multiplied by hours worked, so the figures only need hours to have risen.

questions.prompt: A newsreader says: GDP per person rose 0.7% in the year to June 2026, so the typical household is about 0.7% better off. What is the strongest objection?
hints: GDP per person adds up everyone's share of output and divides. What does that leave out about who gets what?
Think about what an average cannot tell you about how the income was divided up.

acceptedIdeas: GDP per person is an average, so it cannot show how evenly the income was shared out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GDP per person is an average, so it cannot show how evenly the income was shared out

choices.label: GDP per person is an average, so it cannot show how evenly the income was shared out
GDP per person is a nominal figure, so most of the 0.7% is simply higher prices, not output
A rise of 0.7% is too small to count as a real increase in anything at all, whoever got it
GDP per person counts only people with jobs, which leaves out most households altogether

questions.onCorrect: An average can rise while the typical household gains little, or gains more. GDP can't tell you how the income was split, so the gain per person says nothing about any one household.

misconceptions.feedback: The ABS lists GDP per person among its chain volume measures, so price changes have already been taken out.
A small rise is still a rise. The objection is about what an average can hide, and the size of the rise is a separate matter.
It divides by the whole population, with and without jobs. The trouble is that an average can hide who receives the income.

questions.prompt: After a cyclone, a coastal town spends heavily on rebuilding houses and roads, and GDP in the next quarter is higher as a result. What follows?
hints: Is paid rebuilding work production? Think about whether anyone is producing something and being paid for it.
Then ask whether the town ends up with more than it had before the cyclone.

acceptedIdeas: GDP is higher because the rebuilding is production, yet it only replaces what was lost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GDP is higher because the rebuilding is production, yet it only replaces what was lost

choices.label: The town is better off by the full amount of the extra spending, since GDP measures welfare
GDP is unchanged, because rebuilding only restores what existed before the cyclone hit
GDP is higher because the rebuilding is production, yet it only replaces what was lost
GDP falls, because the cyclone destroyed output and rebuilding can't make up for it

questions.onCorrect: Paid rebuilding is production, so GDP counts it, but it puts the town back where it started. A rise in GDP doesn't tell you whether people are better off.

misconceptions.feedback: GDP measures what is produced and not how well off people are. The spending replaces buildings and roads the town already had.
Rebuilding is work paid for at market prices, so it is counted in the quarter it happens. That it restores what was lost doesn't keep it out of GDP.
The destruction itself isn't production, and the rebuilding is, so the spending adds to GDP in the quarter it takes place.

questions.prompt: A small country's GDP rose 6% in dollars over a year. Its prices rose about 5% and its population about 3% (invented figures). Which statement do these figures best support?
hints: Take the price rise out of the 6% first. What is left?
Then ask how that growth compares with the growth in the number of people sharing it.

acceptedIdeas: Real output rose only a little, but population grew faster, so output per person fell
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Real output rose only a little, but population grew faster, so output per person fell

choices.label: Output per person rose about 3%, because 6% growth less 3% population growth is 3%
Real output rose about 1%, so the average person produced about 1% more than before
Real output rose about 6%, because the dollar figure shows how much was produced
Real output rose only a little, but population grew faster, so output per person fell

questions.onCorrect: Taking the price rise out of 6% leaves only a little real growth, and sharing that over a population that grew by 3% leaves less per person. Each row of the ABS table removes a different thing.

misconceptions.feedback: The 6% is in dollars, so it still contains the 5% price rise. Taking prices out leaves about 1% real growth, and the population then takes that below zero per person.
Real growth of about 1% is right, but it is shared over 3% more people, so each person's share fell.
A dollar figure rises with prices too. With prices up about 5%, most of the 6% was higher prices and real output rose only about 1%.

questions.prompt: GDP counts what is produced and sold at a price. Which of these does it count, and which does it leave out?
hints: Ask of each item whether anyone pays for the work or the product.
Unpaid work can be useful and still fall outside GDP.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Counted: the repair for a fee, the café's coffee and the paid house building. Not counted: cooking for the family, mowing your own lawn and the free software.

items.label: A mechanic repairs a customer's car for a fee
items.explanation: It is a service sold at a price, so it is counted.

items.label: A café sells coffee to its customers
items.explanation: It is sold at a market price, so it is counted.

items.label: A builder is paid to put up a new house
items.explanation: It is production that someone pays for, so it is counted.

items.label: Someone cooks dinner for their own family
items.explanation: It is unpaid household work, which Wikipedia says GDP excludes.

items.label: Someone mows their own lawn on a Sunday
