items.explanation: The work is unpaid and nobody buys it, so GDP leaves it out.

items.label: A volunteer writes software and gives it away
items.explanation: Wikipedia quotes Diane Coyle on free digital work such as open-source software, which clearly has great economic value although its price is zero, and GDP leaves it out.

questions.onCorrect: GDP counts work that is paid for at a price. Work done for nothing, however useful, is outside it.

questions.prompt: A union argues that because GDP rose 2.1% in the year to June 2026, each worker produced 2.1% more and should be paid 2.1% more. Which reading of the ABS rows is best?
hints: A claim about what each worker produces needs a row that divides by something about workers.
Which of the ABS rows divides by hours worked, and which way did it move?

acceptedIdeas: Total output rose mainly on more hours and output per hour fell, so the claim confuses the two
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Total output rose mainly on more hours and output per hour fell, so the claim confuses the two

choices.label: Total output rose mainly on more hours and output per hour fell, so the claim confuses the two
Output per person rose 0.7%, so each worker is 0.7% more productive and the claim is half right
Current price GDP rose 5.3%, so the claim understates how much more each worker produced
The ABS rows contradict each other, so no claim about workers can be tested against them

questions.onCorrect: The per hour row fell 0.2%. The year's growth came mainly from more hours, so total output is the wrong figure for a claim about each hour of work.

misconceptions.feedback: Output per person divides by the whole population, with and without jobs, so it isn't a measure of how much a worker produces. The per hour row is, and it fell.
The dollar figure includes price rises, so it overstates growth in output. It says nothing about what each worker produced either.
The rows answer different questions and fit together: more hours worked can raise total output while output per hour slips.

questions.prompt: The ABS recorded GDP up 0.9% in current prices and 0.8% in chain volume measures in the June quarter of 2025, and 1.9% and 0.5% in the September quarter. A commentator says the economy sped up. What do the rows suggest?
hints: Compare the volume row across the two quarters, then the dollar row.
If the dollar figure rose and the volume figure fell, what must have happened to the third thing in the dollar figure?

acceptedIdeas: Dollar growth sped up while output growth slowed, so the extra dollars came from higher prices
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dollar growth sped up while output growth slowed, so the extra dollars came from higher prices

choices.label: The economy sped up, because the dollar figure more than doubled between the two quarters
Output sped up as well, because a rise of 0.5% is still a rise in the economy's output
Dollar growth sped up while output growth slowed, so the extra dollars came from higher prices
Output sped up and prices fell, because the volume row is the smaller of the two

questions.onCorrect: Output growth slowed from 0.8% to 0.5%, and dollar growth rose from 0.9% to 1.9%, so a larger share of the dollar growth was prices.

misconceptions.feedback: The dollar figure includes prices. The volume row, which follows output, went from 0.8% to 0.5%, so output grew more slowly.
Output grew in both quarters, but it grew by less in the second, 0.5% against 0.8%. Speeding up needs a larger rise, and only the dollar figure shows one.
A smaller volume row means prices rose, not fell, since the dollar figure is volume and prices together.

questions.prompt: A newsreader says: "The unemployment rate was 4.9% in October 2026, so about one in twenty Australians had no job." What is wrong with that sentence?
hints: Ask what the rate is a percentage of. Is it everyone, or a smaller group?
Think of someone with no job who is not trying to find one. Should the rate count them?

acceptedIdeas: The rate is a share of the labour force, so it leaves out people without jobs who are not looking
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rate is a share of the labour force, so it leaves out people without jobs who are not looking

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, because the rate is the share of all Australians who have no job
The rate is a share of the labour force, so it leaves out people without jobs who are not looking
The rate counts only people claiming unemployment payments, so it misses many who are out of work
The rate also counts part-time workers who want more hours, so it overstates people with no job

questions.onCorrect: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people as a share of the labour force, which is made up of people who have jobs or are looking for them.

misconceptions.feedback: The rate is not a share of everyone. It is a share of the labour force, and a person with no job who isn't looking for one is outside the labour force.
The ABS doesn't use payment claims. It surveys about 50,000 people each month and asks what they did in a reference week.
Part-time workers who want more hours are employed, and the ABS counts them in a separate measure, the underemployment rate.

questions.prompt: Why is the unemployment rate worked out as a share of the labour force and not of everyone aged 15 and over?
hints: Who is the unemployment rate about: everyone, or people who want work?
A student who is not looking for work is not failing to find a job. Should the rate count them?

acceptedIdeas: It shows how many people trying to work are not finding jobs, so people not looking are left out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It shows how many people trying to work are not finding jobs, so people not looking are left out

choices.label: It makes the rate smaller, which is how the ABS keeps the headline figure from alarming people
The ABS has no information about people outside the labour force, so they cannot be counted at all
It shows how many people trying to work are not finding jobs, so people not looking are left out

questions.onCorrect: The rate describes people who are trying to work. A retiree or a full-time student who isn't looking is not part of that, so the denominator is the labour force.

misconceptions.feedback: The choice of denominator comes from what the rate is meant to show. The ABS defines it as the number of unemployed people as a share of the labour force.
The survey sorts everyone aged 15 and over into three groups, including those outside the labour force, and the participation rate uses them.

questions.prompt: The ABS sorts everyone aged 15 and over into three groups from what they did in a reference week. Where does each of these six people belong?
hints: Check each person against three tests: did they work an hour for pay, did they look in the past four weeks, and could they start?
A person who is waiting to start a job within four weeks, and could have started, is treated as looking.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Employed: the two hours of babysitting and the cafe worker who wants 30 hours. Unemployed: the person who applied for three jobs and the person with a job starting in two weeks. Not in the labour force: the full-time student and the person who stopped looking.

items.label: Worked two hours of paid babysitting last week
items.explanation: The ABS test for employment is one hour or more of paid work in the reference week.

items.label: Works 12 hours a week at a cafe and wants 30
items.explanation: A person with a job is employed. Wanting more hours makes them underemployed, which is a separate measure.

items.label: Has no job, applied for three jobs this month and could start next week
items.explanation: No job, actively looked in the past four weeks and available to start: all three tests are met.

items.label: Has accepted a job that starts in two weeks and could have started last week
items.explanation: The ABS counts a person waiting to start a job within four weeks, and able to have started, as unemployed.

items.label: Is studying full time and is not looking for work
items.explanation: With no job and no job search, the person is outside the labour force.

items.label: Looked for a year, stopped looking, and would take a job tomorrow
items.explanation: Not looking means not unemployed by the ABS test. The RBA calls this hidden unemployment.

questions.onCorrect: A job of one hour or more makes a person employed, and looking while available makes a person unemployed. Everyone else is outside the labour force.

questions.prompt: Now compare the new unemployment rate with the earlier 5.3%. Which way did it move?
hints: Work out the new number unemployed and the new size of the labour force.
Put the first over the second, and compare with 5.3%.

acceptedIdeas: It rose with no job lost, because the labour force grew along with the unemployed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rose with no job lost, because the labour force grew along with the unemployed

choices.label: It rose with no job lost, because the labour force grew along with the unemployed
It stayed at 5.3%, because employment is unchanged and no jobs were lost, so the rate cannot move
It fell, because the labour force is larger now and a larger base always lowers any rate
It cannot be known without counting how many jobs are vacant, which the rate depends on

questions.onCorrect: The extra jobseekers raise both the numerator and the denominator, and the rate rises from 5.3% to 6.0%. Participation rises too, from 66.5% to 67.0%.

misconceptions.feedback: The rate has two parts. The number unemployed rose from 0.7 to 0.8 million and the labour force from 13.3 to 13.4 million, so the share moved.
A larger labour force lowers the rate only if the number unemployed stays put. Here the unemployed rose by the same 0.1 million that the labour force did.
The rate needs only the number unemployed and the size of the labour force, and both are given.

questions.prompt: This is how the RBA describes the effect of JobKeeper in 2020. What does it imply about reading that year's unemployment rate?
hints: Read the second sentence of the extract. Were employees on the subsidy counted as unemployed?
The first sentence says what the rate would have done without the subsidy. Was the rate higher or lower because of it?

acceptedIdeas: The rate left out some lost work, because employees kept on the subsidy with no hours were not counted as unemployed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rate left out some lost work, because employees kept on the subsidy with no hours were not counted as unemployed

choices.label: The rate overstated the damage, because employees kept on the subsidy with no hours were counted as unemployed
The rate was unaffected, because the survey records only hours worked and ignores any link to an employer
The rate showed the damage in full, because everyone who worked no hours was counted as out of work
The rate left out some lost work, because employees kept on the subsidy with no hours were not counted as unemployed

extracts.text: The unemployment rate would have increased by even more had it not been for the JobKeeper Payment and the way that the unemployment rate is measured. The JobKeeper Payment was a wage subsidy paid by the Australian Government to eligible employers to help them keep their employees; even if these employees did not work any hours, they were not counted as unemployed because they were still connected to their employer.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Explainer "The COVID-19 Pandemic, 2020 to 2021" (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: An explainer published by the central bank for the public

questions.onCorrect: The unemployment rate follows rules about looking and being connected to a job, so a large fall in hours can sit behind a smaller rise in the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says the reverse. These employees were not counted as unemployed, so the rate would have been higher without the subsidy.
The unemployment tests ask whether a person has a job and is looking. A link to an employer mattered, which is why the RBA says the rate would have risen by more.
A person with no hours was still not unemployed if connected to an employer, so the rate did not show the whole fall in work.

questions.prompt: The same ABS table gives the October fall in the participation rate as 0.2 points, with a 95% confidence interval of -0.4 to 0.0 points. A headline says "Australians are giving up looking for work." What is the best reading?
hints: Does the interval -0.4 to 0.0 rule out a change of exactly nothing?
Ask whether one month with this much uncertainty would be enough to name a reason.

acceptedIdeas: A fall is likely but could be nil, so one month is thin evidence that people are giving up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fall is likely but could be nil, so one month is thin evidence that people are giving up

choices.label: The fall is certain, because the whole interval sits at or below zero and so shows a decline
Nothing can be learned from it, because the results of a sample survey are never reliable
A fall is likely but could be nil, so one month is thin evidence that people are giving up
The headline is right, because falling participation always means people have given up

questions.onCorrect: The interval leans towards a fall but reaches zero, so one month is weak evidence. A run of months is better evidence than any single figure.

misconceptions.feedback: An interval that ends at 0.0 still allows a change of nothing. About one chance in twenty is left for values outside it, so a fall is likely and not certain.
The interval is the survey's own statement of its reliability. It tells you the likely range, and here the range leans towards a small fall.
A fall in participation can have other causes, such as retirements, and one month with an interval touching zero cannot say which.

questions.prompt: In the ABS series the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate read 4.1% in January 2024, 3.7% in February, 3.9% in March and 4.1% in April, while the trend rate sat at 3.9% to 4.0% throughout. A commentator says unemployment fell sharply in February and rebounded by April. What is the best reading?
hints: Compare the size of the monthly swings with how far the trend moved.
The ABS says which series gives the best measure of underlying behaviour. Which is it?

acceptedIdeas: Most of the dip and rebound is month-to-month noise, because the trend barely moved over the same months
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of the dip and rebound is month-to-month noise, because the trend barely moved over the same months

choices.label: Unemployment really fell 0.4 points in a month and then rebounded, since the adjusted series is the accurate one
Most of the dip and rebound is month-to-month noise, because the trend barely moved over the same months
The trend series must be wrong, because it fails to show the dip that the adjusted series records
The two series conflict, which means the ABS has made an error in one of them

questions.onCorrect: A fall and rebound inside a few months with a flat trend is what sampling noise looks like. The ABS recommends caution with short-term changes and says trend is the best guide.

misconceptions.feedback: A swing that large in one month doesn't show up in the trend, which stayed near 4.0%. The ABS advises caution with short-term changes.
The trend is built to leave out month-to-month variability, so not showing the dip is what it is for.
The series differ because they are meant to. The adjusted series keeps each month's variation and the trend smooths it away.

questions.prompt: In October 2026 the unemployment rate rose 0.1 points to 4.9% and the underemployment rate fell 0.1 points to 6.2%, while the underutilisation rate stayed at 11.1% (seasonally adjusted). What explains the unchanged underutilisation rate?
hints: The underutilisation rate adds two groups together. Which two?
Check which way each group moved in October, and whether the moves cancel.

acceptedIdeas: The rise in the unemployed was roughly offset by a fall in the underemployed, and underutilisation adds the two
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rise in the unemployed was roughly offset by a fall in the underemployed, and underutilisation adds the two

choices.label: Underutilisation counts only people without jobs, so a fall in underemployment cannot move it
The two rates always move in opposite directions by the same amount, so their total never changes
The rise in the unemployed was roughly offset by a fall in the underemployed, and underutilisation adds the two
The ABS publishes underutilisation as a trend measure, so it is not recalculated each month

questions.onCorrect: Underutilisation is the unemployed plus the underemployed as a share of the labour force, so a rise in one and a fall in the other can leave the total where it was.

misconceptions.feedback: Underutilisation is the unemployed plus the underemployed, as a share of the labour force, so a fall in either part moves it.
They move independently, and in other months both can rise or both can fall. In October a small rise in one matched a small fall in the other.
The October release gives underutilisation in seasonally adjusted terms, recalculated each month, and says it remained at 11.1%.

questions.prompt: A monthly release shows an unchanged unemployment rate and an underemployment rate up half a point (invented figures). A commentator says the labour market did not change. What is the better reading?
hints: Underemployed people have jobs but want more hours. What does a rise in their share say about how much work is on offer?
The unemployment rate counts only one group. Is it the only group that matters for the labour market?

acceptedIdeas: It looks weaker, because more people in work want hours they cannot get, though no more are jobless
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It looks weaker, because more people in work want hours they cannot get, though no more are jobless

choices.label: Nothing changed, because people who are underemployed have jobs and so sit outside every measure of weakness
Unemployment must really have risen, because underemployment is unemployment that the ABS counts later
It improved, because a higher underemployment rate means more people have found jobs
It looks weaker, because more people in work want hours they cannot get, though no more are jobless

questions.onCorrect: The RBA reads a higher underemployment rate as a sign of weaker labour demand. A single measure can stay still while another shows a change.

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA treats a high underemployment rate as a sign that labour demand is weak against supply. Having a job doesn't mean getting enough hours.
Underemployed people are employed, and the ABS counts them in a separate measure at the same time as it counts the unemployed.
A higher underemployment rate means more people in work want more hours. It says nothing about people finding jobs.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants to know what share of everyone aged 15 and over is either working or looking for work. Which ABS rate answers that?
hints: The question counts both people who have jobs and people who are looking. Which group is that?
The rate compares that group with the whole working-age population.

acceptedIdeas: participation rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The participation rate: the share of the working-age population that is in the labour force.

questions.onCorrect: The participation rate is the labour force, the employed plus the unemployed, as a percentage of the population aged 15 and over.

misconceptions.feedback: The employment-to-population ratio counts only people with jobs. This question also includes people looking for work.
The unemployment rate is the unemployed as a share of the labour force. It says nothing about how much of the population is in the labour market.
Those two measures describe people whose time is not fully used. The question is about how many are in the labour market at all.

questions.prompt: A news site headlines this release "Inflation 0.8%". Why is that a poor comparison with the RBA's target of 2 to 3 per cent?
hints: The target is stated for a particular length of time. Which one?
Look in the extract for the figure that covers the same length of time as the target.

acceptedIdeas: The target is an annual rate and 0.8% is one month's change, while the 12-month figure was 4.3%
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The target is an annual rate and 0.8% is one month's change, while the 12-month figure was 4.3%

choices.label: The monthly figure is always revised away later, so it cannot be set against any target
The target applies only to the trimmed mean, so the monthly CPI figure is the wrong series altogether
The target is an annual rate and 0.8% is one month's change, while the 12-month figure was 4.3%
The figure of 0.8% already sits below the 2 to 3 per cent band, so there is nothing to compare here

extracts.text: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 4.3%, up from 4.0% in the 12 months to August 2026. Trimmed mean inflation was 3.6%, up from a revised 3.5% in the 12 months to August 2026. In the month of September, the CPI rose 0.8% in original and 0.6% in seasonally adjusted terms.
extracts.who: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Consumer Price Index, Australia (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A statistical agency's key statistics for the month, written for the general public

questions.onCorrect: The target is for annual CPI inflation, so the 12-month figure of 4.3% is the one to hold against it. A month's change shows only how prices moved since the month before.

misconceptions.feedback: Monthly figures are published and used. The trouble is the period they cover: a month's change is not an annual rate.
The RBA's target is for annual CPI inflation, the headline figure. The trimmed mean is a second measure the RBA watches beside it.
Comparing 0.8% with the band mixes a month with a year. Over the 12 months the CPI rose 4.3%, which is above the band.

questions.prompt: Why isn't the basket's inflation just the plain average of 2.5% and 4.7%?
hints: Think about which item a typical household spends more money on, books or childcare.
If one item takes up most of the spending, should its price change count the same as the other's?

acceptedIdeas: Households spend more on childcare, so its price change should count for more in the basket
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Households spend more on childcare, so its price change should count for more in the basket

choices.label: Households spend more on childcare, so its price change should count for more in the basket
Averages of percentages are never allowed, so the ABS has to use a different method
Books are cheap, so the ABS leaves them out of the basket once their price changes by under 3%
The plain average would round to 4%, and the ABS always reports whole numbers for the CPI

questions.onCorrect: The CPI weights each item by how much households spend on it, so a big spending item has more say. Here childcare's 73% share lifts the basket to 4.1%.

misconceptions.feedback: Averages of percentages are fine. A plain average gives each item equal say, and the basket is meant to follow what households actually spend.
The ABS has no such rule, and books stay in the basket with a small weight. The weights come from how much households spend on each item.
The ABS reports the CPI to one decimal place, as the 4.3% for September shows, and the issue here is weighting and not rounding.

questions.prompt: The ABS reports annual headline CPI inflation of 4.3% and trimmed mean inflation of 3.6% for September 2026. What does the gap suggest?
hints: The trimmed mean sets aside the items with the largest price changes. If headline is higher, what kind of items might be in the part set aside?
Compare 3.6% with the top of the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent target range.

acceptedIdeas: A few very large rises lift headline above underlying, and even the 3.6% is still above the target
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A few very large rises lift headline above underlying, and even the 3.6% is still above the target

choices.label: Trimmed mean is the accurate figure and headline is wrong, so inflation is 3.6% and the gap is a mistake
Underlying inflation is back inside the 2 to 3 per cent band, so the pressure on prices has passed
Inflation is falling, because the trimmed mean is the lower figure and the lower figure is the trend
A few very large rises lift headline above underlying, and even the 3.6% is still above the target

questions.onCorrect: Headline counts every price, so a few very large rises can lift it above underlying. The trimmed mean at 3.6% still sits above 3%, so broad pressure remains.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither is wrong. Headline measures all prices, and the trimmed mean sets aside the largest movers, so the two answer different questions.
At 3.6% the trimmed mean is above the top of the band. The lower figure shows less pressure than headline, not none.
A gap between two measures at one date says nothing about direction. Both rose from August, headline from 4.0% to 4.3% and trimmed mean from 3.5% to 3.6%.

questions.prompt: Which measure would have registered that jump in banana prices most fully in the month it happened?
hints: Which of the measures sets the largest price changes aside, and which does not?
An item's weight decides how much of a jump reaches headline CPI. What would a jump in one fruit's price do to the whole basket?

acceptedIdeas: Headline CPI, because it includes every item in the basket, bananas at their weight
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Headline CPI, because it includes every item in the basket, bananas at their weight

choices.label: The trimmed mean, because it gives the items with the largest price changes the most weight
Headline CPI, because it includes every item in the basket, bananas at their weight
The weighted median, because it follows the item whose price changed by the most
All three equally, because each is built from the same prices collected by the ABS

extracts.text: Supply disruptions because of unusual weather: For example, in 2006 Tropical Cyclone Larry destroyed banana crops in Queensland. As a result of this significant reduction in supply, the price of bananas temporarily increased by 400 per cent.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Explainer "Inflation and its Measurement" (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: An explainer published by the central bank for the public

questions.onCorrect: Headline CPI includes every item, so the jump reaches it in proportion to bananas' weight. The trimmed mean and the weighted median are built to see past a one-item change like this.

misconceptions.feedback: The trimmed mean does the opposite. It ranks items by price change and sets the largest ones aside, so a one-item jump barely moves it.
The weighted median is the change of the item in the middle of the ranking, so an extreme item at the top has almost no effect on it.
They start from the same prices but treat the largest changes differently. Headline includes them in full and the two underlying measures set them aside.

questions.prompt: The ABS says electricity prices rose 12.8% over the 12 months to September 2026, largely because Commonwealth electricity rebates ended during the year. How does the RBA's approach treat a change like this?
hints: Ask whether the rise is spread across many items or sits in one category with a stated cause.
The RBA looks through temporary changes in inflation. Does this rise look like a sign of a shift in broad conditions?

acceptedIdeas: As a step in one category with a known cause, which lifts the annual figure without showing broad pressure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a step in one category with a known cause, which lifts the annual figure without showing broad pressure

choices.label: As a step in one category with a known cause, which lifts the annual figure without showing broad pressure
As proof that demand is overheating, because a 12.8% rise in one price must reflect excess demand
As irrelevant to inflation, because prices set by government are not part of the CPI
As a reason to raise the cash rate on its own, because any large price rise must be offset by higher rates

questions.onCorrect: The rebate ending lifts one category's price, and so the annual figure, for a time. The RBA looks for broad and persistent price rises before it responds.

misconceptions.feedback: A rise in one category with a known cause says little about demand. Overheating shows up as price rises across a broad range of items.
Electricity prices are in the CPI, and the ABS reports them under housing. The CPI measures the prices households pay, whoever sets them.
The RBA separates temporary changes from persistent ones and looks through temporary ones. One category's step doesn't call for a response on its own.

questions.prompt: In the month of September 2026 the ABS reports recreation and culture up 3.8%. It attributes the rise to strong demand over the school holidays and major sporting events, with domestic holiday travel and accommodation up 8.0%. How should a reader treat that rise?
hints: Does the ABS give a specific, short-lived reason for the rise? What is it?
Compare how widely the rise is spread across the groups of the CPI.

acceptedIdeas: As a temporary change tied to the school holidays, which the RBA would look through unless it lasts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a temporary change tied to the school holidays, which the RBA would look through unless it lasts

choices.label: As evidence that the whole economy is overheating, because prices rose 3.8% in just a single month
As unimportant, because the CPI counts only annual changes and monthly figures are then discarded
As a temporary change tied to the school holidays, which the RBA would look through unless it lasts
As a reason to cut the cash rate, because holiday spending is the part of inflation that rates control

questions.onCorrect: A rise in one group with a short-lived cause, such as school holidays, is a temporary change. The RBA looks through temporary changes and watches for persistent, broad ones.

misconceptions.feedback: One group in one month, with a stated reason, is a narrow signal. The RBA looks for rises across many items that persist.
The ABS publishes the CPI monthly and the annual figure is built from monthly data. A monthly change is still evidence, but a narrow one.
Nothing in the release links the rise to anything a cash rate change controls, and a rise tied to the school holidays is the kind the RBA looks through.

questions.prompt: In the ABS series headline inflation was 4.6% and the trimmed mean 3.3% in March 2026, and headline was 1.9% and the trimmed mean 2.8% in June 2025. What does that pattern show?
hints: In which of the two dates was headline higher than the trimmed mean, and in which was it lower?
Think about which items the trimmed mean sets aside. Could they be price falls as well as rises?

acceptedIdeas: The gap can run either way, because very large price changes can push headline above or below underlying
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gap can run either way, because very large price changes can push headline above or below underlying

choices.label: Headline always runs above the trimmed mean, so the June 2025 figures must contain an error
The trimmed mean is the better figure, because it moved much less than headline did between the two dates
The two measures should be equal, so any gap between them means the ABS has miscounted
The gap can run either way, because very large price changes can push headline above or below underlying

questions.onCorrect: In March 2026 headline was 1.3 points above the trimmed mean and in June 2025 it was 0.9 points below. Large movers in either direction pull headline away from underlying.

misconceptions.feedback: Headline was below the trimmed mean in June 2025, and nothing says that is an error. Large falls in some prices can pull headline down.
Moving less doesn't make it better. It answers a different question, and the RBA watches both.
The measures are built differently, so they differ in most months. The size and sign of the gap carry information.

questions.prompt: The ABS builds the trimmed mean from the price changes of all 87 items in the CPI basket. Put the steps in order.
hints: The trimming can't happen until the items have a position in a ranking.
The average comes last, because it is taken over what remains.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: First each item's price change is worked out, then the items are ranked, then the largest and smallest are set aside, and last the middle 70 per cent of items are averaged, weighted by spending.

items: Work out each item's price change over the month
Rank the items from the smallest change to the largest
Set aside the items at both ends of the ranking
Average the price changes of the middle 70 per cent of the basket, using spending weights

questions.onCorrect: Each step needs the one before it: the changes give a ranking, the ranking shows what to set aside, and what remains is averaged.

questions.prompt: A table shows CPI index numbers of 130 for bus fares and 155 for haircuts (invented figures). A friend says that proves a haircut costs more than a bus fare. What is wrong with that?
hints: An index number sets a base period at 100. What does 155 say about haircuts?
Does a number measured from each item's own base tell you what a haircut costs against a bus fare?

acceptedIdeas: An index shows how far each price has risen from its base, not which item costs more today
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An index shows how far each price has risen from its base, not which item costs more today

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, because a higher index number always means a higher price in dollars
The index covers capital cities only, so it cannot be used to compare haircuts with bus fares here
An index shows how far each price has risen from its base, not which item costs more today
Haircuts are in the CPI basket and bus fares are not, so the two index numbers cannot be compared

questions.onCorrect: An index shows how much a price has risen since its base period. Haircuts have risen more than bus fares since then, but the index says nothing about which costs more today.

misconceptions.feedback: An index number is a price relative to a base period, so two items' numbers can't be compared as prices. They show only how much each has risen.
Coverage is a real limit of the CPI, but it isn't what is wrong here. The problem is reading index numbers as price levels.
Both are in the basket. The difficulty is that each index number is measured against its own base, so it shows a rise and not a price.

questions.prompt: Two towns both see prices rise about 5% in a year (invented). In town A shops are busy and employers cannot find staff. In town B shops are quiet and some employers are laying staff off. Which statement is best supported?
hints: Think about what strong demand does to sales and hiring, and what dearer inputs do.
Ask whether output and jobs are moving in the same direction as prices in each town.

acceptedIdeas: Demand looks the likelier driver in town A, and rising costs the likelier driver in town B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Demand looks the likelier driver in town A, and rising costs the likelier driver in town B

choices.label: Both towns have the same cause, because the same 5% rise in prices points to the same cause
Costs look the likelier driver in town A and demand in town B, because busy shops face dearer inputs
Demand looks the likelier driver in town A, and rising costs the likelier driver in town B
Nothing can be said about either town, because a price rise does not say anything about its cause

questions.onCorrect: Rising prices with strong sales and hiring suggest demand pressing on capacity. Rising prices with weak sales and layoffs suggest a fall in supply from higher costs.

misconceptions.feedback: The same price rise can have different causes. What separates them is what happens to output and jobs alongside prices.
Busy shops and scarce staff are signs of strong demand. Quiet shops and layoffs alongside rising prices point to costs.
A price rise alone doesn't, but the evidence around it does. Output and jobs moving with prices suggest demand, and moving against them suggest costs.

questions.prompt: The RBA notes that major cyclones and floods can damage large volumes of crops and so raise the price of processed food and meals out for a time. Which cause of inflation is that, and what happens to the output of the affected goods?
hints: Did the event raise demand, or did it cut what could be supplied?
When supply of a good falls, what happens to how much of it is produced?

acceptedIdeas: Cost-push, because supply of the affected goods falls, so prices rise while their output falls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cost-push, because supply of the affected goods falls, so prices rise while their output falls

choices.label: Cost-push, because supply of the affected goods falls, so prices rise while their output falls
Demand-pull, because shoppers rush to buy, so prices and output of the affected goods both rise
Expectations, because people expect dearer food and the expectation alone raises prices
None of the three, because weather lies outside what the RBA counts as a cause of inflation

questions.onCorrect: A disruption that cuts supply is cost-push. Prices rise and output of the affected goods falls, and the RBA calls such periods temporary.

misconceptions.feedback: Demand has not risen. The crop damage cuts supply, which is why prices rise while less of the affected goods is produced.
Expectations can reinforce a price rise, but here the price rise starts from damaged supply. The RBA classes it as cost-push.
The RBA names supply disruptions from unusual weather or natural disasters as a source of cost-push inflation.

questions.prompt: These items quote the Monetary Policy Board's statements of September and November 2026. Which cause of inflation does each one describe?
hints: Ask of each sentence whether it is about spending pressing on capacity, the cost of inputs, or beliefs about future prices.
Capacity is what the economy can produce, so pressure on it means demand is strong against supply.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Demand-pull: the two items about pressure on domestic capacity. Cost-push: the oil supply disruptions and firms raising prices because of cost pressures. Expectations: the two items about inflation expectations.

items.label: 29 September: the Board says "there remains pressure on domestic capacity".
items.explanation: Capacity pressure is demand pressing on what the economy can sustainably produce, which is the RBA's demand-pull case.

items.label: 3 November: domestic capacity pressures are judged to be "a little tighter than earlier thought".
items.explanation: Tighter capacity means demand is pressing harder on supply, so it belongs with demand-pull.

items.label: 29 September: global oil supply disruptions keep up the "pressure on global and domestic energy prices".
items.explanation: Dearer energy raises the cost of producing and moving goods, which is cost-push.

items.label: 3 November: liaison with firms finds many "experiencing cost pressures" and either raising their prices in response or planning to.
items.explanation: Firms raising prices because their costs rose is the RBA's description of cost-push.

items.label: 29 September: of the measures of inflation expectations, the short-term ones "remain elevated".
items.explanation: Expectations are what households and firms believe about future prices, and measures of them are the evidence.

items.label: 3 November: there are "upside risks to inflation expectations", with some measures judged to have risen lately.
items.explanation: The item is about beliefs regarding future prices, which makes it an expectations point.

questions.onCorrect: Each sentence is about one cause: demand against capacity, the cost of inputs, or beliefs about future prices.

questions.prompt: In June 2026 the Board linked an oil price shock to slowing demand. Why would a decision about interest rates matter for a price rise that began in the oil market?
hints: The Board says it wants to stop inflation becoming embedded. What does embedded mean for later prices and wages?
A cash rate decision acts on spending, not on the cost of oil. How could slower spending help?

acceptedIdeas: Rates cannot lower oil prices, but slower demand makes it harder for the rise to spread into prices
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rates cannot lower oil prices, but slower demand makes it harder for the rise to spread into prices

choices.label: Higher rates lower the world price of oil, because Australian demand for fuel falls enough to move it
Rates cannot lower oil prices, but slower demand makes it harder for the rise to spread into prices
The Board ignores supply shocks by rule, so the statement was only a comment on the oil market
Higher rates cut what importers pay for fuel, so the price at the pump falls as a direct result

extracts.text: The Board remains focused on ensuring that inflation does not become embedded once the impulse from higher oil prices has passed through. To achieve this, growth in demand needs to slow to reduce capacity pressures and help bring inflation back to target.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement by the Monetary Policy Board (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A media release giving the Board's decision and reasons

questions.onCorrect: The oil price rise itself is outside the Board's reach. Slower demand reduces capacity pressure and makes it harder for firms to pass costs on and for expectations to rise.

misconceptions.feedback: The Board's statements describe the oil price rise as a global supply matter, so Australian interest rates don't set it. The aim is to stop the rise spreading.
The statement says what the Board is focused on, which is stopping inflation from becoming embedded. It doesn't follow a rule of ignoring supply shocks.
Rates don't change what fuel costs to import. They work through demand, which affects whether firms can pass costs on and whether wages chase prices.

questions.prompt: A firm's wage bill per worker rises 4% over a year, and each worker produces 4% more (invented figures). According to the RBA, what happens to the labour cost of each unit it sells?
hints: Cost per unit depends on the wage per worker and on how much each worker produces.
If both rise by the same proportion, what happens to the cost of labour in each unit?

acceptedIdeas: It does not rise, because labour cost per unit rises only when wages outgrow productivity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It does not rise, because labour cost per unit rises only when wages outgrow productivity

choices.label: It rises by 4%, because every wage rise is passed straight into the cost of each unit sold
It falls by 4%, because higher productivity always lowers the cost of each unit it sells
It cannot be judged without knowing the cash rate, because the cash rate sets labour costs
It does not rise, because labour cost per unit rises only when wages outgrow productivity

questions.onCorrect: Labour cost per unit follows wages divided by output per worker. Equal growth in the two leaves it unchanged, and it rises only when wages outrun productivity.

misconceptions.feedback: A wage rise raises cost per unit only if output per worker doesn't keep pace. Here output per worker rose by the same 4%.
Productivity growth lowers cost per unit only when it outpaces wages. Here the two are equal, so the cost per unit holds steady.
The cash rate does not set a firm's labour cost. The RBA says it depends on wage growth and the productivity of labour.

questions.prompt: The RBA wrote this in November 2026. What is the inference it draws about the economy's capacity?
hints: If growth slows and unemployment rises but inflation stays high, was the economy's capacity larger or smaller than thought?
Which option still treats unemployment and growth as evidence about capacity?

acceptedIdeas: Capacity is tighter than it had judged, because demand is still pressing on supply while growth slows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Capacity is tighter than it had judged, because demand is still pressing on supply while growth slows

choices.label: The oil price shock alone explains why inflation has lasted this long, so capacity is not in question
Capacity is tighter than it had judged, because demand is still pressing on supply while growth slows
Inflation expectations have fallen, so the price rises that remain are temporary and no concern
Unemployment has no link to inflation, so its rise can be ignored when judging capacity

extracts.text: The persistence of high inflation and cost pressures, despite the easing in GDP growth and the rise in unemployment, suggests that domestic capacity constraints have been tighter than previously assessed.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026: Overview (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The RBA's quarterly assessment of the economy and its outlook

questions.onCorrect: Slower growth and higher unemployment would normally ease inflation. When it persists, the likelier reading is that capacity was tighter than thought.

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says cost pressures persisted along with high inflation, and that the persistence points to tighter capacity, so it doesn't put it all on oil.
The extract says nothing of expectations falling. The Board's November statement reports some measures of expectations as having risen.
The RBA uses unemployment as evidence about capacity, and a rise in it while inflation persists is part of the reasoning.

questions.prompt: After a large rise in fuel prices, surveys show households and firms still expect inflation to settle back inside the 2 to 3 per cent range within a couple of years (invented). What does the RBA call expectations that behave this way?
hints: The word the RBA uses suggests something held firmly in place.
The opposite word describes expectations that drift away from the target.

acceptedIdeas: anchored
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Anchored: expectations stay tied to the target after a spike.

questions.onCorrect: Expectations that stay tied to the target whatever current inflation does are anchored, so a spike from a cost shock is likely to fade.

misconceptions.feedback: Unanchored expectations move away from the target after a spike. In this case people still expect inflation to return to the range.
Embedded describes inflation that has become built into prices and wages. The question asks about the expectations, which are tied to the target.

questions.prompt: Fuel prices jump, but surveys show expectations of inflation two years ahead unchanged near the middle of the target range, and firms report little pass-through to other prices (invented). What does the RBA say the Board may be more likely to do?
hints: Which of the three causes of inflation is steady in this case?
The RBA says expectations are the main consideration when a supply shock hits. What do steady expectations imply for the response?

acceptedIdeas: Look through the shock and wait, because inflation should come back down once the shock has passed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Look through the shock and wait, because inflation should come back down once the shock has passed

choices.label: Raise the cash rate by a large amount, because any supply shock must be met with higher rates
Cut the cash rate to offset the dearer fuel, because lower rates reduce the cost of fuel
Look through the shock and wait, because inflation should come back down once the shock has passed
Take no interest in the shock, because prices that rise for one reason are outside its mandate

questions.onCorrect: If expectations stay steady after a supply shock, the Board may be more likely to look through it. If they rise, it may need to raise the cash rate to bring them back down.

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says the response turns on expectations. If they stay steady, the Board is more likely to look through the shock.
Rates don't set the cost of fuel. With expectations steady, the likelier course is to look through the shock, not to add stimulus.
The Board does watch the shock, because it could push up expectations. It is likelier to look through it when expectations remain steady.

questions.prompt: A worker's pay rose 3.5% over the 12 months to September 2026 (an invented figure), and the ABS reports that consumer prices rose 4.3% over the same months. The employer says the rise is above the top of the RBA's target range. What happened to the worker's purchasing power?
hints: Compare the pay rise with the rise in prices over the same period.
Does the target range say what prices did to this worker over the past year?

acceptedIdeas: It fell a little, because prices rose by more than her pay over the year
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It fell a little, because prices rose by more than her pay over the year

choices.label: It rose, because 3.5% is above the top of the RBA's range of 2 to 3 per cent
It rose by 3.5%, because that is the size of the pay rise she was given
It fell a little, because prices rose by more than her pay over the year
It stayed the same, because both her pay and prices went up over the year

questions.onCorrect: Purchasing power moves with pay less inflation. A rise of 3.5% against inflation of 4.3% leaves her able to buy a little less than a year earlier.

misconceptions.feedback: The target range describes what the RBA aims for on average. What matters for her pay is how much prices actually rose, which was 4.3%.
A 3.5% rise in dollars buys 3.5% more only if prices stay still. Here prices rose 4.3%, which takes more than the whole rise away.
Two rises cancel only if they are the same size. Her pay rose by less than prices did, so what she can buy fell.

questions.prompt: Why is the inflation rate subtracted from the pay rise to find the change in purchasing power?
hints: The pay rise is measured in dollars. What does a rise in prices do to what each dollar buys?
If prices rose by exactly as much as pay, would the worker be able to buy more?

acceptedIdeas: Pay growth is in dollars, and inflation shows how much of that growth dearer prices use up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pay growth is in dollars, and inflation shows how much of that growth dearer prices use up

choices.label: Inflation is a charge that the Government takes from every pay rise before it reaches the worker
Pay growth is in dollars, and inflation shows how much of that growth dearer prices use up
The ABS publishes only real pay, so nominal pay has to be corrected before comparing it

questions.onCorrect: A nominal pay rise buys more only to the extent that it outruns prices. Taking inflation off the pay rise gives the change in what the pay can buy.

misconceptions.feedback: Inflation isn't a charge or a tax. It is a rise in prices, which means each dollar buys less.
Pay is reported in dollars at the prices of the time. The comparison with inflation is what turns it into a real figure.

questions.prompt: Each of these is a cost the RBA attaches to inflation that is too high or to inflation that is too low. Which is which?
hints: Ask whether each case would be worse or better if prices were rising faster, then whether it would be worse if they were hardly rising at all.
Expected price falls and the difficulty of cutting real pay belong with very low inflation.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Too high: the bakery repricing monthly, the fridge bought early and the deposit that buys less. Too low: shoppers waiting for lower prices, the factory unable to cut real pay and the central bank unable to push real rates below zero.

items.label: A bakery reprints its price list every month, and customers compare three shops before buying
items.explanation: Businesses need to update prices more often and shoppers spend more time comparing them, which the RBA lists as a cost of high inflation.

items.label: A family buys a fridge this month because they expect it to cost more by Christmas
items.explanation: Expecting higher prices can pull purchases forward, which distorts spending decisions.

items.label: An investor finds that the interest on a fixed deposit buys less than she expected
items.explanation: Higher inflation reduces the real return on an investment.

items.label: Shoppers hold off buying a laptop because prices have been falling and they expect more falls
items.explanation: Expected falls in prices can delay purchases and lower spending.

items.label: A struggling factory can only cut its workers' real pay by cutting their dollar pay, so it lays off staff
items.explanation: With very low inflation there is little room to cut real wages through slow nominal growth, so firms may cut jobs instead.

items.label: In a deep downturn the central bank would like real interest rates below zero and cannot get there
items.explanation: A very low inflation target makes it harder to push real interest rates below zero.

questions.onCorrect: Each cost comes from prices rising too quickly, or too slowly to leave room for adjustment.

questions.prompt: A household agreed a fixed-rate loan expecting about 2.5% inflation. Inflation then runs well above that for several years. Who is better off than they expected?
hints: The loan fixes the dollars to be repaid. What happens to what those dollars buy if prices rise faster than expected?
Think about the borrower and the lender separately. Which one repays and which one receives?

acceptedIdeas: The borrower, who repays in dollars that buy less than was expected
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The borrower, who repays in dollars that buy less than was expected

choices.label: The lender, who collects more dollars in interest than was expected
Neither, because a fixed rate fixes the real value of the loan as well
Both, because prices rose and each side's income rose along with them
The borrower, who repays in dollars that buy less than was expected

questions.onCorrect: A fixed repayment is worth less in real terms when prices rise faster than expected. The borrower gains and the lender receives less purchasing power than planned.

misconceptions.feedback: The dollars of interest are fixed by the loan, so the lender collects what was agreed. Prices rose, so those dollars buy less than the lender planned.
A fixed rate fixes the dollar amounts only. Their real value depends on inflation, so it moved.
Incomes may not keep pace, and the loan terms are fixed in dollars, so the gain falls on one side and the loss on the other.

questions.prompt: A commentator says zero inflation is the obvious target, since only prices that never change treat everyone fairly. Which reply fits the RBA's reasoning best?
hints: The RBA's reasons concern what monetary policy and firms can do when inflation is very low. What are they?
The CPI uses a fixed basket. Does that make it overstate or understate price rises?

acceptedIdeas: At zero there is little room to cut real rates or real wages, and the CPI overstates inflation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At zero there is little room to cut real rates or real wages, and the CPI overstates inflation

choices.label: Zero inflation cannot be measured, because the CPI is only defined for positive rates of inflation
At zero there is little room to cut real rates or real wages, and the CPI overstates inflation
Prices should always rise, because falling prices are always a sign that an economy is failing
The Government prefers some inflation, because it reduces what the Government owes to lenders

questions.onCorrect: Near zero, policy and firms have little room to cut real interest rates or real wages. The fixed basket also makes the CPI overstate inflation a little, so the target has to allow for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The CPI can show zero or negative inflation, and falling prices are a recognised case that the RBA discusses. Measurement is not the problem.
The RBA doesn't say falling prices always signal failure. It says expected falls can delay spending, which is a risk of very low inflation.
The RBA gives no such reason. Its reasons concern the room for policy and wages to adjust, and the CPI's upward bias.

questions.prompt: Two retirees each receive $1,000 a fortnight. Inflation then rises to 4.3% for a year. One pension is indexed to prices and the other is not (invented). What happens to their purchasing power over the year?
hints: Indexation adjusts a payment when prices change. What does that do to what it buys?
For the unindexed pension, ask how many goods $1,000 buys after prices rise 4.3%.

acceptedIdeas: The indexed pension keeps its purchasing power, and the unindexed one buys less
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The indexed pension keeps its purchasing power, and the unindexed one buys less

choices.label: Both lose about the same, because inflation reduces the buying power of every dollar alike
Neither loses, because the dollar amount of each pension stays the same or rises
The indexed pension keeps its purchasing power, and the unindexed one buys less
Only the indexed pension loses, because indexation makes it fall when prices rise

questions.onCorrect: An unindexed pension buys less after a year of 4.3% inflation, while an indexed pension is adjusted with prices. Fixed nominal incomes lose when inflation is higher than expected.

misconceptions.feedback: An indexed pension is adjusted with prices, so it keeps pace and doesn't lose. The unindexed one stays at $1,000 and buys less.
The dollar amount staying the same is the loss. At 4.3% inflation the same $1,000 buys less.
Indexation moves a pension up with prices, not down. It protects the retiree against inflation.

questions.prompt: Worker A's pay rises 5% in a year when prices rise 6%. Worker B's pay is frozen in a year when prices rise 2% (invented figures). Whose purchasing power fell by more?
hints: For each worker, take the inflation rate away from the pay rise.
Compare the two results. Which is further below zero?

acceptedIdeas: Worker B's, because a frozen wage loses more than a pay rise that nearly keeps up with prices
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Worker B's, because a frozen wage loses more than a pay rise that nearly keeps up with prices

choices.label: Worker B's, because a frozen wage loses more than a pay rise that nearly keeps up with prices
Worker A's, because inflation of 6% is the larger inflation figure of the two
Both fell by the same amount, because neither worker got a real pay rise
Worker A's, because a pay rise that fails to keep up is worse than no rise at all

questions.onCorrect: Taking inflation off the pay rise gives roughly -1% for A and -2% for B. B lost more, even though prices rose less.

misconceptions.feedback: What counts is each worker's pay relative to the prices. A's 5% rise offsets most of the 6%, and B's freeze offsets none of the 2%.
Neither got a real rise, but the falls differ in size. A is short by about 1 point and B by about 2.
A loss is its size. A falls behind by about 1 point, and B, with no rise at all, falls behind by about 2.

questions.prompt: The RBA describes a loop that can follow inflation that is too high. Put its steps in order.
hints: The loop opens with the effect on what people can afford.
A cost to firms comes before firms respond to it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Prices outrun incomes first, workers then seek bigger pay rises, firms' costs rise as a result, and firms respond by raising prices further or cutting staff.

items: Prices rise faster than people's nominal incomes
Workers seek larger wage increases to make up the lost purchasing power
Higher wage growth raises firms' costs
Firms raise prices further or employ fewer workers

questions.onCorrect: Each step causes the next: lost purchasing power leads to pay claims, pay claims raise costs, and firms respond with higher prices or fewer workers.

questions.prompt: Average CPI inflation was 9.3% in 1976 to 1984, 6.3% in 1985 to 1992 and 2.6% in 1993 to 2024. What can you say from those averages alone?
hints: An average over many years can hide the years above and below it. Which option claims more than an average can show?
A comparison of two periods shows a change. Does it show what caused it?

acceptedIdeas: Inflation was far lower after targeting began, but the averages do not show what caused that
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inflation was far lower after targeting began, but the averages do not show what caused that

choices.label: Targeting caused the fall, and the averages prove it, because the figure dropped when targeting began
Inflation never exceeded 3% after 1993, and that is why the target is judged to have worked
Inflation was close to zero for most of 1993 to 2024, so the target looks to have been set too low
Inflation was far lower after targeting began, but the averages do not show what caused that

questions.onCorrect: The averages show that inflation was lower in the targeting period. They don't show why, and an average can hide years above or below it.

misconceptions.feedback: A before and after comparison shows that inflation fell. It cannot rule out other causes that arrived at the same time.
An average of 2.6% leaves room for years above 3% and years below 2%. An average says nothing about the highest year.
An average of 2.6% is inside the 2 to 3 per cent range, and it is not close to zero.

questions.prompt: A bank approves a $30,000 car loan and credits the money to your account the same afternoon. Before you spend any of it, what has the bank done?
hints: Think about what a bank has in writing once it agrees to lend: your promise to repay, and an account balance in your name. Which of the two does the bank own, and which does it owe?
Ask whether any other customer's balance has to fall for yours to appear.
questions.onCorrect: A loan adds an asset, the promise to repay, and a liability, the new balance. That is why the RBA says a bank that makes a loan typically creates a deposit.

acceptedIdeas: It has recorded your promise to repay as something it is owed, and your balance as something it owes you
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has recorded your promise to repay as something it is owed, and your balance as something it owes you

choices.label: It has moved $30,000 out of other customers' accounts into yours, so their balances are now lower
It has taken $30,000 of banknotes from its vault and locked them against your account until you spend them
It has recorded your promise to repay as something it is owed, and your balance as something it owes you
It has received $30,000 from the Reserve Bank, which supplies the money for each loan a bank approves

misconceptions.feedback: A loan does not draw down anyone else's balance. The RBA says a bank that makes a loan typically creates a deposit, so the balance in your account is new and nothing has to be taken from another customer's.
The bank's cash stays where it is until a customer withdraws it or pays it away. In the RBA's case study, Bank A's cash is still $100 straight after it credits an $80 loan.
In the RBA's account the bank creates the deposit itself when it lends. The Reserve Bank issues banknotes and holds the banks' own accounts, but it does not fund each loan first.

questions.prompt: Bank A has credited $80 to the borrower's account, yet its cash is still 100. Why has no cash left the bank?
hints: Think about what the bank has done so far: it has written two entries. Has anyone taken cash out of the vault?
Cash changes when someone withdraws or pays it away. Has the borrower done that yet?
questions.onCorrect: Crediting a deposit is a bookkeeping entry. Cash moves only when the borrower draws on the deposit.

acceptedIdeas: The credit is only an entry on the books, and cash leaves when the borrower withdraws it or pays it away
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The credit is only an entry on the books, and cash leaves when the borrower withdraws it or pays it away

choices.label: The bank has paid the $80 out of other customers' deposits, so its own cash has not been touched
The Reserve Bank supplied the $80, so Bank A did not need to use any of its own cash
The loan is paid out in cash only after the first repayment has come in from the borrower
The credit is only an entry on the books, and cash leaves when the borrower withdraws it or pays it away

misconceptions.feedback: A loan does not draw on other customers' balances. The deposit is a new entry, and the bank's cash changes only when the borrower takes cash out.
The RBA's case has Bank A creating the deposit itself. Its cash falls only once the borrower withdraws, as the next line shows.
Payment does not wait for a repayment. The borrower can withdraw straight away, and in the case they withdraw $75 at once.

questions.prompt: In the case you just followed, the business paid its $75 into Bank B. Suppose it had banked at Bank A, the bank that made the loan. Once the $75 is paid in, how do total deposits across the banks compare with the case you followed?
hints: Write down which accounts at Bank A hold a deposit once the business has paid in, and add them up.
Compare the total with the 80 that the loan created. Does paying the money into a different bank change how much was created?
questions.onCorrect: Which bank holds the deposit depends on where the payment lands. The total depends on the loan, and the loan was 80.

acceptedIdeas: They are the same as in the case you followed, but every dollar of it now sits at Bank A
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are the same as in the case you followed, but every dollar of it now sits at Bank A

choices.label: They are the same as in the case you followed, but every dollar of it now sits at Bank A
They are lower, because cash coming back into Bank A cancels part of the loan it made
They are higher, because Bank A has now taken in a deposit as well as having credited one
They are only 5, which is all that was left in the borrower's account

misconceptions.feedback: Cash paid into Bank A becomes a deposit that the bank owes the business. The loan is cancelled only when the borrower repays it.
The $75 the business pays in is the money the borrower withdrew, so the deposit has moved from the borrower's account to the business's. It is not a second 75 on top of the first.
The 5 is only one of the two deposits. The business's 75 is a deposit too, so the total is 80.

questions.prompt: Bank C, a lender invented for this question, makes a $60 loan to a builder, who pays a supplier that banks at Bank D. In what order do these steps happen?
hints: A loan cannot be spent until it is on the bank's books. What has to happen between the request and the payment?
At each step, ask whose account holds the $60 and at which bank.
questions.onCorrect: The deposit exists from the second step, before anything is spent. The fourth step only moves it to another bank.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The builder asks, Bank C records the loan and credits the account, the builder pays the supplier, Bank D credits the supplier, and across the two banks loans and deposits have each risen by $60.

items: The builder asks Bank C for a $60 loan
Bank C records the loan and credits $60 to the builder's account
The builder pays the supplier $60 from that account
Bank D credits $60 to the supplier's account
Across the two banks, loans and deposits have both risen by $60

questions.prompt: Tamsin, an invented borrower, repays $10,000 of a personal loan by a transfer from her everyday account to her bank. What happens to the total amount of money in the economy?
hints: Think about what the loan created when it was made. What would undo that?
After the transfer, does Tamsin's deposit still exist anywhere, or has it gone along with the loan?
questions.onCorrect: Making a loan creates a deposit and repaying it removes one. The RBA describes repayment as typically extinguishing deposits.

acceptedIdeas: It falls by $10,000, because her deposit and her loan are both cancelled
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls by $10,000, because her deposit and her loan are both cancelled

choices.label: It stays the same, because the money has only moved to her bank
It rises by $10,000, because the bank now holds the money and can lend it out again
It falls only if she repays in cash, because a transfer between accounts creates nothing
It falls by $10,000, because her deposit and her loan are both cancelled

misconceptions.feedback: The bank does not end up holding a new deposit. The RBA says repaying a loan typically extinguishes deposits, and Tamsin's balance disappears as the loan is cleared.
A later loan would create a new deposit, but that is a different event. The repayment itself removes the deposit.
The form of payment makes no difference here. Her deposit is used up either way, and the amount of money falls by the same $10,000.

questions.prompt: Bank B has just credited a $40 deposit to its second borrower, who now withdraws the whole $40 in cash to pay a merchant. Which lines of Bank B's balance sheet change?
hints: Cash goes out of the vault. What does the bank no longer owe once it has paid it?
A balance sheet has to keep matching, so every fall on one side needs a matching change somewhere.
questions.onCorrect: The withdrawal pays off the deposit with cash, so one asset and one liability shrink by the same amount and the loan stays.

acceptedIdeas: Its cash and the deposit it owes the borrower both fall by 40
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its cash and the deposit it owes the borrower both fall by 40

choices.label: Its loan and its equity both fall by 40, because the borrower has taken the loan away with the cash
Its cash and the deposit it owes the borrower both fall by 40
Its cash falls by 40 and its loan rises by 40, because the cash has now been lent out
Only its cash falls, because the loan is still owed and nothing else on the sheet is touched

misconceptions.feedback: The loan is still owed by the borrower, and equity is the owners' money. Neither changes when the borrower takes cash out.
The loan was recorded when the deposit was credited, and it is still 40. Withdrawing cash does not make a second loan.
Cash cannot fall on its own. The bank owed the borrower a deposit of 40, and paying out cash settles that debt, so the deposit falls by the same amount.

questions.prompt: The merchant pays the $40 into Bank A. Adding up both banks, how do loans and deposits compare?
hints: List each bank's loans and then each bank's deposits, and add each list.
Think about which transaction created the deposits, and whether the merchant's payment created any more.
questions.onCorrect: Each loan created a deposit of the same size, and payments only moved the deposits between banks, so the two totals stay equal.

acceptedIdeas: They are equal, because the lending created deposits that match the loans
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are equal, because the lending created deposits that match the loans

choices.label: They are equal, because the lending created deposits that match the loans
They are equal only at Bank B, because Bank A made no loan the second time
Deposits are larger, because each payment into a bank adds a deposit on top of the loan
Loans are larger, because the banks' own cash is also lent out

misconceptions.feedback: Equal totals appear across the system, not bank by bank. Bank A holds a deposit of 45 against a loan of 80, and Bank B holds a deposit of 75 against a loan of 40.
A payment moves a deposit from one account to another. The 40 the merchant pays in is the deposit the borrower already had, so it adds nothing.
Loans are only what borrowers owe. Cash stays on the banks' books as an asset, and the loans of 120 are matched by deposits of 120.

questions.prompt: The two sources below both describe what limits bank lending. How do they relate?
hints: Ask what each source says a bank needs in order to lend, and what each says must be there from the other side.
Check whether either source mentions a multiplier.
questions.onCorrect: A bank needs the cash and capital to lend, and somebody has to want the loan. The RBA's own case study names both kinds of limit.

extracts.text: Deposit-taking institutions need to hold sufficient liquid assets to meet withdrawals from depositors (to ensure that repayment obligations can be met without selling illiquid assets); assets (loans) needs to be backed by capital (to absorb any losses arising from defaults or other sources)
extracts.who: Doherty, Jackman and Perry, "Money in the Australian Economy", RBA Bulletin (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: An introduction to money written by Reserve Bank staff

extracts.text: The constraining factor on bank lending recognized today is largely the number of available borrowers willing to create loan contracts.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Money creation" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: They cover two sides of lending: A the cash and capital a bank needs, and B the borrowers who must want a loan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They cover two sides of lending: A the cash and capital a bank needs, and B the borrowers who must want a loan

choices.label: They cover two sides of lending: A the cash and capital a bank needs, and B the borrowers who must want a loan
They contradict each other, so at least one of them must be wrong about how Australian banks lend today
Source B shows that cash and capital no longer limit a bank, since Australia has no reserve requirement now
Source A describes a reserve multiplier, which is the very idea that Wikipedia says has been abandoned

misconceptions.feedback: They answer different parts of the question. The RBA's case study itself says lending depends on the borrower's decision as well as on the bank's liquidity and capital.
No reserve requirement removes one old rule, the reserve multiplier. Liquidity and capital still limit a bank, and Source A names both.
Source A mentions no multiplier. It lists liquid assets and capital, which are the limits that replaced the reserve requirements.

questions.prompt: In an invented case, the Government pays a $2,000 grant into a household's bank account. It raises the money by selling bonds to a superannuation fund, which pays for them from its own bank account. What happens to the total amount of money in the economy?
hints: Follow each account in turn. Whose balance goes up, and whose goes down?
Money is created when the total of deposits and currency rises. Does the total rise here, or does one account gain what another loses?
questions.onCorrect: Money is created when a bank lends, not when money changes hands. Here the household gains what the fund loses.

acceptedIdeas: It is unchanged: the household's deposit rises by $2,000 and the fund's falls by $2,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is unchanged: the household's deposit rises by $2,000 and the fund's falls by $2,000

choices.label: It rises by $2,000, because the household now holds a deposit that did not exist before the grant
It rises by $2,000, because a government can spend money before it has collected it from anyone
It falls by $2,000, because the fund's deposit disappears when it pays for the bonds it buys
It is unchanged: the household's deposit rises by $2,000 and the fund's falls by $2,000

misconceptions.feedback: The household's deposit is matched by a fall in the fund's. The RBA says a government payment does not create money, because a bond sale or taxation has to pay for it and each takes a deposit away somewhere else, as the bond sale does from the fund here.
The RBA says a government transfer has to be funded by issuing bonds or by taxation, and both reduce deposits somewhere else, so the total does not rise.
The fund's deposit does not disappear. The money ends up in the household's account, so one deposit falls and another rises by the same amount.

questions.prompt: A columnist writes: "The Reserve Bank has to create the money first. Banks only pass it on to borrowers." Which reply is best supported by the RBA's account?
hints: Which kind of money makes up most of what people hold, and who owes it to them?
Check whether the RBA says a bank waits for the Reserve Bank before it credits a borrower's account.
questions.onCorrect: Deposits are the largest part of money, and a bank creates one when it lends. The Reserve Bank's own role is narrower.

acceptedIdeas: Most money is bank deposits, and a bank creates one itself when it lends, so lending does not wait for the Reserve Bank
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most money is bank deposits, and a bank creates one itself when it lends, so lending does not wait for the Reserve Bank

choices.label: The columnist is right in outline, since every dollar a bank lends was first issued by the Reserve Bank and handed on
The columnist is right about loans, because banks must hold the money in reserve before any loan can be approved
Most money is bank deposits, and a bank creates one itself when it lends, so lending does not wait for the Reserve Bank
The columnist is wrong that the Reserve Bank matters, because it plays no part in banks' payments or in the money supply

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says deposits make up the greatest share of money, and that banks create them when they lend. Banknotes are the Reserve Bank's own liability, and they are the smaller part.
Wikipedia's article says Australia has no reserve requirement, and the RBA's limits on lending are liquidity and capital. A loan is not held back until reserves exist.
The Reserve Bank issues banknotes, holds the banks' settlement accounts and can create deposits when it buys bonds. It does not fund each loan first, and it still has a part to play.

questions.prompt: Five invented banks each face a problem. Which of the RBA's limits on lending does each problem show?
hints: Ask what the bank would need in order to lend more: cash it could pay out, owners' funds to absorb losses, or a person who wants a loan.
Cash on hand points to liquidity, owners' funds point to capital, and a lack of takers points to borrowers.
questions.onCorrect: The RBA lists these as separate limits, and a bank that is short of any one of them stops lending.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bank E and Bank H are short of liquidity, Bank F and Bank J are about capital, and Bank G has no willing borrowers.

items.label: Bank E's customers withdraw more in a week than the cash and other liquid assets it holds
items.explanation: It cannot meet withdrawals, which is the cash side of lending.

items.label: Bank F has lent so much against so little of its owners' money that a few defaults would use all of it up
items.explanation: Losses are absorbed by capital, and here there is too little of it.

items.label: Bank G has plenty of cash and owners' funds, but hardly anyone wants a loan at the rates it charges
items.explanation: No borrower approaches, so no loan is made and no deposit is created.

items.label: Bank H could repay its depositors only by selling loans it cannot sell quickly
items.explanation: The RBA says a bank needs liquid assets so that it can repay without selling illiquid ones.
