items.label: Bank J's regulator requires it to keep the owners' funds above a minimum amount against its loans
items.explanation: Minimum capital requirements reinforce the capital limit.

questions.prompt: Which of these transactions adds to the total amount of money in the economy?
hints: Check each transaction for a new loan. Money is created when lending makes a deposit that was not there before.
Where an account gains, look for another account that loses the same amount.
questions.onCorrect: Only the loan creates a deposit that did not exist before. The other three move or swap money that was already there.

acceptedIdeas: A bank approves a loan to a boat builder and credits the firm's account
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bank approves a loan to a boat builder and credits the firm's account

choices.label: A shopper takes $400 in notes out of an ATM
A bank approves a loan to a boat builder and credits the firm's account
An employer pays a worker's wages from its account into hers
A customer pays a $900 electricity bill from her account to the power company's account at another bank

misconceptions.feedback: Her deposit falls by $400 and her notes rise by $400, which swaps one form of money for the other and leaves the total as it was.
The worker's deposit rises by what the employer's falls, so the total stays the same.
A deposit moves from one account to another, and the total is the same. It only changes bank.

questions.prompt: The Board lifts its target for the cash rate by 25 basis points. Which statement about the variable rate on a home loan is best supported by the RBA's account?
hints: The Board makes one decision. Ask who decides the other interest rates people pay, and what else might enter their decision.
Would a bank want to match a change in the cash rate exactly, in every case and on the same day?
questions.onCorrect: The Board sets the target for one rate. Each bank then sets its own rates, and the cash rate is a strong influence on them without fixing them.

acceptedIdeas: Your bank sets it, and the cash rate is a strong influence on it without being the only influence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Your bank sets it, and the cash rate is a strong influence on it without being the only influence

choices.label: The Reserve Bank sets it directly, so it rises by exactly 25 basis points on the day of the decision
The Government sets it, using the Reserve Bank's decision as the guide for how far it should move
Your bank passes on every change in full and at once, because the cash rate is its only funding cost
Your bank sets it, and the cash rate is a strong influence on it without being the only influence

misconceptions.feedback: The Board sets a target for the cash rate, the rate on overnight loans between banks. The RBA says the cash rate is not the only determinant of other interest rates, and each bank sets its own lending rates.
Banks set their lending rates, to make lending as profitable as they can within the risk they accept. The Government has no part in it, and the Board itself acts independently of the Government.
The RBA says banks' funding costs do not always change by the same amount, or as fast, as the cash rate, and that competition and credit risk also affect lending rates.

questions.prompt: The target is 4.85 per cent, so the Reserve Bank pays 4.75 per cent on balances that banks leave with it. Bank P, an invented bank, has spare balances, and Bank Q, also invented, offers to borrow them overnight at 4.50 per cent. What does the corridor give Bank P a reason to do?
hints: Compare what Bank P would earn from Bank Q with what the Reserve Bank pays on balances left with it.
The corridor is made of two rates the Reserve Bank offers to every bank. Which one is relevant to a bank with spare balances?
questions.onCorrect: The floor of the corridor is the rate the Reserve Bank pays on balances, so no bank has a reason to lend for less than that.

acceptedIdeas: Leave the balances with the Reserve Bank, which pays more than Bank Q is offering for them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leave the balances with the Reserve Bank, which pays more than Bank Q is offering for them

choices.label: Leave the balances with the Reserve Bank, which pays more than Bank Q is offering for them
Lend to Bank Q anyway, since earning any interest at all is better than earning none
Refuse, because the Reserve Bank has made it illegal to lend at less than the target
Lend to Bank Q, because the cash rate is simply whatever two banks agree between themselves

misconceptions.feedback: Bank P is not choosing between interest and none. The Reserve Bank pays 4.75 on the balances, which is more than Bank Q offers.
The corridor works by incentive and not by rule. Banks are free to trade at any rate, and they have no reason to accept less than the floor.
Two banks are free to agree a rate, but the floor limits what a lender will accept, because it can always earn the floor from the Reserve Bank.

questions.prompt: After the Board raises the cash rate target, what is the best-supported expectation about the interest a bank pays on a savings account?
hints: The RBA separates rates that follow the cash rate quickly from rates that respond more slowly. Which group does a deposit rate belong to?
Ask who decides the rate paid on a savings account, and whether that decision has to wait for the Board.
questions.onCorrect: Deposit rates respond less directly than market rates, and each bank has discretion over its own.

acceptedIdeas: It may change by a different amount from the cash rate and a little later, because the bank decides it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It may change by a different amount from the cash rate and a little later, because the bank decides it

choices.label: It rises by the same amount on the same day, because the cash rate fixes every rate a bank pays
It may change by a different amount from the cash rate and a little later, because the bank decides it
It does not move at all, because only the rates on loans are affected by the cash rate
It can change only on the day of the Board's decision, because banks never move deposit rates on their own

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says the cash rate acts less directly on deposit rates, which tend to respond after some delay, and that rates on different sources of funds can differ in size and timing.
The RBA says the cash rate has a strong influence over deposit rates as well as lending rates. It acts on both, at different speeds.
The RBA says a bank can lift its deposit rates without any change in the cash rate, for example to attract more deposits.

questions.prompt: Four bodies appear in a story about interest rates. Which of them does each job?
hints: Ask which body decides each thing, and which one only reports or uses it.
The Board sets one rate and explains why. Other rates are set by the lenders and savings providers themselves.
questions.onCorrect: Each body has its own job, and the Board's is narrower than headlines suggest.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Board sets the cash rate target and explains it at a media conference, the ABS publishes the CPI, the Government delivers the Budget, and a commercial bank sets credit card and savings rates.

items.label: Sets the target for the cash rate
items.explanation: The Monetary Policy Board makes the decision about monetary policy, by majority vote.

items.label: Explains each decision at a media conference once the meeting is over
items.explanation: The Reserve Bank explains its decisions in public, with the Governor taking the media conference.

items.label: Calculates and publishes the consumer price index every month
items.explanation: The ABS, and not the Reserve Bank, calculates and publishes the CPI.

items.label: Delivers the Budget
items.explanation: The Budget is the Government's own account of its taxes and spending.

items.label: Decides the interest rate on a credit card
items.explanation: Banks set their own lending rates, and a credit card is a loan.

items.label: Decides how much interest to pay on a savings account
items.explanation: Banks have discretion over their deposit rates.

questions.prompt: The Board raised the target on 3 February, 17 March and 5 May and left it unchanged on 16 June. A commentator says the hold shows the Board had finished raising rates. What does the Board's statement of that day support?
hints: Look for the Board's view of inflation in the sentence, and for what it says it is waiting to learn.
Would a Board that thought inflation was back on target write that it is still too high?
questions.onCorrect: In June the Board held while it assessed the effect of its earlier rises and the oil disruption, and it raised the target again on 29 September.

extracts.text: But inflation is still too high and the Board judged that it was appropriate to leave the cash rate target unchanged while it assesses the response to previous interest rate rises and the impact of the oil supply disruption.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement by the Monetary Policy Board (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A media release giving the Board's decision and reasons

acceptedIdeas: Inflation was still too high, and the Board was waiting to see how its rises were working
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inflation was still too high, and the Board was waiting to see how its rises were working

choices.label: Inflation was still too high, and the Board was waiting to see how its rises were working
Inflation had returned to the target band, so the Board judged that no further rise was needed
The Board had decided that rate rises do not work, so it would stop using them in future
The Government had asked the Board to pause, so that households could adjust to the earlier rises

misconceptions.feedback: The statement says inflation is still too high. The Board left the target unchanged for a different reason, which is that it wanted to see the effect of what it had already done.
The statement gives no such view. It says the Board is assessing the response to the earlier rises, which treats them as having some effect still to be seen.
The Board sets policy independently of the Government, and the statement gives its own reasons for the hold. The Government's wishes are not among them.

questions.prompt: Both of these decisions raised the target by 25 basis points. What do the two votes show?
hints: Work out the margin in each vote by taking the smaller number from the larger.
The RBA's explainer says decisions are made by majority vote, and that the chair has an additional casting vote if one is required. Was one required here?
questions.onCorrect: A majority decides, and the margin tells you how close the call was.

extracts.text: Today’s policy decision was made by majority: five members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.10 per cent; four members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 3.85 per cent.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement by the Monetary Policy Board (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A media release giving the Board's decision and reasons

extracts.text: Today’s policy decision was by majority: six members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent; three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement by the Monetary Policy Board (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A media release giving the Board's decision and reasons

acceptedIdeas: Both decisions stand, and March was closer: the margin was one vote then and three in November
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both decisions stand, and March was closer: the margin was one vote then and three in November

choices.label: The March decision carried less force, because a vote of five to four is not enough to bind the Board
The Governor decided both times, since the chair has a casting vote and so the other votes only advise
Both decisions stand, and March was closer: the margin was one vote then and three in November
November was the closer call, because more members in March voted to raise the target

misconceptions.feedback: A decision made by majority binds the Board in the same way as a unanimous one. The split shows how close the call was, and nothing more.
The chair's additional casting vote is for when one is required, and a vote of five to four or six to three already has a majority.
A closer call is a smaller margin. Five to four is a margin of one vote and six to three is a margin of three, so March was the closer.

questions.prompt: A bank, invented for this question, raises its variable home loan rate by 0.40 of a percentage point soon after the Board raises the target by 0.25. A customer says the Board must have set the loan rate. What does the RBA's account suggest?
hints: Compare 0.40 with 0.25. Does anything in the RBA's account say the two have to match?
Ask who chooses the rate on a home loan, and what the RBA says about the gap between that rate and the cash rate.
questions.onCorrect: The Board's target is a strong influence on lending rates. Each bank still chooses its own, and the gap between the two varies.

acceptedIdeas: The bank set it, and the gap between the cash rate and a loan rate can widen or narrow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The bank set it, and the gap between the cash rate and a loan rate can widen or narrow

choices.label: The Board set it, since a bank must pass on a rise in the cash rate in full and no more than that
The bank set it, and the gap between the cash rate and a loan rate can widen or narrow
The bank has made an error, since a lending rate cannot rise by more than the cash rate does
The Government set it, since it has to approve any change a bank makes to a lending rate

misconceptions.feedback: No rule makes banks pass on the exact amount. The RBA says the spread between the cash rate and other rates varies over time, because banks set their own rates.
A lending rate can move by more or by less. The RBA lists competition, credit risk and financial market conditions among the reasons the gap changes.
The RBA describes banks setting their lending rates to make lending as profitable as they can, within an appropriate exposure to the risk of default. No approval is mentioned.

questions.prompt: Suppose the Board were to lower the target by 25 basis points. In what order do these things follow?
hints: The Board decides first. Which things does the Reserve Bank itself control, and which are left to others?

questions.onCorrect: The Board and the corridor come first, then the market reference rates, then the choices banks make for themselves.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Board announces the target, the corridor moves with it, market reference rates fall quickly, banks decide on their own deposit and lending rates, and customers see rates that differ from bank to bank.

items: The Board announces a lower target for the cash rate

Market reference rates fall quickly
Banks decide how far and how fast to cut their deposit and lending rates
Borrowers and savers see new rates that differ from bank to bank

questions.prompt: These two sources describe the Monetary Policy Board. Which conclusion do both of them support?

extracts.kind: An explainer published by the central bank for the public

extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: The Government has a say in who sits on the Board, and the Board still decides the target on its own judgement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Government has a say in who sits on the Board, and the Board still decides the target on its own judgement

choices.label: The Government has a say in who sits on the Board, and the Board still decides the target on its own judgement
The Treasurer effectively sets the cash rate, since the Treasurer appoints most of the Board's members
The Board cannot be independent, because the Secretary to the Treasury has a seat and so Treasury controls the vote

questions.prompt: By 16 June 2026 the Board had raised the cash rate target three times since February, and its statement still said inflation was too high. A commentator says the rises have failed. What does the RBA's explainer on how policy reaches the economy imply?
hints: The explainer gives an estimate of how long it takes for a change in the cash rate to have its maximum effect. What is it, and how sure does the RBA say it is?
Ask whether inflation still being high after a few months tells you the rises have failed, or only that they have not finished working.
questions.onCorrect: The explainer puts the maximum effect at one to two years and says the estimates are very uncertain, so high inflation after a few months does not show failure.

acceptedIdeas: It is too early to say: the maximum effect is estimated at one to two years, with large uncertainty
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is too early to say: the maximum effect is estimated at one to two years, with large uncertainty

choices.label: Yes, because rises that were working would already have brought inflation down within a few months of the first rise
It is too early to say, because a rate rise has no effect at all until its second year
It is too early to say: the maximum effect is estimated at one to two years, with large uncertainty
No, because rate rises work only through the exchange rate, which responds within days

misconceptions.feedback: The explainer says households and businesses take time to adjust, so the effects of a change build up over a much longer period than a few months.
The RBA puts the maximum effect between one and two years out, which does not mean nothing happens before that. The 16 June statement itself reports signs that consumer spending was already slowing.
The explainer lists four channels and the exchange rate is only one of them. Each channel takes its own time.

questions.prompt: Eight things follow a run of rate rises. Which of the RBA's four channels does each one belong to?
hints: Ask what the thing that changes actually is: a repayment, a price of an asset, the cost of a loan or saving, or the exchange rate.
Cash left over each month is the cash-flow channel, and the value of what people own is the wealth channel.
questions.onCorrect: Each channel starts from a different place, and a single rate rise sets off all four.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dearer loans and better deposit rates are the saving and investment channel, higher repayments are the cash-flow channel, falling home values are the asset prices and wealth channel, and the dollar is the exchange rate channel.

items.label: A builder postpones a block of flats because the loan to build it now costs more
items.explanation: A dearer loan is a weaker incentive to invest, which is the saving and investment channel.

items.label: A household that had been spending its savings puts more of them into a deposit that now pays more
items.explanation: A higher deposit rate gives more reason to save, and that is also part of this channel.

items.label: A family with a variable-rate mortgage sees its repayment rise and cuts back on eating out
items.explanation: Higher repayments leave less cash to spend, which is the cash-flow channel.

items.label: A small firm with a variable-rate loan has less cash left after paying interest each month
items.explanation: The cash-flow channel works for businesses as well as households.

items.label: Home values fall, and owners feel less well off and spend less
items.explanation: Falling asset prices reduce wealth, and households spend some share of their wealth.

items.label: A property that has lost value gives a bank less to lend against
items.explanation: Asset values are the collateral that banks lend against, so a fall makes borrowing harder.

items.label: Australian exports become dearer for overseas buyers
items.explanation: A higher Australian dollar makes Australian goods dearer abroad.

items.label: Imported goods become cheaper in Australian dollars, which holds back inflation
items.explanation: The RBA says a lower exchange rate adds to inflation because imports cost more, and a higher one does the reverse.

questions.prompt: A retired couple, invented for this question, live on interest from bank deposits and have no debt. After the Board raises the target, what happens to their cash flow, and what does the RBA expect this channel to do to spending across the economy?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their interest income tends to rise, but borrowers' loss of cash flow is the larger effect, so total spending falls

choices.label: Their interest income falls, because banks cut deposit rates when the cash rate rises, so total spending falls
Their interest income tends to rise, but borrowers' loss of cash flow is the larger effect, so total spending falls
Their income is unchanged, because the cash-flow channel works only on people who borrow, so only borrowers cut spending
Their interest income rises, and since it is the larger effect, total spending in the economy rises with it

misconceptions.feedback: Deposit rates follow the cash rate in the same direction, though slowly. The cash-flow channel gives savers more interest when rates rise.
The cash-flow channel works on savers as well. The RBA says higher rates reduce what borrowers have to spend and add to what savers receive.
The RBA says the borrowers' effect is the larger one, so the net effect through this channel is lower spending and not higher.

questions.prompt: These are two sentences from the RBA's assessment of housing and borrowing in its November 2026 Statement on Monetary Policy. What does the mix of evidence show about the effect of the rises so far?

questions.prompt: An Australian winemaker, invented for this question, sells most of its wine overseas and has no debt. After a run of cash rate rises the Australian dollar rises against other currencies. Through which channel do the rises reach this business, and how?

questions.prompt: The RBA's explainer walks through the effect of a cut in interest rates. Put its steps in order.
hints: A cut works on demand first. What can supply not do as fast as demand?
Prices rise because demand is greater than supply, and inflation is what you see once firms have raised their prices.
questions.onCorrect: Lower rates raise demand, supply is slower to respond, and the gap pushes prices up. A rise in rates sets the chain going in the opposite direction.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lower rates stimulate spending, supply takes time to respond, demand runs ahead of supply, firms raise prices more quickly, and inflation rises.

items: Lower interest rates for households and businesses stimulate spending
Supply takes time to respond, because firms need to find workers and equipment
Demand runs ahead of supply, which puts upward pressure on prices
Businesses raise their prices more quickly
Inflation rises

questions.prompt: A central bank, invented for this question, raised its rate twice, in March and in April. In October its report says new housing loans have fallen sharply, house prices have begun to fall, consumer spending growth is slowing and inflation is unchanged. A reader says the rises did nothing. Which response does the RBA's account support?
hints: Sort the four signs into those that have already moved and the one that has not. Which one are the rises ultimately aimed at?
Count the months from the rises to October, and compare them with the RBA's estimate of when the maximum effect arrives.
questions.onCorrect: Some channels respond sooner than others, and the effect on inflation can take one to two years to arrive.

acceptedIdeas: Housing and spending have begun to respond, and the main effect on inflation may be months away
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Housing and spending have begun to respond, and the main effect on inflation may be months away

choices.label: The reader is right, because inflation is what the rises were meant to change and it has not moved
Housing and spending have begun to respond, and the main effect on inflation may be months away
The reader is right, because a rise that works shows up in prices within a few months
The reader is wrong, because falling house prices show that the rises have worked in full

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says the effect on inflation builds up over one to two years. Unchanged inflation after six or seven months is what a lag would produce, so it does not show the rises did nothing.
The RBA does not say prices respond within a few months. It says households and businesses take time to adjust, and puts the maximum effect at one to two years.
Housing is one channel. The effect on spending and inflation is still building, and falling house prices do not show that the rises have finished working.

questions.prompt: The ABS measured real GDP growth of 0.7 per cent for the June 2021 quarter, -1.8 per cent for September and 3.7 per cent for December. By the newspapers' rule of two quarters in a row of falling real GDP, was Australia in recession in the September quarter?
hints: The rule the newspapers use has a number in it. How many negative quarters does it need, and how are they arranged?
Write the three quarterly figures in a row and mark which are negative.
questions.onCorrect: The technical test needs two consecutive negative quarters. September 2021 was one, between two rises, so it is not a technical recession.

acceptedIdeas: No: GDP fell in only one quarter, and the rule needs two quarters in a row to call a recession
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: GDP fell in only one quarter, and the rule needs two quarters in a row to call a recession

choices.label: No: GDP fell in only one quarter, and the rule needs two quarters in a row to call a recession
Yes, because a fall of 1.8 per cent in a quarter is large enough to count as a recession
Yes, because any quarterly fall that is followed by a rebound shows the economy had a downturn
It cannot be said without the unemployment rate, which is what the rule is based on

misconceptions.feedback: The rule does not look at the size of one fall. It asks for two negative quarters in a row, and the quarters on either side of September were positive.
A rebound does not turn one fall into two. The technical test counts consecutive negative quarters, and here there was one.
The two-quarter rule uses real GDP only. Unemployment belongs to the RBA's broader description and to unemployment rules, which are other tests.

questions.prompt: The ABS series shows real GDP growth of -0.2 per cent in the March quarter of 2020, -6.8 in June, then 3.4 in September and 3.4 in December. In which quarter did output reach its lowest level?
hints: Output is at its lowest at the point where it stops falling and starts to rise. Look for the quarter after which the figures turn positive.
A negative figure means output fell during that quarter and a positive one means it rose. Which quarter's fall was followed by a rise?
questions.onCorrect: The RBA says a contraction ends with a trough. Output kept falling to June 2020 and began to rise in September, so June is the trough.

acceptedIdeas: June quarter 2020: output fell up to then and began to rise again in September
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: June quarter 2020: output fell up to then and began to rise again in September

choices.label: March quarter 2020, because that was the first quarter in which output fell
June quarter 2020: output fell up to then and began to rise again in September
September quarter 2020, because it was the first quarter of recovery
December quarter 2020, because output was still below where it started the year

misconceptions.feedback: The first fall starts the contraction. Output kept falling in June, by far more, so the lowest level came later.
Growth of 3.4 per cent means output rose during September. It rose from a level that was already at its lowest, in June.
Output was still below its December 2019 level in December 2020, but it had risen in both quarters since June. The lowest level is the one before the rises began.

questions.prompt: A first estimate shows real GDP falling two quarters in a row. A later release revises the first of those quarters to growth of 0.1 per cent. What does that show about the technical test?
hints: The RBA lists weaknesses of the technical test. Which one concerns how GDP figures change after they are first published?
After the revision, are there still two negative quarters in a row?
questions.onCorrect: The RBA lists revision among the weaknesses of the technical test, so a call based on early figures may not last.

acceptedIdeas: A recession call from it can change as the figures are revised after they are published
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A recession call from it can change as the figures are revised after they are published

choices.label: A recession call from it can change as the figures are revised after they are published
Nothing, because the first estimate of GDP is always the one that stands and is never changed later
That the economy recovered, because a revised quarter is a new quarter of growth
That GDP cannot be used to identify a recession at all, so the technical test is worthless as a guide

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says GDP is re-measured as more data arrive, so a quarter that first looked negative can be revised up, and one that first looked positive can be revised down.
A revision changes the estimate for the same quarter. It records a better measurement, not a new period of growth.
Revision is one of three weaknesses the RBA lists. It does not rule out using GDP, and the RBA says most recessions do show two negative quarters.

questions.prompt: The ABS reports real GDP growth of 0.3 per cent in the March quarter of 2026 and 0.4 in June, GDP per person of -0.1 and then nil, and a seasonally adjusted unemployment rate of 4.9 per cent in October, 0.6 of a point higher than a year before. Which of these tests do those figures meet?
hints: Take the tests that give a clear yes or no first. For each, compare the figure the rule needs with the figure the ABS reports.
Two of the rules are invented, with different amounts. The same 0.6 of a point can pass one and fail the other.
questions.onCorrect: The data pass or fail each clear rule at once, and the broader description turns on how much weakness and how large a rise count.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The technical test and its per-person version are not met, the invented 0.5-point rule is met and the 1-point rule is not, and the RBA's description depends on a judgement about weakness and size.

items.label: The technical test: two quarters in a row of negative real GDP growth
items.explanation: Both quarters grew, by 0.3 and 0.4 per cent.

items.label: The same test applied to GDP per person
items.explanation: GDP per person fell by 0.1 per cent in March and was nil in June, so there were not two negative quarters.

items.label: An invented rule: a recession when unemployment rises by more than 0.5 of a point in a year
items.explanation: The rise was 0.6 of a point, which is more than the rule's amount.

items.label: An invented rule: a recession when unemployment rises by more than 1 point in a year
items.explanation: The rise was 0.6 of a point, which is less than the rule's amount.

items.label: The RBA's description: sustained weak or negative growth with a significant rise in unemployment
items.explanation: Whether growth of 0.3 and 0.4 per cent is weak enough, and a rise of 0.6 of a point large enough, is for the reader to judge.

questions.prompt: An invented economy has a long boom in property lending that drives prices up for years. Its central bank raises its rate sharply to slow the boom. Two years later many borrowers cannot repay, lenders fail, output falls and unemployment rises. Which of the RBA's Australian episodes does it most resemble?
hints: Look for what started the trouble in the invented economy: a cost shock from abroad, a tightening against a boom, a financial collapse or a shutdown.
Compare the key words in each answer with the key words in the case.
questions.onCorrect: The RBA says the early 1990s recession mainly resulted from efforts to curb excess demand and speculation in property markets, and rates went very high.

acceptedIdeas: The early 1990s: efforts to curb excess demand and property speculation, with rates raised very high
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The early 1990s: efforts to curb excess demand and property speculation, with rates raised very high

choices.label: The early 1980s: central banks tightened against entrenched inflation, and weak global demand and drought added to it
The mid-1970s: a global oil price shock raised costs of production and cut demand from overseas
2020: many activities were suspended at once to manage a public health emergency
The early 1990s: efforts to curb excess demand and property speculation, with rates raised very high

misconceptions.feedback: That episode had drought and weak global demand as extra causes. A boom in property lending and speculation points to the early 1990s.
The 1970s began with a shock to the cost of oil. The invented economy's trouble began at home, with lending and a tightening against it.
The 2020 downturn was driven by a sudden suspension of activity, and output fell within months. Nothing like that happens in the invented case.

questions.prompt: In the global financial crisis of 2008 to 2009, the RBA says, Australian real GDP fell in only one quarter, yet unemployment climbed to nearly 6 per cent and underemployment jumped. Which statement fits the tests?
hints: Apply the technical test first. How many quarters fell?
Then ask what the other two tests would make of the rise in unemployment, and whether all three agree.
questions.onCorrect: The RBA says that, in part because of the different definitions, economists disagree about whether some weak episodes were recessions.

acceptedIdeas: The technical test is not met, as one quarter fell, while the rise in unemployment points the other way
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The technical test is not met, as one quarter fell, while the rise in unemployment points the other way

choices.label: The technical test is not met, as one quarter fell, while the rise in unemployment points the other way
It was a recession by every test, because unemployment rose and the economy slowed down at the time
It was not a recession by any test at all, because real GDP fell in only one quarter during the whole crisis
No test can be applied, because the figures are too old to be compared with the figures for 2026

misconceptions.feedback: A single negative quarter does not meet the technical test. The tests can disagree, and this is an episode where they do.
That is true of the technical test only. The RBA's description and an unemployment rule also look at unemployment, which rose to close to 6 per cent.
The tests do not depend on how recent the data are. The RBA applies them to older episodes, such as 1974-75 and 1991-92.

questions.prompt: In the RBA's account of the depression of the 1890s, a long resource and property boom ended, foreign investors withdrew their funds, wool prices collapsed and there was a run on the banks. Which kind of shock does it most resemble?
hints: Look for what set the trouble off: a cost shock, a central bank's tightening, a collapse in lending and deposits, or a deliberate shutdown.
Which words in the account describe banks and investors?
questions.onCorrect: A boom ended, investors withdrew, banks were run on and wool prices collapsed. The RBA calls it Australia's deepest financial crisis.

acceptedIdeas: A financial bust: a long boom ended, and lending and deposits collapsed along with it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A financial bust: a long boom ended, and lending and deposits collapsed along with it

choices.label: A supply shock: the cost of an essential input jumped, as with oil in the mid-1970s
A financial bust: a long boom ended, and lending and deposits collapsed along with it
A tightening against inflation: the central bank raised rates to bring down prices, as in the early 1980s
A shutdown: activity was suspended to manage a health emergency, as in 2020

misconceptions.feedback: The 1890s began with the end of a boom and a withdrawal of funds. The oil shock of the 1970s began with the price of an input.
Nothing in the account of the 1890s has a central bank tightening to reduce inflation. The trouble began with a boom ending and funds leaving.
No activity was suspended on purpose in the 1890s. A run on banks and a collapse in prices caused the crisis.

questions.prompt: An invented warehouse worker loses her job in a recession and is still looking for work two years after output has recovered. Which reason does the RBA give for why long-term unemployment can last after a recovery?
hints: The RBA gives reasons that concern the unemployed person and reasons that concern how the economy is changing. Which does the right answer include?
Check each wrong answer against what the RBA actually says, not against what sounds plausible.
questions.onCorrect: The RBA says skills can fade with disuse, that employers may think they have, and that a recession can hasten structural change.

acceptedIdeas: Her skills may have faded with disuse, or employers may think so, and a recession can hasten structural change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her skills may have faded with disuse, or employers may think so, and a recession can hasten structural change

choices.label: Unemployment figures are revised downward for years after a recession, so the persistence is a statistical effect
Output stays below potential for years after every recession, because the business cycle has no turning point
Her skills may have faded with disuse, or employers may think so, and a recession can hasten structural change
Employers always cut wages during a recovery, so people turn down the work that is on offer

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA gives no such reason. It says unemployment settles higher after each recession and falls slowly, which is a real effect on people.
The RBA describes the cycle as having a trough followed by an expansion. Long-term unemployment lasts for the reasons the RBA gives, skills and structural change, whatever output does.
The RBA does not say this. It gives skills that fade with disuse, what employers believe about that, and faster structural change as the reasons.

questions.prompt: Six invented economies each report real GDP growth for a few quarters and the change in the unemployment rate over the year. Which of the two tests does each one meet?
hints: Take the technical test first: look for two negative quarters side by side. Then check whether unemployment rose by a lot or hardly at all.
The RBA's description asks for weak or negative growth together with a significant rise in unemployment. Does the economy have both?
questions.onCorrect: The two tests look at different things, so the same figures can pass one and fail the other.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first and last economies meet both tests, the second and the fifth meet only the RBA's description, the third meets only the technical test, and the fourth meets neither.

items.label: Real GDP falls 0.5 per cent and then 0.8 per cent in two quarters in a row, and unemployment rises 2 points
items.explanation: Two negative quarters in a row meet the technical test, and weak output with a large rise in unemployment fits the broader description.

items.label: Real GDP grows 0.1, 0.1 and 0.0 per cent over three quarters, and unemployment rises 1.5 points
items.explanation: Growth is weak but never negative, so the technical test is not met, while weak growth with a large rise in unemployment fits the broader description.

items.label: Real GDP falls 0.4 per cent and then 0.3 per cent in two quarters in a row, and unemployment does not change
items.explanation: Two negative quarters meet the technical test, but with no rise in unemployment the broader description does not fit.

items.label: Real GDP grows 0.8 per cent and then 0.6 per cent, and unemployment rises 0.1 of a point
items.explanation: Growth is positive and unemployment has hardly moved, so neither test is met.

items.label: Real GDP falls 0.2 per cent, rises 0.3 per cent and falls 0.2 per cent again, and unemployment rises 1.2 points
items.explanation: The two falls are not in a row, so the technical test is not met. Weak output and a significant rise in unemployment fit the broader description.

items.label: Real GDP falls 0.6 per cent and then 0.2 per cent in two quarters in a row, and unemployment rises 1.8 points
items.explanation: Two negative quarters in a row and a large rise in unemployment meet both tests.

questions.prompt: The 2026-27 Budget shows a deficit of $31.5 billion. Which comparison does most to show whether that is large?
hints: A dollar figure means more when it is set against something. What in the Budget table could the deficit be compared with?
The deficit is one year's gap. Which other figures in the table say how much has built up and what carrying it costs?
questions.onCorrect: A deficit is judged against the size of the economy, and then against the debt it adds to and the interest the debt costs.

acceptedIdeas: The deficit as a share of GDP, read alongside the debt and the interest bill
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The deficit as a share of GDP, read alongside the debt and the interest bill

choices.label: The deficit as a share of GDP, read alongside the debt and the interest bill
The dollar figure on its own, because a deficit of billions of dollars is plainly very large
The year the Government expects the budget to be back in balance, because a later year means a bigger deficit
The cash rate, because the Reserve Bank's interest rate decisions set the size of the Government's deficit

misconceptions.feedback: A dollar figure needs a scale. The same $31.5 billion would be huge for a small economy and modest for a large one, which is why the Budget also gives it as a share of GDP.
A date says when a projected deficit ends and says nothing of how large it is in any year. The Budget gives that date as a projection, not as a measure of size.
The Government's deficit is receipts less payments. It is not set by the Reserve Bank, which sets the cash rate target independently.

questions.prompt: In the Budget table, gross debt rises from $928.6 billion in 2024-25 to $1,249.0 billion in 2029-30, about a third more, while gross debt as a share of GDP goes from 33.4 to 35.6 per cent, a much smaller rise. What explains the gap between the two?
hints: A share has two parts, the debt and the thing it is divided by. If the share grew by much less than the debt, what must have happened to the second part?
Check what the row is headed. What is the debt being divided by?
questions.onCorrect: A share of GDP divides the dollar figure by the size of the economy. If the share rises by less than the dollars, the economy has grown as well.

acceptedIdeas: GDP has grown too, so debt has risen much less when it is set against the size of the economy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GDP has grown too, so debt has risen much less when it is set against the size of the economy

choices.label: One of the two rows must be wrong, because the same debt cannot rise by two different amounts
The share row leaves out some of the debt, so it has grown more slowly than the dollar row
GDP has grown too, so debt has risen much less when it is set against the size of the economy
The share row compares debt with the Government's receipts, which have grown faster than debt

misconceptions.feedback: Both rows are right. They measure the same debt in different ways: one in dollars and one divided by the size of the economy.
Both rows are gross debt, and the share row divides the same dollars by GDP. Nothing is left out.
The row is headed per cent of GDP, so the debt is compared with the size of the economy, and not with what the Government collects.

questions.prompt: A reader wants to know the total the Government must hand back to the holders of its bonds when they mature. Which measure in the Budget table answers that, and why?
hints: Look at the definitions in the notes under the table. One of them mentions what is paid back at maturity.
A measure that subtracts assets will be smaller than one that does not. Which of the two figures in the table is smaller?
questions.onCorrect: Gross debt is the face value of the securities, which is the amount repaid to investors at maturity. Net debt takes off selected financial assets.

acceptedIdeas: Gross debt, because it is the face value of the securities, which is repaid at maturity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Gross debt, because it is the face value of the securities, which is repaid at maturity

choices.label: Gross debt, because it is the face value of the securities, which is repaid at maturity
Net debt, because it is the broader measure and so counts everything the Government owes in total
Net interest, because it is the part of the debt that has to be paid back in each single year
Either one, because the two measures differ only in how the same figures are rounded off in the table

misconceptions.feedback: Net debt subtracts some of the financial assets the Government holds and counts securities at market value. It is a different measure, and it is not the amount repaid at maturity.
Net interest is the interest paid less the interest received. It is a cost of carrying the debt and not the amount borrowed.
The measures differ in what they count. Net debt takes off selected financial assets, which is why it is the lower of the two in every year of the table.

questions.prompt: From 2026-27 to 2029-30, gross debt rises from 34.0 to 35.6 per cent of GDP, while net interest payments rise from 0.6 to 0.9 per cent of GDP. Which grows faster, and what does the Budget excerpt say about why?
hints: Work out how much each figure has risen compared with where it started, not by how big it is.
The question asks what the excerpt says about why. Does it give a reason, or only the figures?
questions.onCorrect: The interest bill rises by about half and the debt ratio by under 5 per cent. The excerpt shows the figures and does not give the reason.

acceptedIdeas: The interest bill grows much faster, and the excerpt gives no reason for it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The interest bill grows much faster, and the excerpt gives no reason for it

choices.label: The debt ratio grows faster, because 35.6 is a much bigger number than 0.9
The interest bill grows much faster, and the excerpt gives no reason for it
They grow at the same pace, because the interest bill is a fixed share of whatever debt there is
The interest bill grows faster because the Government borrows more each year than the economy grows

misconceptions.feedback: Growth is measured against the starting figure. The debt ratio rises by under 5 per cent of itself, while the interest figure rises by half.
The two rows show different growth, so the interest bill is not a fixed share of the debt ratio. The ratio is nearly flat while the interest bill rises.
The excerpt gives no such cause, and the debt ratio is nearly flat over these years. A reader should not supply a reason that the document does not give.

questions.prompt: In 2025-26 the Budget's cash deficit is 1.0 per cent of GDP and its structural deficit peaks at 1.6 per cent. Why is the structural deficit the larger of the two?
hints: The structural balance removes the estimated effects of cyclical factors. In which direction do they push the cash balance in 2025-26?
If something temporary is making the cash result look better, what happens to the figure when it is taken out?
questions.onCorrect: Commodity prices are adding to the cash balance for now. Taking the temporary help out leaves a larger deficit.

extracts.text: Cyclical factors are estimated to have a positive contribution to the underlying cash balance in 2025–26 and 2026–27, in large part due to elevated commodity prices.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia, Budget Paper No. 1, 2026-27, Statement 3 (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The Government's own account of its Budget

acceptedIdeas: Commodity prices are lifting this year's cash balance, and the structural figure strips out that help
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Commodity prices are lifting this year's cash balance, and the structural figure strips out that help

choices.label: Commodity prices are lifting this year's cash balance, and the structural figure strips out that help
The structural measure adds spending the Government has planned but not yet paid, so it comes out bigger
The two measures are the same figure counted in two ways, so one of the printed numbers must be wrong
Commodity prices are hurting the cash balance, and the structural measure leaves those effects out

misconceptions.feedback: The structural balance is the cash balance with cyclical effects removed. It does not add planned spending.
They differ because the structural measure removes the estimated temporary effects of commodity prices and the economic cycle. The numbers are both as the Budget states them.
The extract says cyclical factors make a positive contribution, mostly because commodity prices are high. High prices help the cash balance.

questions.prompt: Seven sentences are reworded from the same Budget paper. What kind of statement is each one?
hints: Ask whether the sentence says what a term means, looks ahead, assesses the Government's own work, or reports someone else's view.
A forecast says what is expected and depends on assumptions. A judgement says something is good or bad, or that it works.
questions.onCorrect: The Government is the author throughout, and what a reader does with each sentence depends on its kind: look up a definition, test a forecast's assumptions, weigh a judgement and check a report of others.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two sentences about net debt and net interest are definitions, the two about gross debt and balance are forecasts, the two about the fiscal position and inflation are judgements, and the IMF sentence reports what another body expects.

bins.label: A report of what others say

items.label: Net debt counts what the Government owes at market value, less some of the financial assets it holds
items.explanation: It says what a term in the table means, and the notes under the table give the same.

items.label: Net interest payments are the interest the Government pays, less the interest it receives
items.explanation: It is a definition of a row in the table.

items.label: Gross debt should peak in 2028-29, at 35.8 per cent of GDP, and then drop to 27.2 per cent by 2036-37
items.explanation: It is a projection that depends on assumptions about growth, prices and policy.

items.label: The budget should come back into balance in 2034-35
items.explanation: A date in the future is a projection, not something that has been observed.

items.label: This update delivers big improvements in the fiscal position
items.explanation: It is the Government's own assessment of its work, and a reader can argue with it.

items.label: This update takes pressure off inflation
items.explanation: It is the Government's claim about what its budget does, and the table does not measure it.

items.label: The International Monetary Fund expects Australia's budget balance to rank third among G20 countries in 2027
items.explanation: It reports what another body expects, and a reader can check it with that body.

questions.prompt: An invented radio host says, "The Government should run its books like a household, or the debt will sink us." What can you say about that, using this passage?
hints: Read what the passage says about commentators, and then what it says about economists. Which does it report as the majority view?
Ask whether the passage claims that the host is wrong, or only reports that the comparison is challenged.
questions.onCorrect: The article says economists generally challenge the comparison. That is a reason to ask the host for another argument.

extracts.text: In public discourse, politicians and commentators frequently draw parallels between government debt and household debt, as they argue that a government taking on debt is akin to a household taking on debt. However, economists generally challenge this analogy, as the functions and constraints of governments and households are vastly dissimilar.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Government debt" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: The article reports that economists generally challenge the comparison, so the host needs another argument
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The article reports that economists generally challenge the comparison, so the host needs another argument

choices.label: The article reports that economists generally challenge the comparison, so the host needs another argument
The passage shows that debt can never be a problem for any government, so the host is simply wrong about debt
The passage backs the host, because it says that politicians and commentators often draw this parallel
The passage tells us nothing, because a Wikipedia article cannot report what economists think about debt

misconceptions.feedback: The passage does not go that far. It reports that economists challenge the analogy, and elsewhere the article describes risks from debt.
Describing what commentators say is not endorsing it. The passage then reports that economists generally challenge the comparison.
The article is a summary by volunteer editors, and its claim should be attributed to the article. It is still evidence of what the editors report economists to say.

questions.prompt: Two invented countries report budget deficits. Country X has a deficit of 50 billion dollars and a GDP of 2,000 billion. Country Y has a deficit of 5 billion and a GDP of 40 billion. Which has the larger deficit compared with its economy?
hints: Divide each deficit by its country's GDP, roughly, and compare the two shares.
Why does the Budget give the deficit as a share of GDP as well as in dollars?
questions.onCorrect: Y's deficit is about 12.5 per cent of its GDP and X's is 2.5 per cent, so Y's is five times as large relative to its economy.

acceptedIdeas: Y, because its deficit is a much larger share of its GDP than X's is
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Y, because its deficit is a much larger share of its GDP than X's is

choices.label: X, because a deficit of 50 billion dollars is ten times larger than one of 5 billion
Neither can be judged, because a deficit means nothing unless the debt is known as well
They cannot be compared, because the two economies are different sizes
Y, because its deficit is a much larger share of its GDP than X's is

misconceptions.feedback: The dollar sizes are not comparable on their own. X's economy is fifty times larger than Y's, so its larger deficit is a smaller share of its GDP.
Debt matters for the full picture, but the question is about the deficit relative to the economy, and the share of GDP answers it.
Different sizes are the reason for using a share of GDP. It puts deficits from economies of any size on one scale.

questions.prompt: The structural budget balance removes the estimated temporary effects of the economic cycle and of commodity prices. For each change below, does the structural balance take it out or leave it in?
hints: Ask whether the change is temporary and tied to prices or to the state of the economy, or lasting and tied to a policy.
The Budget says the structural balance leaves out the short-lived effects of the cycle and of prices.
questions.onCorrect: The structural balance strips out the temporary effects of prices and the cycle and keeps the lasting effects of policy.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The iron ore, unemployment payments and commodity price changes are cyclical and taken out, while the tax cut, the new annual payment and the saving measure are lasting and stay in.

bins.label: Taken out of the structural balance

items.label: Iron ore prices are above their long-run level, so company tax receipts are higher than usual
items.explanation: A price deviation from its long-run level is a cyclical effect on receipts, and it is estimated and removed.

items.label: Economic activity is below its long-run level, so more people receive unemployment payments
items.explanation: A deviation of activity from its long-run level is a cyclical effect on payments.

items.label: Commodity prices are temporarily below their long-run level, so receipts are lower than usual
items.explanation: The adjustment works in both directions. A temporary shortfall is taken out as well.

items.label: The Government cuts an income tax rate permanently, so receipts are lower in every future year
items.explanation: A lasting policy change is not a temporary cyclical effect, so it remains in the structural balance.

items.label: A new payment is legislated to continue every year
items.explanation: A permanent payment changes the structural position, so the structural balance keeps it.

items.label: A saving measure cuts a program's spending in every future year
items.explanation: A lasting change to spending is a structural effect.

questions.prompt: A reader quotes this sentence to argue that Australia's debt is dangerous. The Budget's Table 3.1 gives gross debt peaking at 35.8 per cent of GDP, and it covers the Australian Government general government sector. Which reading is the most careful?
hints: Compare the number in the sentence with the number in the Budget, and ask what the sentence claims: a rule or some evidence?
The sentence is about government debt in general. Ask whether the Budget table measures the same thing.
questions.onCorrect: The sentence is a report of some evidence, and the Budget's figure is well below it. The table's coverage is narrower than government debt as a whole.

extracts.text: Some evidence suggests growth rates are lower for countries with government debt greater than around 80 percent of GDP.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Government debt" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: It reports some evidence, and 35.8 is well below 80, though the table covers only the Australian Government
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It reports some evidence, and 35.8 is well below 80, though the table covers only the Australian Government

choices.label: It proves that debt above 80 per cent always lowers growth, so Australia is safe whatever happens below it now
It reports some evidence, and 35.8 is well below 80, though the table covers only the Australian Government
It shows Australia's debt is dangerous, because the Budget has gross debt rising to a peak
It can be ignored, because anything written in an encyclopedia article is simply an opinion

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence says some evidence suggests it. A report of some evidence does not prove a rule or make everything below the level safe.
The peak in the Budget is 35.8 per cent, which is well under the 80 per cent in the sentence. A rise to a peak is not itself a danger.
The article should be attributed and weighed, and not ignored. Here it reports evidence about debt and growth that a reader can compare with the table.

questions.prompt: Suppose a recession pushes up unemployment and Parliament passes no new law about taxes or payments. What is the likeliest effect on the Government's budget deficit?
hints: Think about what happens to the tax people pay, and to who receives payments, when jobs are lost.
Ask whether the change needs anyone to decide anything, or whether the existing rules produce it.

acceptedIdeas: It widens, because less tax comes in and more payments go out under existing rules
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It widens, because less tax comes in and more payments go out under existing rules

choices.label: It stays the same, because a deficit changes only when Parliament votes to change it
It widens, because less tax comes in and more payments go out under existing rules
It narrows, because a weaker economy leaves the Government with less to spend on
It widens, but only because Ministers have decided to spend a good deal more

questions.onCorrect: Tax collected falls with incomes and payments rise with unemployment, so the deficit widens under rules that are already in place.

misconceptions.feedback: Some changes need a vote, but tax and payment rules also respond on their own. Income tax collected falls with incomes and more people qualify for payments, so the deficit moves without a new law.
Payments rise in a downturn and tax revenue falls. Both push the deficit up, so a weaker economy widens it.
Ministers may decide to spend more, though the deficit widens without that. Falling tax revenue and rising payments do it under rules already in place.

questions.prompt: Is each of these measures automatic or discretionary? The last one is an invented case.
hints: Ask of each measure whether anyone has to decide something new for it to happen.
A rule that is already in place and moves with incomes or prices is automatic.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Automatic: income tax collected falling with incomes, more people qualifying for unemployment payments and payments rising with indexation. Discretionary: the three-month excise cut, a new tax offset and a one-off bonus payment.

items.label: Income tax collected falls as people's incomes fall
items.explanation: The tax rules are already in place and the amount collected follows incomes, so no decision is needed.

items.label: More people qualify for unemployment payments in a downturn
items.explanation: The entitlement exists already, and more people meet it when jobs are lost.

items.label: Payments rise because they are indexed to prices
items.explanation: Indexation is a rule, so the rise follows from the price index with no new decision.

items.label: Excise on petrol and diesel is cut for three months
items.explanation: The 2026-27 Budget more than halved the excise for a temporary period, which was a decision.

items.label: Parliament passes a new tax offset for workers
items.explanation: A new offset is a change to the law that someone chose to make.

items.label: A one-off bonus payment is announced for households (invented case)
items.explanation: An announcement is a decision, even though the payment goes out through existing systems.

questions.onCorrect: Measures that follow from rules already in place are automatic, and those that someone announces or legislates are discretionary.

questions.prompt: In the wind farm town, suppose the people who are paid save 8 of every 10 extra dollars and spend only 2. Compared with the first $10 million, what happens to the total rise in GDP?
hints: Work out the second round: if 2 of every 10 dollars are spent, how much of the first $10 million is passed on?
Each round is a fifth of the one before, so ask how many rounds are big enough to matter.

acceptedIdeas: It is a little above $10 million, because each round passes on very little
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a little above $10 million, because each round passes on very little

choices.label: It is still about $50 million, because the first $10 million is the same
It is far above $50 million, because the money that is saved gets spent later
It is a little above $10 million, because each round passes on very little
It is below $10 million, because saved money leaves the economy altogether

questions.onCorrect: Only 2 of every 10 dollars is passed on, so the rounds are $10m, $2m, $0.4m and so on, about $12.5m in all.

misconceptions.feedback: The first round is the same, and the later rounds are not. With only 2 of every 10 dollars passed on, they shrink almost at once.
In this example, saved money drops out of the chain of spending. Each round passes on only 2 of every 10 dollars, so the total is small.
The first $10 million has already been spent and counts, so the total can't be below it. Saving only cuts the later rounds short.

questions.prompt: The same A$1 billion of extra government spending is announced in two invented economies. Economy A has high unemployment and idle factories. In Economy B every worker and factory is already in use and demand is outrunning supply. What is most likely?
hints: Ask in each economy whether there are idle workers and machines that the extra demand could put to work.
Where nothing is idle, extra demand has to bid for resources already in use. What does bidding do to prices?

acceptedIdeas: More output and jobs in A and more price rises or crowded-out spending in B, because A has idle resources
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More output and jobs in A and more price rises or crowded-out spending in B, because A has idle resources

choices.label: More output and jobs in A and more price rises or crowded-out spending in B, because A has idle resources
The same rise in output in both, because a dollar of spending has the same multiplier everywhere
No effect in A and a large effect in B, because idle resources cannot respond and busy firms can
Output falls in both, because extra government spending always pushes up interest rates and crowds out investment

questions.onCorrect: Idle resources can meet extra demand with extra output. At capacity the same demand competes for resources already in use, so more of it shows up in prices and imports.

misconceptions.feedback: A multiplier isn't a fixed number. Idle resources let extra demand become extra output, and fully used resources don't.
This reverses the role of spare capacity. Idle resources are what allow extra demand to turn into output and jobs.
Crowding out depends on conditions. With plenty of spare capacity the extra demand doesn't have to compete for resources, and Wikipedia says the stimulus is then much more effective.

questions.prompt: A government can raise payments to low-income households or cut taxes for high-income households, by the same total amount. Wikipedia reports it may be argued that one of these has the larger multiplier. Which one, and why?
hints: The total cost is the same, so look at what each group does with an extra dollar.
Which group is likelier to be short of money and so to spend most of what it receives?

acceptedIdeas: Payments to low-income households, because they spend more of each extra dollar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Payments to low-income households, because they spend more of each extra dollar

choices.label: Tax cuts for high-income households, because each of them receives a larger amount
Neither, because households don't change their spending when their income changes in the short run
They are equal, because the same number of dollars enters the economy either way
Payments to low-income households, because they spend more of each extra dollar

questions.onCorrect: Wikipedia's argument is that households held back by their incomes spend a bigger share of anything extra, and spend it sooner.

misconceptions.feedback: The two options cost the same in total, so the cheque size doesn't decide it. What matters is how much of each dollar is spent, which starts the next round.
Wikipedia says the multiplier depends on the marginal propensity to consume, which is the response of spending to extra income. It is larger for households whose spending is constrained by income.
The same dollars enter, and the first round is the same size. The difference is how much is spent rather than saved, and it grows with each round.

questions.prompt: Fuel prices have jumped and demand in the economy is strong. How does the Government's three-month cut to fuel excise differ from the RBA raising the cash rate as a response?
hints: Ask which price each tool changes directly, and which it changes only by way of spending.
One of the two tools was announced as temporary. What does that say about how long its effect on the price lasts?

acceptedIdeas: The cut lowers the pump price directly for three months, while a rate rise acts on spending across the economy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cut lowers the pump price directly for three months, while a rate rise acts on spending across the economy

choices.label: Both work only by slowing demand, so the cut acts through the economy in the same way a rate rise does
The cut lowers the pump price directly for three months, while a rate rise acts on spending across the economy
The cut lowers inflation for good, while a rate rise lowers it only for the three months of the cut
The cut has no effect on the price at the pump, because the price of oil is set in markets overseas, not here

questions.onCorrect: The two tools act on different parts of the problem: one lowers a price for a limited time and costs the Budget, the other restrains spending across the economy.

misconceptions.feedback: An excise cut removes tax from the pump price, so the price falls directly. A rate rise works by raising borrowing costs and slowing spending.
This reverses the time frames. The cut is temporary by design, and the cash rate stays where the Board puts it until the Board changes it.
The Budget says the cut lowers the cost of a 65-litre tank by nearly $23, so excise is part of the price drivers pay.

questions.prompt: A boost to spending is announced in each of these situations. Does the situation send more of the boost into output and jobs, or less?
hints: Go back to the four things that change the size: spare capacity, who spends, leakages and the central bank.
For each situation, ask whether it leaves the next round of spending larger or smaller.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More into output: idle builders and equipment, pensioners spending locally, and a central bank that holds rates. Less: households that save nearly everything, spending on imports, and a central bank that raises rates.

items.label: Builders and equipment sit idle across a region when a road project is announced
items.explanation: Idle resources can be put to work without bidding up prices, so the extra demand turns into output.

items.label: Pensioners receive extra payments and spend them in local shops
items.explanation: Wikipedia says low-income households spend a large share of extra income, and that pensioners' spending tends to go to local businesses.

items.label: The central bank holds interest rates where they are while the extra spending works through
items.explanation: Wikipedia says the strength of a stimulus depends on how accommodating the central bank is.

items.label: A tax cut goes to households that save nearly all of any extra income
items.explanation: Saving is a leakage, so very little is passed on to the next round.

items.label: Most of what households buy with a new payment is imported
items.explanation: Imports are a leakage: the spending pays producers overseas and doesn't become income at home.

items.label: The central bank raises interest rates to head off overheating from the extra spending
items.explanation: Higher rates offset part of the stimulus, which lowers its effect on output.

questions.onCorrect: Spare capacity, spending at home and a central bank that doesn't lean against the boost make a larger effect on output. Saving, imports and higher interest rates make a smaller one.

questions.prompt: Source A is the Government's judgement of its own Budget. Source B is the RBA's description of the economy. A reader says Source B confirms Source A. What does Source B give someone weighing the claim?

extracts.text: This budget update helps to take the pressure off inflation, delivers substantial improvements in the fiscal position, and cuts taxes for workers and businesses.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia, Budget Paper No. 1, 2026-27, Statement 3 (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The Government's own account of its Budget

extracts.text: The economy is currently operating with excess demand and is judged to reach balance next year, slightly later than previously thought, with spare capacity emerging in 2027.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026: Overview (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The RBA's quarterly assessment of the economy and its outlook

hints: Ask what Source B is describing: the Budget, or the condition of the whole economy?
What would you need to know to say how much a Budget changes inflation, and is it in either extract?

acceptedIdeas: A picture of how fully resources are in use, which bears on the claim without testing it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A picture of how fully resources are in use, which bears on the claim without testing it

choices.label: An estimate, in percentage points, of how much the Budget has lowered inflation in the year
A rejection of Source A, because excess demand shows that the Budget has pushed prices up
A picture of how fully resources are in use, which bears on the claim without testing it
A confirmation of Source A, because both documents are official and both are about inflation

questions.onCorrect: Source B says the economy has excess demand. That is context for judging a claim about inflation, and it leaves the size of the Budget's effect untested.

misconceptions.feedback: Source B has no estimate of the Budget's effect. It describes the economy, and a claim about the Budget needs a separate measure of what the Budget does.
Excess demand describes the economy and doesn't show what the Budget did to prices. Source B can't refute the claim any more than it can confirm it.
Two official documents on the same subject don't confirm each other. Source B says nothing about what the Budget does.

questions.prompt: A state government's new rail project hires most of a region's available engineers when the region is already at full employment, and private firms that planned their own projects cannot find staff (an invented case). What do economists call it when government activity displaces private activity in this way?
hints: Think about who gets the engineers when there are none to spare.
The word describes private activity being pushed aside, as if the government took up the room.

acceptedIdeas: crowding out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Crowding out: the government's project uses resources that private firms would have used.

questions.onCorrect: At full employment the government project competes for scarce engineers, so private projects are displaced. That is resource crowding out.

misconceptions.feedback: The multiplier is the ratio of the final rise in GDP to the first change in spending. The term wanted names what happens when government activity uses resources private firms would have used.
A leakage takes part of each round out of domestic spending through saving, taxes or imports. Here the resources are being used by the government and the private firms are the ones left short.
An automatic stabiliser is a budget rule that responds to the economy without a decision. This project was chosen, and the effect on private firms is something else.
Crowding in is the opposite: extra demand encourages private spending. Here private projects are the ones that lose out.

questions.prompt: Suppose AUD/USD is 0.75, so that A$1 exchanges for 75 US cents. The rate then moves to 0.70. What has happened?
hints: Read the quote as the RBA does: how many US cents does one Australian dollar buy?
Compare what A$1 buys at 0.75 with what it buys at 0.70.

acceptedIdeas: The Australian dollar has lost value, because it now buys 70 US cents where it bought 75
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Australian dollar has lost value, because it now buys 70 US cents where it bought 75

choices.label: The Australian dollar has gained value, because a smaller number means a stronger currency
The Australian dollar has lost value, because it now buys 70 US cents where it bought 75
The US dollar has lost value, because AUD/USD counts Australian dollars per US dollar
Nothing has happened to its value, because an exchange rate is only a ratio of two numbers

questions.onCorrect: At 0.70 one Australian dollar converts into 70 US cents instead of 75, so it has lost value against the US dollar. The RBA calls that a depreciation.

misconceptions.feedback: A smaller AUD/USD number means each Australian dollar buys fewer US cents, so the Australian dollar is worth less.
AUD/USD gives the US cents you receive for one Australian dollar, as the 0.75 example shows. This option reads the quote the other way round.
The ratio is the price of one currency in the other. When it falls, the Australian dollar buys less US currency, so its value has changed.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes how the value of the Australian dollar is set?
hints: Recall what the RBA says about the regime Australia has had since 1983.
Ask whether any single body sets the price, or whether it moves with buyers and sellers.

acceptedIdeas: Buyers and sellers of currency set it, with the RBA stepping in only on rare occasions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers and sellers of currency set it, with the RBA stepping in only on rare occasions

choices.label: The RBA sets it at each Board meeting, alongside its decision on the cash rate target
It is pegged to the US dollar, at a rate that the Government announces in each Budget
The Government adjusts it each year, so that Australia's exports stay above its imports
Buyers and sellers of currency set it, with the RBA stepping in only on rare occasions

questions.onCorrect: A floating dollar is priced by the market, and the RBA steps in only on rare occasions, such as when trading becomes disorderly.

misconceptions.feedback: The dollar has floated since 1983. The cash rate is one influence on it, because it affects interest rate differentials, but the Board doesn't set the exchange rate.
A peg ties a currency to another one, as the Danish krone is tied to the euro. Australia has had a floating rate since 1983.
No government adjusts the Australian dollar by decision. It floats, so buyers and sellers of currency determine it.

questions.prompt: Source A is an ABS figure for the June quarter of 2026 and Source B is the RBA's view in November. Over the year the Board also raised the cash rate target at five meetings. By the RBA's own rules about what moves the dollar, which fact points the same way as the appreciation?

extracts.text: The terms of trade fell 1.6%.
extracts.who: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Australian National Accounts: National Income, Expenditure and Product (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The ABS's key statistics for the June quarter 2026

extracts.text: The Australian dollar has appreciated since the start of the year and is judged to be around estimates of its long-run equilibrium.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026: Overview (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The RBA's quarterly assessment of the economy and its outlook

hints: Take each fact in turn and ask which way the RBA says it moves the dollar, all else being equal.
The terms of trade compare export prices with import prices. Is a fall in it good or bad news for the demand for Australian dollars?

acceptedIdeas: The cash rate rises, because higher Australian interest rates tend to lift the dollar
