answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cash rate rises, because higher Australian interest rates tend to lift the dollar

choices.label: The cash rate rises, because higher Australian interest rates tend to lift the dollar
The fall in the terms of trade, because it shows that Australian goods have become cheaper to foreign buyers
Both of them, because any news about prices raises the value of a currency
Neither of them, because the RBA sets the exchange rate and ignores these factors

questions.onCorrect: The RBA says higher Australian interest rates support a higher dollar and a fall in the terms of trade goes with a lower one, so the two facts pull in opposite directions.

misconceptions.feedback: A drop in the terms of trade goes with a weaker dollar, so it points the other way. It means export prices fell against import prices.
The RBA's rules give each driver a direction. A rise in interest rates supports the dollar, and a fall in the terms of trade goes with a lower dollar.
The RBA floats the dollar and doesn't set it, and its explainer lists interest rate differentials and the terms of trade among the drivers of its value.

questions.prompt: Is each of these parties helped or hurt by a rise in the value of the Australian dollar?
hints: For each party, ask whether a higher dollar makes what they buy cheaper or what they sell dearer.
A higher dollar makes foreign goods cheaper for Australians and Australian goods dearer for foreigners.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Helped: the household buying imports, the firm repaying foreign-currency debt and the family on holiday overseas. Hurt: the exporter, the manufacturer competing with imports and the hotel selling to overseas tourists.

items.label: A household buying imported goods
items.explanation: Imports cost fewer Australian dollars, so the household's money goes further.

items.label: An Australian exporter selling to overseas buyers
items.explanation: Its goods become dearer in foreign currency, which makes the exporter less competitive.

items.label: A firm repaying a loan in a foreign currency
items.explanation: Each Australian dollar buys more of that currency, so fewer are needed to repay. The RBA describes the reverse for a depreciation.

items.label: A local manufacturer competing with imports
items.explanation: Imports become cheaper, so the manufacturer's price advantage shrinks.

items.label: An Australian family on holiday overseas
items.explanation: The RBA says an appreciation means Australian tourists need fewer Australian dollars to pay for meals and hotels overseas.

items.label: A Cairns hotel that sells rooms to overseas tourists
items.explanation: Its rooms cost visitors more in their own currency, so fewer may come.

questions.onCorrect: A higher dollar makes foreign goods and currencies cheaper for Australians and Australian goods dearer for foreigners, which helps buyers of foreign things and hurts sellers abroad.

questions.prompt: Six months after the Australian dollar fell sharply, a commentator notes that the trade balance has worsened and says a lower dollar can't help exporters. What does the RBA's account of the J-curve suggest about that conclusion?
hints: Separate the effect on prices, which is immediate, from the effect on volumes, which comes later.
Does a worse trade balance after six months rule out an improvement after more time?

acceptedIdeas: It is premature, because net exports are likely to fall first and improve as volumes respond
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is premature, because net exports are likely to fall first and improve as volumes respond

choices.label: It is sound, because a falling dollar always makes imports dearer and so always widens the deficit
It is mistaken, because a fall in the dollar improves the trade balance as soon as it happens
It is premature, because net exports are likely to fall first and improve as volumes respond
It is beside the point, because the exchange rate has no effect on the trade balance at all

questions.onCorrect: In the short run a falling dollar tends to lower the value of net exports, and the RBA says the volume response lifts it later.

misconceptions.feedback: Imports do cost more at once, which is the direct effect. The RBA says export and import volumes respond later, and that tends to improve the balance over time.
The RBA says the opposite happens first: the direct effect of dearer imports comes at once and the volume response comes with a lag.
The RBA treats the exchange rate as a main influence on the value of exports and imports, through both prices and volumes.

questions.prompt: A retailer pays an overseas car maker $2 million for a shipment of cars, using money in its Australian bank account. (This is an invented case.) How does the balance of payments record it?
hints: The RBA's Bali holiday example is the model: a service was bought and the payment came from a bank account.
Ask what came in, what went out, and which account records changes in who holds money and assets.

acceptedIdeas: An import in the current account and a matching entry in the financial account, because every transaction has two entries
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An import in the current account and a matching entry in the financial account, because every transaction has two entries

choices.label: One entry only, an import in the current account, because paying from a bank isn't a transaction with the rest of the world
An import in the current account and a matching entry in the financial account, because every transaction has two entries
Two entries, both in the current account, because the cars and the payment are both part of the same trade
An export in the current account, because the retailer's money has left Australia in payment

questions.onCorrect: The cars are an import in the current account, and the payment is the offsetting entry in the financial account, so the two cancel.

misconceptions.feedback: The payment moves money held in an Australian bank into overseas hands, and the financial account records that. Every transaction has two entries.
The cars are trade and belong in the current account. The payment changes who holds the deposits, so it belongs in the financial account.
The cars came into Australia, which makes them an import. The money leaving is the payment side, and it is recorded in the financial account.

questions.prompt: The Australian dollar falls sharply on a Monday. A retailer sells imported appliances that it prices in Australian dollars. Which pattern for its prices over the next year or two fits the RBA's account best?
hints: Which direction does a depreciation push the price of imports?
The retailer sets its own prices. What might make it wait before passing a cost increase on?

acceptedIdeas: Prices rise gradually, because firms wait to see if the fall lasts, and the full effect takes one to three years
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Prices rise gradually, because firms wait to see if the fall lasts, and the full effect takes one to three years

choices.label: Every imported price rises by the full amount on Monday, because costs rise as soon as the currency falls
Prices fall, because a lower dollar makes foreign goods cheaper for Australian buyers to import
Prices stay the same, because the value of the dollar affects only the exporters and not importers
Prices rise gradually, because firms wait to see if the fall lasts, and the full effect takes one to three years

questions.onCorrect: Firms often wait until a move looks lasting, and households and firms then take time to change what they buy, so the full effect builds over one to three years.

misconceptions.feedback: The cost does rise at once, but the RBA says firms pricing in Australian dollars decide when to pass it on, and many wait until a move looks lasting.
A lower dollar makes imports dearer, since more Australian dollars are needed for the same foreign currency. Prices are pushed up, not down.
The RBA says a depreciation raises the prices of imported goods and services, which contributes to inflation in two ways.

questions.prompt: Share prices fall in markets around the world this week. Nothing has changed in Australian interest rates or in the prices of Australia's exports. By the RBA's account, what would you expect for the Australian dollar, and why?
hints: Think of the driver that matters over short periods, and what it tracks.
The question says the other two drivers haven't changed, so what is left?

acceptedIdeas: A fall, because it tends to move with global share prices as the appetite for risk shifts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fall, because it tends to move with global share prices as the appetite for risk shifts

choices.label: A fall, because it tends to move with global share prices as the appetite for risk shifts
A rise, because nervous investors move their money into Australian assets that they see as safe
No change, because nothing has changed in Australia's own economy this week, so nothing moves
A fall, but only if the RBA cuts the cash rate in response to the news from overseas markets

questions.onCorrect: The RBA says the dollar tracks other financial markets over short periods, so it typically falls when global shares do.

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says the Australian dollar typically weakens when global share prices fall, because it moves with investors' willingness to take risk.
The dollar is priced in global markets. The RBA says it moves with global markets and with investors' appetite for risk, whatever is happening at home.
The link to risk sentiment works directly, without a change in the cash rate. Interest rate differentials are a separate driver.

questions.prompt: A commentator says Australia's current account deficit means the country is losing money to the rest of the world every year. Using what the RBA says, what is the best reply?
hints: Recall what the RBA says about the sum of the current account and the capital and financial account.
Ask what Australia has tended to do about funding its investment, and what that implies for the income it pays abroad.

acceptedIdeas: The commentator is wrong, because the deficit is matched by capital flowing in to invest in or lend to Australia
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The commentator is wrong, because the deficit is matched by capital flowing in to invest in or lend to Australia

choices.label: The commentator is right, because a deficit means more money leaves than returns and nothing offsets it
The deficit is cancelled by a budget surplus, because the Government's accounts balance the nation's accounts
The commentator is wrong, because the deficit is matched by capital flowing in to invest in or lend to Australia
The accounts record only trade, so a deficit simply means imports were bigger than exports in the year

questions.onCorrect: The two accounts offset each other. Australia has tended to borrow from overseas to invest, and part of the deficit is the interest it pays on that borrowing.

misconceptions.feedback: The RBA says the two accounts always sum to zero, so a deficit in the current account comes with a surplus in capital flowing in.
The offsetting entry is in the capital and financial account of the balance of payments. The Government's budget is a separate account.
The trade balance is one part of the current account. The account also records income paid abroad, and the financial account matches it.

questions.prompt: Prices of Australia's coal exports rise while the prices of the goods it imports stay about the same. What do economists call the ratio of Australia's export prices to its import prices?
hints: The measure compares what Australia gets for its exports with what it pays for its imports.
The RBA says it has moved closely with the dollar's value for many years.

acceptedIdeas: terms of trade
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The terms of trade, which rise when export prices rise faster than import prices.

questions.onCorrect: With export prices up and import prices steady, the terms of trade rise, which the RBA says tends to go with a higher dollar.

misconceptions.feedback: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. The measure asked about compares export prices with import prices, although the RBA says the two have moved closely together.
The trade balance is the value of exports less imports. The ratio asked about compares export prices with import prices.
The current account is the whole record of goods, services and income with the rest of the world, which is much wider than a ratio of prices.
The trade-weighted index measures the dollar against a basket of currencies. The ratio asked about is a ratio of prices.

questions.prompt: Two invented economies each report GDP growth of 3% over a year. In Economy P hours worked rose 3% and output per hour was unchanged. In Economy Q hours worked were unchanged and output per hour rose 3%. If each kept growing this way for many years, which statement is best supported?
hints: Compare what each economy used more of: hours of work, or output from each hour.
Ask which kind of growth could be repeated every year if people could not work more hours each time.

acceptedIdeas: Economy Q's growth could go on without more labour, because each hour of work now produces more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Economy Q's growth could go on without more labour, because each hour of work now produces more

choices.label: Both would be growing equally well, because 3% growth in GDP means the same whatever lies behind it
Economy Q's growth could go on without more labour, because each hour of work now produces more
Economy P's growth is the stronger kind, because more hours of work add more to total output
Economy Q's figures must contain a mistake, because output cannot rise when hours stay the same

questions.onCorrect: In Q, output grew because each hour produced more, so the same growth could be repeated without more labour. P's growth needed more hours, and hours can't rise every year without limit.

misconceptions.feedback: The totals match, and the sources differ. P's growth needs more hours every year, which can't rise without limit, while Q's comes from getting more out of each hour.
More hours does add to total output, as it did in P, but hours can't keep rising every year. The question is what could go on for many years.
Output can rise with hours unchanged when each hour produces more. That is what a rise in output per hour means, and it is what happened in Q.

questions.prompt: Does each of these add more inputs, or raise output from the same inputs?
hints: Ask of each item whether anything new is being used, or whether the same things are producing more.
More people, more machines and more hours are all inputs. A better method is not.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More inputs: more people joining the labour force, a new mine and longer hours. More output from the same inputs: software, competition reform and shared know-how.

bins.label: More output from the same inputs

items.label: More people join the labour force
items.explanation: A larger workforce is more labour, which is an extra input.

items.label: Software lets the same staff process more claims
items.explanation: The staff and equipment are the same and the output is larger, so productivity has risen.

items.label: A new mine is built
items.explanation: A mine is more capital. Output rises because more is being used, and no more is made from each unit.

items.label: Competition reform pushes firms to use inputs more efficiently
items.explanation: The RBA names microeconomic reform as one way to raise efficiency, which means more output from the same inputs.

items.label: Workers share know-how when they change jobs
items.explanation: The RBA lists knowledge sharing through workers changing jobs as a source of productivity spillovers.

items.label: Workers put in longer hours
items.explanation: More hours is more labour input. Output per hour hasn't changed.

questions.onCorrect: Growth from more labour, capital or hours is extensive, and growth from using the same inputs better is intensive. Only the second is a rise in productivity.

questions.prompt: The bakery's output index is 104 and its combined input index is 106. What has happened to its multifactor productivity?
hints: MFP is output divided by combined inputs. Which index is bigger in year 2?
If inputs grow by 6 and output by only 4, is more or less being made from each unit of input?

acceptedIdeas: It has fallen, because inputs grew by more than output did
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has fallen, because inputs grew by more than output did

choices.label: It has fallen, because inputs grew by more than output did
It has risen, because the bakery's output index went up
It is unchanged, because both of the indexes went up
It can't be said without knowing how much profit the bakery made

questions.onCorrect: Inputs rose by 6 and output by 4, so each unit of input produces less than before and MFP has fallen.

misconceptions.feedback: Output did rise, and so did inputs, by more. MFP compares the two, and a larger rise in inputs means less is made from each unit of them.
Both indexes rose, but not by the same amount. MFP stays the same only if output and inputs grow at the same rate.
MFP is calculated from the volume of output and the volume of inputs, as the RBA's toy factory shows, and profit isn't needed.

questions.prompt: A report says: 'ABS figures show that multifactor productivity in health care has fallen.' Using the extract, what should a careful reader say?

extracts.text: The ABS does not provide MFP estimates for non-market industries, namely public administration and safety, education and training, and health care and social assistance.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Explainer "Productivity" (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: An explainer published by the central bank for the public

hints: Read the extract for which industries the ABS leaves out, and check whether health care is one of them.
If there is no MFP estimate for an industry, can a report cite one?

acceptedIdeas: It can't be tested with that measure, because the ABS publishes no MFP estimate for health care
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It can't be tested with that measure, because the ABS publishes no MFP estimate for health care

choices.label: It is probably true, because health care is a large industry whose costs keep rising year after year
It is false, because productivity never falls when it is measured properly
It can be checked in the ABS's MFP tables, which cover every industry in the economy
It can't be tested with that measure, because the ABS publishes no MFP estimate for health care

questions.onCorrect: The ABS doesn't estimate MFP for non-market industries such as health care, so a claim about a fall in it needs a different source.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says no MFP estimate exists for health care, so there is no figure to show a fall. Rising costs are a different matter from MFP.
Measured productivity can fall, and the RBA says it often does in a downturn. The point here is that the ABS gives no MFP estimate for health care.
The extract says the ABS gives MFP estimates for market industries only, and health care is among the industries it names as excluded.

questions.prompt: A country keeps adding machines per worker but gains no new technology. What does the Solow model, as Wikipedia describes it, predict about growth in output per worker?
hints: Recall what the model says about each extra unit of capital added to the same workers.
A steady state is where investment in capital just matches what wears out. What happens to growth as it is approached?

acceptedIdeas: It slows towards a steady level, because each extra machine adds less than the one before
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It slows towards a steady level, because each extra machine adds less than the one before

choices.label: It speeds up without limit, because every machine adds as much as the one before
It is unaffected, because machines never change what a worker can produce
It slows towards a steady level, because each extra machine adds less than the one before
It turns negative at once, because capital wears out faster than it is added

questions.onCorrect: With diminishing returns and no new technology, output per worker eventually reaches a steady state, so adding machines alone can't keep growth going.

misconceptions.feedback: The model assumes diminishing returns to capital. Each extra machine adds less than the last, so growth can't speed up without limit.
Capital does raise output per worker, up to a point. The model's point is that the gains from adding it shrink.
Depreciation is part of the model, but it only stops growth at the steady state, where investment equals depreciation. Growth slows without turning negative at once.

questions.prompt: Read this sentence from Wikipedia. What can you conclude from the sentence alone?

extracts.text: In 1957 South Korea had a lower per capita GDP than Ghana, and by 2008 it was 17 times as high as Ghana's.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Economic growth" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

hints: Ask what the sentence reports and what it leaves out, such as the reasons.
Does one pair of countries show what always happens, or what can happen?

acceptedIdeas: Income rankings can reverse, because growth kept up for decades lets a poor country overtake a richer one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Income rankings can reverse, because growth kept up for decades lets a poor country overtake a richer one

choices.label: Income rankings can reverse, because growth kept up for decades lets a poor country overtake a richer one
Poor countries always catch up quickly, because capital flows to wherever it is scarce in the world
Rankings of income never change, because rich countries always stay ahead of poor ones
South Korea's success was caused by its exports, because they grew faster than Ghana's

questions.onCorrect: The sentence shows that a gap in growth, kept up for decades, can reverse an ordering. It doesn't say why, and it doesn't show that every poor country catches up.

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence is one pair of countries and says nothing about all poor ones. Wikipedia says elsewhere that in practice convergence was rarely achieved.
The sentence is a counter-example: a country poorer than Ghana in 1957 ended 17 times as rich in 2008.
The sentence gives the outcome and no cause. Any explanation of why Korea grew faster would need other evidence.

questions.prompt: A firm's output falls by 10% in a downturn, but it cuts its labour and equipment use by only 3%. (This is an invented case.) What happens to its measured productivity, and what should we make of it?
hints: Work out roughly what happened to the ratio of output to inputs when output fell by more than inputs did.
Think about why a firm can't cut inputs as quickly as its sales fall.

acceptedIdeas: It falls, because inputs can't be cut as fast as output, so it says little about the trend
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls, because inputs can't be cut as fast as output, so it says little about the trend

choices.label: It rises, because the firm is now using fewer inputs than it was using before the downturn
It falls, because inputs can't be cut as fast as output, so it says little about the trend
It is unchanged, because productivity depends only on the technology the firm uses
It falls, which shows that the firm's workers have become less skilled during the year

questions.onCorrect: Output fell by more than inputs, so measured productivity falls. Economists look over long periods because the cycle moves the short-run figure.

misconceptions.feedback: Productivity is output relative to inputs, and output fell by more than inputs did. The firm gets less from each unit of input.
Measured productivity moves with the cycle as well, since firms can't adjust their inputs as fast as demand changes.
The RBA says productivity tends to fall in a downturn because inputs adjust slowly. That doesn't mean skills have fallen.

questions.prompt: Potential growth is how fast the economy's capacity to produce can grow. What does the sentence imply for the pressure on prices when demand grows at a given pace?

extracts.text: In Australia, weak productivity growth continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the extent and economic effects of the downturn in the housing market.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement by the Monetary Policy Board (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: A media release giving the Board's decision and reasons

hints: Think of capacity as a ceiling on what the economy can supply, and ask how quickly the ceiling is rising.
If demand grows at the same pace but the ceiling rises more slowly, what happens to the gap between them?

acceptedIdeas: The pressure is greater, because capacity grows slowly and demand meets its limit sooner
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pressure is greater, because capacity grows slowly and demand meets its limit sooner

choices.label: The pressure is smaller, because slower potential growth lowers what it costs firms to produce
There is no link, because productivity and prices are measured by different agencies
The pressure is greater, because capacity grows slowly and demand meets its limit sooner
The pressure is greater, because slow growth in capacity means unemployment must be falling

questions.onCorrect: A slower rise in the ceiling on supply means the same growth in demand presses on capacity sooner, and that is the setting in which prices come under pressure.

misconceptions.feedback: Slow growth in capacity doesn't lower costs. It means demand runs into the limit on what the economy can supply sooner.
Who measures them doesn't matter. Capacity sets how much can be supplied, and prices come under pressure when demand outruns it.
Capacity isn't a count of jobs. The sentence is about how fast output can grow, and it says nothing about unemployment.

questions.prompt: A farmer keeps adding workers to a field of fixed size, and each new worker adds less to the harvest than the one before. What name do economists give this pattern?
hints: The field doesn't change, only the number of workers. What happens to the extra output from each one?
The RBA uses a phrase with 'marginal' in it for adding one more unit of an input to the others.

acceptedIdeas: diminishing returns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Diminishing returns: each extra unit of one input, with the others held fixed, adds less than the one before.

questions.onCorrect: Holding the other inputs fixed, each extra worker adds less than the last. That is diminishing returns, and it is why more inputs alone can't keep growth rising.

misconceptions.feedback: Compounding is the way small differences in growth add up over time. The pattern in the question is about the extra output from each extra worker.
Multifactor productivity is output per unit of labour and capital combined. The pattern asked about is the shrinking addition from each extra worker.
Extensive growth is growth from using more inputs. The pattern asked about is why that sort of growth slows.

questions.prompt: The RBA's November forecast table has a row for the cash rate, shown here with its note. The six figures are year averages, running from 2025/26 to 2028. A reader says: 'The RBA has announced that it will raise the cash rate to 4.9 per cent.' The 4.9 is the figure for 2026/27. What do the row and its note support?

extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026: Overview (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: One row of the forecast table, under the year-average columns

extracts.text: (c) The forecasts incorporate several technical assumptions. The cash rate is assumed to move in line with expectations derived from financial market pricing as per 28 October and the daily exchange rate (TWI) is assumed to be unchanged from its level at 28 October 2026 going forward.
extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026: Overview (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The note to the forecast table

hints: Read the note beneath the row. What is the cash rate assumed to follow?
The Board decides the cash rate target at each meeting. Could a table finalised on 28 October announce a decision for 2026/27?

acceptedIdeas: The reader is wrong, because it is a technical assumption taken from market pricing and not a plan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reader is wrong, because it is a technical assumption taken from market pricing and not a plan

choices.label: The reader is right, because the RBA puts a number in its tables only when it intends to deliver it
The reader is right about the level, because 4.9 per cent is the cash rate in force when the forecasts were made
The reader is wrong, because it is a technical assumption taken from market pricing and not a plan
The reader is partly right, because the staff forecast the cash rate in the same way as they forecast inflation

questions.onCorrect: The note says the cash rate is assumed to follow expectations derived from market pricing at 28 October. It records what markets expected, and the Board hasn't announced it.

misconceptions.feedback: The note says the cash rate is assumed to follow expectations from financial market pricing. The number records what markets expected on 28 October, and the Board hasn't announced it.
The cash rate target was 4.60 per cent on 28 October, after the September increase. The 4.9 is an assumed path for a later year.
The note separates the two. Inflation and growth are forecasts, while the cash rate is an assumption taken from market pricing.

questions.prompt: Each of these items quotes or sums up a sentence from the Board's statement of 3 November 2026. Which part of the statement is each?
hints: Ask whether a sentence reports something that has happened, something expected, or something the Board will do.
A sentence about scenarios or forecasts looks ahead, and a sentence about what the data show looks back.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Decision: the increase to 4.85 per cent. Evidence: inflation being broadly based, and the slowing economy and falling housing prices. Outlook: inflation staying above 3 per cent, and the unresolved conflict. Approach: being attentive to the data.

bins.label: What the Board will do next

items.label: The statement opens by saying that the Board has "decided to increase the cash rate target", to 4.85 per cent.
items.explanation: It states what the Board did to the cash rate target, which is the decision itself.

items.label: Inflation "remains elevated", and recent data show it is "broadly based".
items.explanation: It reports what recent data show about inflation, which has already happened.

items.label: The Board says the economy "is slowing" and the unemployment rate "has risen", and that housing prices have fallen "significantly".
items.explanation: It describes the present state of the economy, housing and jobs.

items.label: Inflation is forecast to stay above 3 per cent over the next year, and the Board sees a growing risk that higher inflation expectations become "embedded".
items.explanation: It says what inflation is expected to do and names a risk, so it looks forward.

items.label: The Board treats the Middle East conflict as "unresolved" and describes scenarios in which inflation is higher and activity is lower than forecast.
items.explanation: It describes scenarios that could make the outcome differ from the forecast, which are risks to the outlook.

items.label: The Board says it "will be attentive to the data" and to the outlook and risks, and will use them to guide its decisions.
items.explanation: It says what the Board will pay attention to when it makes later decisions.

questions.onCorrect: The decision is what the Board did, the evidence is what has happened, the outlook is what is expected and what could differ, and the approach is what the Board says it will watch.

questions.prompt: Source A is the GDP growth row of the November forecast table and Source B is the row of previous forecasts printed beneath it. The six figures are for the years ended June 2026, December 2026, June 2027, December 2027, June 2028 and December 2028. How were the GDP growth forecasts revised?

extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026: Overview (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The GDP growth row of the forecast table

extracts.who: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026: Overview (CC BY 4.0)
extracts.kind: The row of previous forecasts printed beneath it

hints: Compare each figure in Source A with the figure beneath it in Source B, one date at a time.
Check whether the direction of the change is the same at the early dates and at the late ones.

acceptedIdeas: Higher through to mid-2027 and lower after that, so stronger activity soon and weaker later
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Higher through to mid-2027 and lower after that, so stronger activity soon and weaker later

choices.label: Higher at every date, so the Bank is more optimistic about growth throughout the forecast period
Lower at every date, because tighter policy is expected to hold growth down all the way through
Revised only at the first date, since later forecasts are simply repeated until new data arrive
Higher through to mid-2027 and lower after that, so stronger activity soon and weaker later

misconceptions.feedback: The last three figures in Source A (1.3, 1.3 and 1.5) are below those in Source B (1.6, 1.6 and 1.8), so they were revised down.
The first three figures in Source A (2.1, 1.6 and 1.6) are above those in Source B (1.9, 1.4 and 1.5), so they were revised up.
Every one of the six figures in Source A differs from the one beneath it in Source B, so the whole path was revised.

questions.prompt: Source A is from the Board's statement of 11 August, when it left the cash rate at 4.35 per cent. Source B is from 29 September, when it raised the rate to 4.60 per cent. Which new information did the Board cite for the change?

acceptedIdeas: The conflict had broadened, energy prices ran well above forecast, and growth and inflation beat expectations
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conflict had broadened, energy prices ran well above forecast, and growth and inflation beat expectations

choices.label: The conflict had broadened, energy prices ran well above forecast, and growth and inflation beat expectations
The Government had cut taxes in the Budget, so the Board raised the rate to offset the extra spending it caused
The dollar had fallen sharply, which made imports dearer and called for a response from the Board in September
Unemployment had fallen below 4 per cent, which showed that the labour market had become very tight

extracts.kind: The voting line of the media release

hints: Read what the three members voted for, and compare it with what the headline says they wanted.
Look at the table: did a split vote, or the wording of a statement, tell you what the next meeting would do?

acceptedIdeas: Only that the Board was divided about this decision, because a vote shows nothing about what comes next
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only that the Board was divided about this decision, because a vote shows nothing about what comes next

choices.label: That another rise is certain, because a majority has already formed in favour of raising rates
Only that the Board was divided about this decision, because a vote shows nothing about what comes next
That a cut is likely soon, because three of the members already wanted a lower cash rate
That the Governor alone decides, because the other members only advise on the day of the meeting

misconceptions.feedback: A majority for this decision doesn't bind the Board next time. In the 2026 table, as the course reads it, neither the votes nor the closing wording lined up with the next decision.

The statement reports that six members voted to raise the rate and three voted against, so the decision was made by a vote.

questions.prompt: Source A is from the Board's statement of 11 August and Source B is from the Statement on Monetary Policy in November. What changed between them?

The Board now expects inflation to take longer to return to the midpoint of its range

flashcards.front: What do we call GDP with the effect of price changes taken out?
flashcards.back: Real GDP. It moves only when the volume produced moves, while nominal GDP also moves with prices.

acceptedIdeas: real gdp
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Real GDP. It moves only when the volume produced moves, while nominal GDP also moves with prices.

flashcards.front: Why can nominal GDP rise in a year when the economy has made nothing extra?
flashcards.back: Nominal GDP is output valued at the prices of the time, so higher prices raise it even if the volume produced stays the same.

flashcards.front: In the ABS national accounts, which measure shows whether each hour of work now produces more than before?
flashcards.back: GDP per hour worked, which the ABS lists under productivity. For the year to June 2026 it fell 0.2%.

acceptedIdeas: per hour worked
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GDP per hour worked, which the ABS lists under productivity. For the year to June 2026 it fell 0.2%.

flashcards.front: Name one thing a rise in GDP would not tell you about whether a typical household is better off, and say why.
flashcards.back: For example who receives the income (GDP is silent on how evenly it is shared), unpaid work (not counted), or spending that only replaces what was lost, such as rebuilding after a natural disaster.

flashcards.front: In the ABS labour force statistics, what word describes people who have a job but want and could work more hours?
flashcards.back: Underemployed. The ABS counts them as employed, so they are in the underemployment rate and not the unemployment rate.

acceptedIdeas: underemployed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Underemployed. The ABS counts them as employed, so they are in the underemployment rate and not the unemployment rate.

flashcards.front: Why can the unemployment rate rise in a month when employment also rises?
flashcards.back: More people who were outside the labour force start looking, so the labour force grows. If some of them don't find work at once, the number unemployed and the labour force both rise, and so does the rate.

flashcards.front: What do we call the number of unemployed plus underemployed people, as a percentage of the labour force?
flashcards.back: The underutilisation rate. For October 2026 the ABS reported 11.1%, seasonally adjusted.

acceptedIdeas: underutilisation rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The underutilisation rate. For October 2026 the ABS reported 11.1%, seasonally adjusted.

flashcards.front: A monthly unemployment rate rises 0.1 points and the ABS gives a 95% confidence interval of -0.1 to 0.3 points for the change. Why is that weak evidence that unemployment is rising?
flashcards.back: The interval includes zero, so the true change could be nothing or a small fall. The ABS advises caution with short-term changes and says the trend is the best guide to underlying behaviour.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the average inflation rate after the items with the largest price changes are trimmed away?
flashcards.back: The trimmed mean: the average price change of the middle 70 per cent of the basket by weight, once the items are ranked by price change.

acceptedIdeas: trimmed mean
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The trimmed mean: the average price change of the middle 70 per cent of the basket by weight, once the items are ranked by price change.

flashcards.front: What decides how much weight each item gets in the CPI basket?
flashcards.back: How much households spend on it. An item that takes more of household spending has a bigger say in the CPI.

acceptedIdeas: household spending
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How much households spend on it. An item that takes more of household spending has a bigger say in the CPI.

flashcards.front: Annual headline CPI inflation is 4.3% and the trimmed mean is 3.6%. What might explain the gap, and what does 3.6% still show?
flashcards.back: A few very large price rises can lift headline above the trimmed mean, which sets the largest movers aside. At 3.6% the trimmed mean is still above the target range of 2 to 3 per cent.

flashcards.front: Why is the CPI not an ideal measure of one household's cost of living?
flashcards.back: It prices an average basket for capital cities, weighted by average spending, so a household that spends differently faces a different rise. The RBA says cost-of-living inflation is the rise in spending a household needs to keep up its standard of living.

flashcards.front: What name does the RBA give inflation that starts when the cost of inputs such as oil rises and firms supply less?
flashcards.back: Cost-push inflation. A fall in aggregate supply from higher input costs pushes prices up while output falls.

acceptedIdeas: cost-push
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cost-push inflation. A fall in aggregate supply from higher input costs pushes prices up while output falls.

flashcards.front: What word does the RBA use for expectations that stay tied to the inflation target even when current inflation is high?
flashcards.back: Anchored. When expectations are anchored a spike from a cost shock is likely to fade.

acceptedIdeas: anchored
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Anchored. When expectations are anchored a spike from a cost shock is likely to fade.

flashcards.front: A rate rise can't lower the price of oil. Why might the RBA still raise rates after an oil price shock?
flashcards.back: Slower demand reduces capacity pressure and makes it harder for the cost rise to be built into later prices and wages, and it helps stop inflation expectations rising. The RBA says the response depends on expectations.

flashcards.front: What is stagflation, and why does it make the RBA's job hard?
flashcards.back: Stagnant output, high or rising unemployment and high inflation together, which a large or persistent supply shock can cause. Price stability and full employment then pull in opposite directions.

flashcards.front: Which word does the RBA use for a dollar value less the effects of inflation?
flashcards.back: A real value. A nominal value is the plain dollar amount, and a real value takes away what rising prices did to it.

acceptedIdeas: real value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A real value. A nominal value is the plain dollar amount, and a real value takes away what rising prices did to it.

flashcards.front: Why does a borrower on a fixed-rate loan gain if inflation turns out higher than expected?
flashcards.back: The repayments are fixed in dollars, so when prices rise faster than expected those dollars buy less. The borrower repays in dollars worth less, and the lender receives less purchasing power than planned.

flashcards.front: Which word does the RBA use for a situation in which prices are falling?
flashcards.back: Deflation. Expected falls in prices can lead consumers to delay purchases, which lowers spending.

acceptedIdeas: deflation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deflation. Expected falls in prices can lead consumers to delay purchases, which lowers spending.

flashcards.front: Give two reasons the RBA does not aim for zero inflation.
flashcards.back: A lower target is costly to achieve, since it would cut output growth and raise unemployment. Near zero there is little room to push real interest rates or real wages down in a downturn, and the CPI is biased upwards a little, so the target must allow for that.

flashcards.front: What are the two main forms of money in Australia, and which makes up the greater share?
flashcards.back: Currency, meaning banknotes and coins, and deposits at banks. Deposits make up the greater share.

flashcards.front: When a bank makes a loan, what two entries go on its balance sheet?
flashcards.back: A loan, which is an asset, and a deposit in the borrower's account, which is a liability. Both are for the same amount.

flashcards.front: What limits how much a bank can lend?
flashcards.back: The cash it needs to meet withdrawals, the capital it needs to absorb losses, a return that covers its costs, and a borrower who wants the loan.

flashcards.front: What does repaying a loan do to deposits, and why?
flashcards.back: It removes them. The borrower's deposit and the loan are cancelled together, so the amount of money falls.

flashcards.front: What is the cash rate, and what does the Board set?
flashcards.back: The cash rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Board sets a target for it.

flashcards.front: How does the policy interest rate corridor keep the cash rate near the target?
flashcards.back: The Reserve Bank pays banks 0.1 points below the target on their balances and lends to them at 0.25 above, so banks have no reason to trade outside that band.

flashcards.front: Which rates follow a change in the cash rate quickly, and which follow it slowly?
flashcards.back: Market reference rates follow quickly. Deposit rates respond less directly and take time, and each bank sets its own lending rate.

flashcards.front: Who sets the cash rate target, and who publishes the CPI?
flashcards.back: The Monetary Policy Board of the Reserve Bank sets the target. The ABS calculates and publishes the CPI.

flashcards.front: What are the two stages of the transmission of monetary policy?
flashcards.back: First, a change in policy moves interest rates across the economy. Second, those rates move activity and inflation.

flashcards.front: Name the RBA's four channels through which interest rates reach spending.
flashcards.back: Saving and investment, cash flow, asset prices and wealth, and the exchange rate.

flashcards.front: How long can it take for a change in monetary policy to have its maximum effect, and how sure is that?
flashcards.back: Some estimates say between one and two years, with a large degree of uncertainty because the economy changes over time.

flashcards.front: Why does a rate rise still lower spending through the cash-flow channel when savers receive more interest?
flashcards.back: The RBA says the borrowers' effect is larger than savers' effect, so the net effect is lower spending.

flashcards.front: What are the four phases of the business cycle, in order?
flashcards.back: Expansion, peak, contraction and trough.

flashcards.front: What is a technical recession, and what is one weakness of that test?
flashcards.back: Real GDP shrinking for two quarters running. Weak growth can hurt without being negative, volatile components can give a false signal, and the figures are revised.

flashcards.front: How does the RBA describe a recession more broadly?
flashcards.back: A prolonged stretch of weak or falling output together with a large rise in unemployment.

flashcards.front: Why can unemployment stay high after output recovers?
flashcards.back: Skills can fade with disuse, employers may think they have, and a recession can hasten structural change.

flashcards.front: What is the underlying cash balance?
flashcards.back: The Government's headline Budget result: receipts less payments, shown as a deficit or a surplus.

flashcards.front: How do gross debt and net debt differ?
flashcards.back: Gross debt is the face value of government securities on issue. Net debt counts the securities at market value and subtracts selected financial assets.

flashcards.front: What does the structural budget balance remove, and what is its limit?
flashcards.back: It removes the estimated temporary effects of commodity prices and the economic cycle. It is estimated and not observed, so it depends on assumptions.

flashcards.front: What kinds of sentence does a Budget paper contain?
flashcards.back: Definitions, forecasts, the Government's own judgements, and reports of what other bodies say. Each is checked in a different way.

flashcards.front: What do we call a budget rule that moves the deficit with the economy, with no new decision?
flashcards.back: An automatic stabiliser. Income tax collected falls with incomes and benefit payments rise with unemployment, which keeps demand up in a downturn.

acceptedIdeas: automatic stabiliser
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An automatic stabiliser. Income tax collected falls with incomes and benefit payments rise with unemployment, which keeps demand up in a downturn.

flashcards.front: A deficit widens in a recession and no law has changed. Why doesn't that show a policy failure?
flashcards.back: Tax revenue falls with incomes and payments rise with unemployment under rules already in place, so the deficit widens with no decision at all.

flashcards.front: In the RBA's wind farm example, why does $10 million of spending lead to $50 million of GDP?
flashcards.back: Each round of spending is income for someone else, who spends 8 of every 10 dollars. The rounds shrink but add up, and the multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5.

flashcards.front: Name three leakages and say what they do to the multiplier.
flashcards.back: Saving, taxes and imports. Each takes part of every round out of domestic spending, so the multiplier is smaller.

flashcards.front: When is a boost to government spending likely to show up in prices and not in output?
flashcards.back: When the economy is at capacity. There are no idle workers or machines, so the extra demand competes for resources already in use and crowds out private spending.

flashcards.front: What do we call a fall in the value of the Australian dollar?
flashcards.back: A depreciation. An appreciation is a rise in its value.

acceptedIdeas: depreciation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A depreciation. An appreciation is a rise in its value.

flashcards.front: AUD/USD moves from 0.80 to 0.78. Which currency has gained, and how do you know?
flashcards.back: The US dollar. One Australian dollar now buys 78 US cents instead of 80, so the Australian dollar has depreciated.

flashcards.front: Name the three drivers of the Australian dollar that the RBA describes, with the direction of each.
flashcards.back: Higher Australian interest rates lift it. Higher export prices raise the terms of trade and lift it. Over short periods it tracks risk sentiment and global share prices, rising and falling with them.

flashcards.front: Why can a depreciation lower the value of net exports at first?
flashcards.back: Import prices rise at once, while export and import volumes respond only with a lag, so the value of net exports tends to fall first and rise later.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't a current account deficit mean money is simply lost?
flashcards.back: The two accounts always sum to zero. Australia has tended to borrow from overseas to invest, so capital flowing in matches the deficit.

flashcards.front: What is output per unit of labour and capital combined called?
flashcards.back: Multifactor productivity, or MFP. Changes in it reflect changes in output that changes in inputs can't explain.

acceptedIdeas: multifactor productivity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multifactor productivity, or MFP. Changes in it reflect changes in output that changes in inputs can't explain.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between extensive growth and intensive growth?
flashcards.back: Extensive growth comes from using more inputs, such as more people or hours. Intensive growth comes from getting more output from the inputs already in use, and only that raises productivity.

flashcards.front: What two ways of raising productivity does the RBA describe?
flashcards.back: Efficiency, which is moving a business up to its frontier, and expanding capacity, which is moving the frontier outward through new technology and knowledge.

flashcards.front: Why can't adding machines alone keep output per worker growing, according to the Solow model?
flashcards.back: Capital has diminishing returns, so output per worker reaches a steady state. Only technological progress lifts it beyond that.

flashcards.front: Why can a growth gap of about a third of a point a year matter?
flashcards.back: Growth compounds. Wikipedia's example is the UK and the US from 1870 to 2008, where 1.47% against 1.80% a year reversed their ranking.

flashcards.front: What is the RBA's quarterly assessment of the economy, with its forecasts and risks, called?
flashcards.back: The Statement on Monetary Policy. It is published quarterly and sets out the assessment the Board considered in making its decision.

acceptedIdeas: Statement on Monetary Policy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Statement on Monetary Policy. It is published quarterly and sets out the assessment the Board considered in making its decision.

flashcards.front: Which parts of a decision statement should you keep apart when you read it?
flashcards.back: The decision, the evidence so far, the outlook with its risks, and what the Board says it will do next. The vote comes at the end.

flashcards.front: The forecast table shows a cash rate for the years ahead. How should you read it?
flashcards.back: As a technical assumption taken from market pricing at the date the forecasts were finalised. It is neither the Board's plan nor a promise.

flashcards.front: What does a split vote tell you about the next meeting?
flashcards.back: Very little. It shows disagreement about this decision. In the 2026 table, which is the course's own reading, neither the votes nor the closing wording lined up with the next decision.

flashcards.front: In two sentences, say what the Board did on 3 November 2026 and the main reason.
flashcards.back: The Board raised its cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, a rise of 25 basis points, by six votes to three. It judged that inflation is broadly based, that capacity pressures are a little tighter than thought and that the risk of higher inflation expectations becoming embedded has increased.
